name: pinneapple_systems

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library
pinneapple_systems.component_library.base
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.base — ``ComponentModel``: a
``BaseModel`` that additionally knows its physical constraint (a
``Physics``) and offers single-call ``.fit()``/``.evaluate()``
convenience, closing the two real gaps found against a plain
``BaseModel``/``PINNBase``:

1. No unified train-this-model-now entry point. ``.fit()`` here is
   deliberately thin — it builds a data+physics ``loss_fn`` and delegates
   to the existing ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer``, which already
   has a stronger set of loss balancers (ReLoBRaLo/SoftAdapt/PCGrad/
   AugmentedLagrangian) than a bespoke EMA balance would be. No training
   loop is duplicated here.
2. No metric computation on the model itself. ``.evaluate()`` is
   genuinely new: RMSE/MAPE/R² against held-out targets.

Composition, not reimplementation: a ``ComponentModel`` wraps an existing
registered ``pinneapple_neural.architectures`` backbone (built via
``ModelRegistry.build``) rather than defining new network layers — a
"pipe" or "pump" is a *physical role* attached to an architecture, not a
new architecture family.

Single-call training, delegating to the shared ``Trainer``.
Returns ``Trainer.fit``'s result dict (``best_val``, ``best_path``,

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc: RMSE / MAPE / R² against ``targets``.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library.benchmark
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.benchmark — train every
architecture registered under one ``component_type`` and rank by final
validation loss (real numbers from ``ComponentModel.fit()``, not a
display placeholder).

Kept as a thin loop over ``ComponentModel.fit()``/``.evaluate()`` rather
than routing through ``pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.Arena``: Arena
benchmarks *problem presets* end-to-end (it builds and trains its own
model from a ``ProblemSpec``), whereas a registered component here is
already a built, physics-attached ``ComponentModel`` — there is no
per-component ``ProblemSpec`` to hand Arena. No training loop is
duplicated at this layer either way, since ``.fit()`` itself delegates to
the shared ``Trainer``.

functions.name: benchmark_component_type
functions.sig: (component_type: str, train_loader, val_loader = None, *, epochs: int = 50, lr: float = 0.001, eval_coords: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None, eval_targets: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None, log_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> ComponentBenchmarkResult
functions.doc:
Trains every architecture registered for ``component_type`` on the
same data and ranks them by final validation loss (ascending — lower
is better). If ``eval_coords``/``eval_targets`` are given, also attaches
RMSE/MAPE/R² per architecture via ``ComponentModel.evaluate()``.

``log_dir`` defaults to a fresh temp directory (never
``TrainConfig``'s own default of ``"runs"``, a relative path that
would otherwise write into — and collide with — whatever the caller's
current working directory happens to be, e.g. a shared repo checkout).

children.summary: Train every architecture registered under one component_type and rank by final validation loss (real numbers from ComponentModel.fit(), not a display placeholder).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library.components
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.components — six reference plant
components. Deliberately six, not padded to ten: each pairs a genuinely
different (physics shortcut, backbone architecture, component_type)
combination rather than near-duplicating the others.

| component_type   | class                     | physics              | backbone       |
|-------------------|---------------------------|-----------------------|----------------|
| pipe              | PipeVanillaPINN           | incompressible_flow   | vanilla_pinn   |
| heat_exchanger     | HeatExchangerVanillaPINN  | heat_conduction       | vanilla_pinn   |
| tank_shell        | TankShellVanillaPINN      | linear_elasticity     | vanilla_pinn   |
| battery_cell      | BatteryCellVanillaPINN    | species_diffusion     | vanilla_pinn   |
| pump              | PumpModifiedMLP           | incompressible_flow   | modified_mlp   |
| valve             | ValveModifiedMLP          | none (data-driven)    | modified_mlp   |

Importing this module registers all six with ``ComponentRegistry`` (see
``pinneapple_systems.component_library.__init__``, which imports it for
its side effect).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library.physics
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.physics — ``Physics``: the thin
attachment layer between a named plant component and the constraint it
must satisfy.

Two ways to build one:

- :meth:`Physics.from_shortcut` wraps one of the generic, closed-form
  residuals already in ``pinneapple_systems.component_modeling
  .physics_residuals`` (incompressible flow, heat conduction, linear
  elasticity, species diffusion) into a ``Trainer``-compatible loss_fn.
  No new physics is implemented here — this only adapts the existing
  ``residual(model, coords, **params) -> Tensor`` contract to the
  ``loss_fn(model, y_hat, batch) -> {"total": Tensor, ...}`` contract
  ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer`` expects.
- :meth:`Physics.from_preset` wraps a registered PDE preset from
  ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment`` via the existing symbolic-PDE
  compiler (``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.compile
  .compile_problem``), for a component whose physics is one of PINNeAPPle's
  ~50 named presets rather than one of the four generic shortcuts.

classes.name: Physics
classes.doc:
A named physical constraint, reduced to a single ``Trainer``-shaped
loss_fn. ``params`` is kept alongside for introspection (e.g. shown on
a Toolbox/Component detail view) even though it is already baked into
``loss_fn`` via closure.

children.summary: Physics: the thin attachment layer between a named plant component and the constraint it must satisfy.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library.registry
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.registry — ``ComponentRegistry``:
a registry of NAMED PLANT COMPONENTS keyed by ``component_type`` (e.g.
"pipe", "pump", "valve") — several competing architectures may register
under the same ``component_type``, mirroring how
``pinneapple_neural.architectures.registry.ModelRegistry`` lets many
architectures register under one ``family``.

Deliberately layered ON TOP of ``ModelRegistry`` rather than replacing it:
every component class is (or wraps) a ``BaseModel``. What ``ModelRegistry``
has no concept of, and this module adds, is the ``(component_type,
Physics)`` attachment — a component is a named, physically-constrained
*thing you can point at a real pipe/pump/valve*, not just an architecture
family.

classes.doc: Central registry for named plant components.

methods.doc: Decorator: ``@ComponentRegistry.register(component_type="pipe", name="PipeVanillaPINN")``.

methods.name: build

Instantiate a registered component, stamping it with the
bookkeeping (``_component_name``/``_init_kwargs``) that
``ComponentModel.save_checkpoint``/``load_checkpoint`` needs to
reconstruct it later from a checkpoint alone — the same job
``pinneapple_hub.hub.from_pretrained`` already does for plain
``ModelRegistry`` architectures, done here at the component layer
instead.

functions.sig: (*, component_type: str, name: str, physics: Optional[Physics] = None, description: str = '', tags: Optional[List[str]] = None)
functions.doc:

as a bare decorator: ``@register_component(component_type=..., name=...)``.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_library.toolbox
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library.toolbox — ``Toolbox``: a named,
versioned, installable bundle of ``component_type``s (e.g. "Fluid
Mechanics Toolbox v1.0" bundling pipe+pump+valve).

Purely an in-repo bookkeeping/dependency-resolution layer, honestly
scoped: there is no external package index or download step here.
``install()``/``uninstall()`` only track an in-memory "installed" set
(mirroring what a real package manager's *resolve* phase would compute)
— they do not fetch or execute any code the component classes don't
already provide via ``ComponentRegistry``.

classes.name: ToolboxRegistry
classes.doc: Registry of :class:`Toolbox` bundles, plus a tiny installed-set.

children.summary: Toolbox: a named, versioned, installable bundle of component_types (e.g. "Fluid Mechanics Toolbox v1.0" bundling pipe+pump+valve).

children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_library — the piece
``pinneapple_systems.component_modeling``'s own docstring says pinneapple
deliberately did NOT build: a registry of NAMED PLANT COMPONENTS (keyed
by ``component_type``, e.g. "pipe"/"pump"/"valve"), each pairing an
existing ``pinneapple_neural.architectures`` backbone with a ``Physics``
constraint, plus versioned installable ``Toolbox`` bundles of component
types.

Everything else a component needs — control (PID/MPC), uncertainty
quantification (ensemble/SWAG/MC-Dropout), edge export, digital-twin
attachment, generic physics residuals — already exists in
``pinneapple_systems.component_modeling`` and
``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin``; this package composes those, it
does not re-implement them:

    from pinneapple_systems.component_library import ComponentRegistry
    from pinneapple_systems.component_modeling import run_mpc, DeepEnsemble
    from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin import DigitalTwin

    pipe = ComponentRegistry.build("PipeVanillaPINN")
    pipe.fit(train_loader, val_loader, epochs=200)
    twin = DigitalTwin(model=pipe, ...)   # DigitalTwin already accepts any nn.Module

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.bayesian
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.bayesian — SWAGApproximation: a
real, architecture-agnostic approximate Bayesian posterior over a model's
weights, via SWAG (Stochastic Weight Averaging Gaussian — Maddox et al.
2019, "A Simple Baseline for Bayesian Uncertainty in Deep Learning").

Why SWAG and not a "Bayesian last layer": a last-layer treatment needs to
identify each architecture's final linear layer + feature extractor, which
is fragile across heterogeneous backbones. SWAG treats the WHOLE parameter
vector uniformly — no architecture-specific hook needed, so it works for any
``nn.Module`` unmodified.

How it works: after reaching a normal point estimate (plain Adam training
against a supplied loss), it takes ``n_snapshots`` further short
optimization runs, recording the running mean and variance of every
parameter across those snapshots. That gives a diagonal Gaussian posterior
N(mean, diag(variance)) over the weights. Prediction resamples weights from
that posterior ``n_samples`` times and reports the resulting predictive
mean/std — real stochasticity from actual weight-space samples, not dropout
or ensemble disagreement (see ``ensemble.DeepEnsemble`` for that other,
structurally different UQ mechanism).

Self-contained: unlike the upstream implementation this was ported from,
this version does not assume the model exposes any particular ``.fit()``
convention — it runs its own minimal Adam training loop against a supplied
``loss_fn(model, coords) -> scalar tensor``.

classes.name: SWAGApproximation
classes.sig: (model: Any)

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (coords: torch.Tensor, targets: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None, *, loss_fn: Optional[Callable[[Any, torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]] = None, epochs: int = 100, lr: float = 0.001, n_snapshots: int = 10, snapshot_epochs: int = 20, snapshot_lr: Optional[float] = None) -> 'SWAGApproximation'

children.summary: SWAGApproximation: a real, architecture-agnostic approximate Bayesian posterior over a model's weights, via SWAG (Stochastic Weight Averaging Gaussian — Maddox et al.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.control
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.control — PID feedback control for
an arbitrary differentiable or black-box component.

Standard control-theory utility: ``PIDController`` implements the textbook
discrete-time law u = Kp*e + Ki*integral(e) + Kd*de/dt, and
``run_closed_loop()`` closes a loop around any single-input/single-output
callable "plant" (a bare Python function, a lambda wrapping one channel of a
trained model, a toy synthetic system, ...). Deliberately decoupled from any
specific model registry or component type — the plant only needs to be a
``float -> float`` callable.

State estimation is NOT reimplemented here: pinneapple already ships
Kalman-family estimators — see ``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.assimilation
.kalman`` (EKF/EnKF for live digital twins) and
``pinneapple_neural.architectures.classical_ts.kalman`` (time-series Kalman/
UKF/EnKF). Wrap one of those into a ``float -> float`` callable and pass it
as ``observer`` below instead of adding a third parallel implementation.

classes.name: PIDController
classes.sig: (kp: float, ki: float, kd: float, setpoint: float, output_limits: tuple[float, float] | None = None, bias: float = 0.0)
classes.doc:
Standard discrete-time PID: u = bias + Kp*e + Ki*integral(e) + Kd*de/dt,
e = setpoint - measurement.

``output_limits=(lo, hi)`` saturates the action like a real actuator and
turns on anti-windup by conditional integration (the integral is frozen
while the output is saturated in the direction the error pushes;
Astrom & Hagglund, "Advanced PID Control", 2006, sec. 3.5). ``bias`` is
the feed-forward / manual-reset term. Without them the controller is the
textbook unbounded law, as before.

functions.name: run_closed_loop
functions.sig: (plant: Callable[[float], float], *, setpoint: float, kp: float = 1.0, ki: float = 0.1, kd: float = 0.0, steps: int = 50, dt: float = 0.1, process_noise: float = 0.0, measurement_noise: float = 0.0, observer: Callable[[float], float] | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, list[float]]
functions.doc:
Closes a discrete-time control loop around ``plant``.

At each step the PID controller computes an action from the (optionally
filtered) measurement, ``plant(action)`` returns the new output, and the
loop repeats. ``plant`` has no notion of "components" or a registry — it
is any scalar callable.

``observer``, if given, must be a ``float -> float`` callable mapping a
raw (noisy) measurement to a filtered estimate — e.g.
``lambda y: kf.step(np.array([y]))["x"][0]`` wrapping an
``ExtendedKalmanFilter``. Without one, the controller acts on the raw
measurement directly.

children.summary: PID feedback control for an arbitrary differentiable or black-box component.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.edge
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.edge — package a trained model as a
self-contained edge-deployment bundle (ONNX graph + manifest.json zipped
together), and a minimal runtime that can execute that bundle with
onnxruntime + numpy alone (no torch/pinneapple import at all).

Builds on ``pinneapple_tools.model_export.export_onnx`` (the existing ONNX
tracing logic) rather than duplicating it — this module only adds the
packaging (manifest + zip) and the torch-free runtime around that export.

``EdgeRuntime`` is genuinely new: the same code path a real edge device
would run, runnable locally for testing/validation before actual
deployment.

classes.name: EdgeRuntime
classes.sig: (zip_path: str)
classes.doc:
Minimal edge-device inference runtime — onnxruntime + numpy only, no
torch/pinneapple import at all. Loads an ``export_edge_package()`` zip
and runs real ONNX inference.

functions.name: export_edge_package
functions.sig: (model: Any, output_dir: str, *, name: str, sample_input: torch.Tensor, opset_version: int = 17, extra_manifest: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Exports `model` to ONNX and zips it with a manifest.json into a
self-contained edge deployment package. Returns
{"manifest": {...}, "onnx_path": ..., "zip_path": ...}.

`model` is used exactly as given (whatever weights it currently holds —
the caller decides whether that's freshly initialized or trained).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.ensemble
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.ensemble — DeepEnsemble: N
independently-initialized copies of the same architecture, trained
separately, combined at inference time.

Ensemble disagreement (across-member std) is genuine epistemic uncertainty —
a different mechanism from MC-Dropout's within-model stochastic-forward-pass
uncertainty (see ``mc_dropout.mc_dropout_uncertainty``) and from
``bayesian.SWAGApproximation``'s weight-space Bayesian posterior. Per Wilson
& Izmailov (2020, "Bayesian Deep Learning and a Probabilistic Perspective of
Generalization"), a deep ensemble is a practical approximation to Bayesian
model averaging.

Decoupled from any specific registry: members are built from a supplied
``model_factory() -> nn.Module`` callable.

classes.name: DeepEnsemble
classes.sig: (model_factory: Callable[[], Any], n_members: int = 5, base_seed: int = 0)

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (coords: torch.Tensor, targets: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None, *, loss_fn: Optional[Callable[[Any, torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]] = None, epochs: int = 100, lr: float = 0.001) -> List[List[float]]
methods.doc:
Trains every member independently (each already has different
initial weights from __init__) on the same data — the only source
of ensemble diversity here is initialization + optimization path,
not bagging/bootstrapping (a legitimate, simpler deep-ensemble
variant per Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017).

methods.name: predict
methods.doc:
Returns (mean, std) across members — std is epistemic uncertainty
from model disagreement, not from any single model's own noise.

children.summary: DeepEnsemble: N independently-initialized copies of the same architecture, trained separately, combined at inference time.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.mc_dropout
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.mc_dropout — MC-Dropout epistemic
uncertainty: n_samples stochastic forward passes with dropout kept active,
reduced to a (mean, std) estimate.

This is the one small capability missing from pinneapple's existing model
base classes (``pinneapple_neural.architectures.base.BaseModel`` /
``pinns.base.PINNBase`` cover checkpointing, ONNX/TorchScript export, and a
physics-loss adapter already; ``pinneapple_neural/trainer/heteroscedastic.py``
covers a *different* UQ mechanism — aleatoric noise via a learned variance
head). Implemented here as a standalone function rather than a new base
class so it works on ANY ``nn.Module`` that has at least one ``nn.Dropout``
submodule, with no inheritance requirement.

functions.name: mc_dropout_uncertainty
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module, x: torch.Tensor, n_samples: int = 50) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]
functions.doc:
Returns (mean, std) over `n_samples` stochastic forward passes with
dropout active. Raises ValueError if `model` has no `nn.Dropout`
submodule (nothing would actually be stochastic).

children.summary: MC-Dropout epistemic uncertainty: n_samples stochastic forward passes with dropout kept active, reduced to a (mean, std) estimate.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.mpc
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.mpc — Model Predictive Control
(receding horizon) around an arbitrary differentiable component.

Real MPC in the textbook sense: at each outer step it optimizes a whole
future control sequence against the plant model over a horizon, applies only
the first action, then re-optimizes at the next step (receding horizon). The
plant itself IS the prediction model — the control sequence is optimized by
gradient descent straight through it (no finite differences, no
linearization), so `plant` must be a differentiable ``nn.Module`` (any
architecture; this module has no notion of a specific component or
registry).

Contrast with ``control.PIDController``: PID is reactive (responds to
current error only); MPC here is predictive (plans ``horizon`` steps ahead,
trading off tracking error against control effort via ``action_weight``).

functions.name: run_mpc
functions.sig: (plant: nn.Module, *, in_dim: int, setpoint: float, control_input_index: int = 0, observed_output_index: int = 0, horizon: int = 10, steps: int = 30, opt_iters: int = 30, lr: float = 0.1, action_weight: float = 0.01, action_bounds: Tuple[float, float] = (-2.0, 2.0), fixed_inputs: Optional[Dict[int, float]] = None, seed: int = 0) -> Dict[str, List[float]]
functions.doc:
Receding-horizon MPC: at each of ``steps`` outer steps, optimize a
length-``horizon`` control sequence (Adam, ``opt_iters`` iterations,
gradients flowing through ``plant`` itself) minimizing::

    sum_k (y_k - setpoint)^2 + action_weight * u_k^2

then apply only the first action. Returns the closed-loop trajectory
``{"time", "setpoint", "action", "output", "planned_cost"}``.

``plant`` is used exactly as given — no pretraining, no assumptions
about its weights. The caller is responsible for supplying a plant whose
``control_input_index -> observed_output_index`` map is meaningful
(trained, hand-built, or otherwise).

children.summary: Model Predictive Control (receding horizon) around an arbitrary differentiable component.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.physics_residuals
children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.physics_residuals — generic,
closed-form PDE residuals for a handful of standard physical constraints,
computed via autograd against any differentiable model's coordinate ->
field(s) map.

Each function has the signature ``residual(model, coords, **params) ->
Tensor`` and returns a residual tensor that should be driven to zero (e.g.
via ``(residual(...) ** 2).mean()`` as a training loss term). They make no
assumption about what `model` represents beyond the shape of its output
columns — no dependency on any particular component, registry, or problem
catalog.

To use with ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.pinns.base.PINNBase``'s
``physics_loss(physics_fn=..., physics_data=...)`` contract, wrap one of
these as::

    def physics_fn(model, data):
        r = heat_conduction_residual(model, data["coords"], k=50.0, Q=0.0)
        return (r ** 2).mean()

    loss_dict = pinn_model.physics_loss(physics_fn=physics_fn,
                                         physics_data={"coords": coords})

A missing/unsatisfiable residual raises a loud ``NotImplementedError`` —
never a silent zero (a silent zero would make the physics loss term
vanish and defeat its purpose).

functions.name: incompressible_continuity_residual
functions.sig: (model: Any, coords: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Mass-conservation (div(u) = 0) residual for a velocity-field output.
Assumes the model's first `dim` output columns are velocity components
aligned with the first `dim` coordinate axes (u, v, [w]).

functions.name: heat_conduction_residual
functions.sig: (model: Any, coords: torch.Tensor, *, k: float = 50.0, Q: float = 0.0) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Steady-state heat diffusion residual: k*laplacian(T) + Q, T = model's
first output column, laplacian summed over every axis of `coords`
(works for any spatial dimension).

functions.name: linear_elasticity_residual
functions.sig: (model: Any, coords: torch.Tensor, *, E: float = 210000000000.0, nu: float = 0.3) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Navier-Lame equilibrium (isotropic linear elasticity, no body force):
(lambda+mu)*grad(div(u)) + mu*laplacian(u) = 0. Assumes the model's first
`dim` output columns are displacement components [u, v, (w)]. Works in
2D or 3D.

functions.name: species_diffusion_residual
functions.sig: (model: Any, coords: torch.Tensor, *, D: float = 1e-05, k: float = 0.0) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Simplified steady-state diffusion-reaction (Fick's second law at
steady state, first-order decay): D*laplacian(C) - k*C = 0. Assumes the
model's first output column is concentration. A generic Fickian
diffusion-reaction constraint — not tied to any specific transport
system.

children.summary: Generic, closed-form PDE residuals for a handful of standard physical constraints, computed via autograd against any differentiable model's coordinate -> field(s) map.

children.doc:
pinneapple_systems.component_modeling — control, optimization, and
uncertainty-quantification tooling that operates on ANY differentiable
component model, independent of what that component represents physically.

This package deliberately does NOT include a component registry, a base
"component model" class, or a mesh/collocation generator — pinneapple
already has more capable, more mature native equivalents for all three:

- Named, buildable model architectures & introspection:
  ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.registry.ModelRegistry``
- A trainable-model contract (checkpointing, ONNX/TorchScript export, a
  physics-loss adapter): ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.base.BaseModel``
  / ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.pinns.base.PINNBase``
- Collocation-point / mesh generation: ``pinneapple_data.collocation``,
  ``pinneapple_design.geometry``
- Multi-architecture comparison: ``pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.Arena``

What IS here is the machinery that was genuinely missing:

- ``control``    — PIDController + a generic closed-loop runner
- ``mpc``        — gradient-based receding-horizon Model Predictive Control
- ``bayesian``   — SWAG: an approximate weight-space Bayesian posterior
- ``ensemble``   — DeepEnsemble epistemic uncertainty
- ``mc_dropout`` — MC-Dropout epistemic uncertainty
- ``physics_residuals`` — generic autograd PDE residuals (incompressible
  flow, heat conduction, linear elasticity, species diffusion)
- ``edge``       — ONNX edge-deployment packaging + a torch-free runtime

Every function/class here works on a plain ``nn.Module`` (or a bare
Python callable, for ``control.run_closed_loop``) supplied by the caller —
none of it references any specific physical component.
children.summary: Control, optimization, and uncertainty-quantification tooling that operates on ANY differentiable component model, independent of what that component represents physically.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.control
pinneapple_systems.control.analysis
children.doc:
Linear analysis of any dynamic model ``dx/dt = f(x, u, d, t)``: trim, linearisation, stability, controllability,
loop margins and step-response metrics.

The model is a plain Python callable. Nothing here knows about a particular plant::

    from pinneapple_systems.control import analysis as A

    f = lambda x, u, d, t: np.array([x[1], -2.0 * x[0] - 0.4 * x[1] + u[0]])
    lin = A.linearize(f, x=[0.0, 0.0], u=[0.0])
    A.stability(lin["A"])["classification"]          # 'stable (oscillatory)'

Finite differences are central, with a step scaled to each variable. :func:`linearize` reports the difference
between two step sizes as an error estimate, so a Jacobian that depends on the step is visible.

Margins (:func:`loop_margins`) are measured on the open loop ``L(jw)``, given as a transfer function or as any
callable ``w -> L(jw)``. The crossings are found on a logarithmic grid and refined by root finding:

* gain margin at the phase crossover;
* phase margin at the gain crossover;
* delay margin = phase margin / gain-crossover frequency;
* peak sensitivity ``Ms = max |1 / (1 + L)|``.

References: Astrom & Murray, *Feedback Systems* (2nd ed., 2021), ch. 5-6 and 10; Skogestad & Postlethwaite,
*Multivariable Feedback Control* (2005), ch. 2.

functions.name: equilibrium
functions.sig: (f: Model, x0: Sequence[float], u0: Sequence[float] | None = None, d0: Sequence[float] | None = None, t: float = 0.0, free: Sequence[int] | None = None, tol: float = 1e-10) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Trim point of ``dx/dt = f(x, u, d, t)``: the state where the derivatives vanish, by root finding.

Parameters
----------
f : callable
    ``f(x, u, d, t) -> dx/dt``.
x0 : array_like
    Initial guess of the state; the components not listed in ``free`` stay fixed.
u0, d0 : array_like, optional
    Input and disturbance held during the search.
t : float [s]
    Time passed to ``f``.
free : sequence of int, optional
    Indices of the state adjusted by the search (default: all). The remaining derivatives must vanish with the
    rest fixed, which ``residual_norm`` reports.

Returns
-------
x : ndarray
    Trim state (units of the caller's state).
residual : ndarray
    ``f`` at the trim state (state units per second).
residual_norm : float
    Euclidean norm of the residual (state units per second).
converged : bool
    Root finder converged and ``residual_norm <= tol``.
message : str
    Root finder message.

functions.name: linearize
functions.sig: (f: Model, x: Sequence[float], u: Sequence[float] | None = None, d: Sequence[float] | None = None, t: float = 0.0, rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Jacobians of ``f`` at ``(x, u, d)``: ``dx/dt ~ A dx + B du + E dd`` by central differences.

Parameters
----------
f : callable
    ``f(x, u, d, t) -> dx/dt``.
x, u, d : array_like
    Operating point (the caller's units).
t : float [s]
    Time passed to ``f``.
rel_step : float [-]
    Finite-difference step relative to ``max(1, |value|)``.

Returns
-------
A : ndarray
    State Jacobian (1/s).
B : ndarray
    Input Jacobian (state units per input unit per second).
E : ndarray
    Disturbance Jacobian (state units per disturbance unit per second).
f0 : ndarray
    ``f`` at the point (state units per second); not zero away from equilibrium.
jacobian_error : float [-]
    Largest relative change of A, B and E when the step is multiplied by 10: a Jacobian that depends on the
    step (non-smooth model, too small a step) shows here.

functions.name: stability
functions.sig: (A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], dt: float | None = None, tol: float = 1e-09) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Eigen-analysis of a linear(ised) system.

Parameters
----------
A : ndarray
    Continuous-time state matrix (1/s), or a discrete-time transition matrix when ``dt`` is given.
dt : float [s], optional
    Sample time of a discrete-time ``A``. Its eigenvalues ``z`` are mapped to ``s = log(z) / dt``.
tol : float [1/s]
    Real parts within ``tol`` of zero count as marginal.

Returns
-------
eigenvalues : ndarray
    Eigenvalues of ``A`` as given (1/s for continuous time, dimensionless for discrete time).
s : ndarray
    Continuous-time equivalents (1/s).
classification : str
    One of 'stable', 'stable (oscillatory)', 'marginal', 'unstable', 'unstable (oscillatory)'.
max_real : float [1/s]
    Largest real part of ``s``.
modes : list of dict
    Per eigenvalue:
    ``s`` (1/s), ``growth_rate`` [1/s], ``time_constant`` [s], ``doubling_time`` [s] (unstable modes),
    ``half_life`` [s] (stable modes), ``frequency`` [rad/s], ``damping_ratio`` [-] and the eigenvector.
unstable_directions : list of ndarray
    Real parts of the eigenvectors of the unstable modes (state units).

functions.name: controllability
functions.sig: (A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], B: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> dict[str, Any]

Kalman controllability matrix ``[B, AB, ..., A^(n-1) B]``.

Returns

rank : int
    Rank of the controllability matrix (full rank = ``n``: every state can be steered).
n : int
    Number of states.
controllable : bool
    ``rank == n``.
condition_number : float [-]
    Ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value: large means some directions need large inputs.

functions.name: observability
functions.sig: (A: Sequence[Sequence[float]], C: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> dict[str, Any]

Returns
-------

    Rank of the observability matrix.
n : int
    Number of states.

    ``rank == n``: every state can be reconstructed from the outputs.
condition_number : float [-]
    Ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value.

functions.name: transfer_function
functions.sig: (A, B, C, D = None, input_index: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Transfer function ``Y(s)/U(s)`` of one input of a state-space model (``scipy.signal.ss2tf``).

Returns
-------
num : ndarray
    Numerator coefficients, highest power first, one row per output.
den : ndarray
    Denominator coefficients, highest power first.
poles : ndarray
    Roots of ``den`` (1/s).
zeros : list of ndarray
    Roots of each output's numerator (1/s).

functions.name: loop_margins
functions.sig: (L, delay: float = 0.0, w_min: float = 0.0001, w_max: float = 10000.0, n: int = 4000) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Classical margins of an open loop ``L(jw)`` under unit negative feedback.

Parameters
----------
L : tuple (num, den) or callable
    Open loop as polynomial coefficients in ``s`` (highest power first), or a callable ``w -> L(jw)``.
delay : float [s]
    Pure transport delay added to the loop (``exp(-j w delay)``).
w_min, w_max : float [rad/s]
    Frequency range searched.
n : int
    Grid points before refinement.

Returns
-------
gain_margin : float [-]
    ``1 / |L|`` at the phase crossover (-180 deg); ``inf`` when the phase never crosses it.
gain_margin_db : float [dB]
    The gain margin in decibels.
phase_crossover : float [rad/s]
    Frequency of the -180 deg crossing (nan when none).
phase_margin : float [deg]
    ``180 + angle(L)`` at the gain crossover (``|L| = 1``); nan when ``|L|`` never crosses 1.
gain_crossover : float [rad/s]
    Frequency where ``|L| = 1`` (nan when none).
delay_margin : float [s]
    Extra delay that removes the phase margin: ``phase_margin [rad] / gain_crossover``.
ms : float [-]
    Peak sensitivity ``max |1/(1+L)|`` on the grid (robustness: Ms < 2 is the usual target).
ms_frequency : float [rad/s]
    Frequency of the sensitivity peak.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.control.cartpole
children.doc:
Inverted pendulum on a cart: energy swing-up from hanging, LQR catch at upright, disturbance rejection.

The cart's acceleration is the input, as when a servo drive tracks an acceleration command. The pendulum is a point
mass at distance ``length`` (l) from the pivot, and the angle is measured from upright:

    p'' = u,          theta'' = (g sin(theta) - u cos(theta)) / l + d

``d`` is an angular-acceleration disturbance (a push).

Pipeline, all on :mod:`pinneapple_systems.control`:

1. :func:`~.analysis.linearize` at upright gives ``A, B``. :func:`~.analysis.stability` finds the real pole at
   ``+sqrt(g/l)`` and its doubling time.
2. :func:`~.tuning.lqr` with ``Q, R`` gives the balance gains and the closed-loop poles.
3. An energy-based swing-up (Astrom & Furuta, *Automatica* 36, 2000) pumps the pendulum's energy towards that of
   upright rest, with ``u = k_E E sign(theta' cos theta)`` limited to ``a_swing``. Near upright, the LQR takes over.
4. A push of ``push`` rad/s^2 lasting ``push_duration`` at ``t_push`` tests the disturbance rejection.

Without control, the open loop is simulated from a small tilt, to show how fast it falls.

classes.name: CartPoleParams
classes.doc:
Parameters of the cart-pole study.

Attributes
----------
g : float [m/s^2]
    Gravity.
length : float [m]
    Pivot to the pendulum's centre of mass.
a_balance : float [m/s^2]
    Cart acceleration limit while balancing.
a_swing : float [m/s^2]
    Cart acceleration limit while pumping energy (gentler, so the swing-up takes several swings).
k_energy : float [1/(m s^2) scaled]
    Gain of the energy pumping law (cart acceleration per unit of energy error, per kg and per m of l).
q_position, q_velocity, q_angle, q_rate : float
    LQR state weights (cart position, cart velocity, angle, angular rate).
r_input : float
    LQR input weight.
catch_angle : float [rad]
    The LQR takes over below this angle from upright.
catch_rate : float [rad/s]
    And below this angular rate.

    from pinneapple_systems.control.cartpole_video import cartpole_animation

Needs matplotlib and ffmpeg (on the PATH, or through ``imageio-ffmpeg``).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.control.loop
children.doc:
Closed loops on any plant: actuators, controllers, a fixed-step simulator, and the linearised closed loop.

The plant is ``dx/dt = rhs(x, u, d, t)`` with a measured output ``y = output(x)`` (:class:`Plant`). Between the
controller and the plant sits an :class:`Actuator`:

* range limits;
* a rate limit;
* a first-order lag;
* a dead band;
* a transport delay;
* optionally *integrating*, where the command is the rate of the applied value. A pump flow is integrating with
  respect to the mass in a tank.

What the controller commands is part of the design. The same PID that holds a plant when it commands a position
(e.g. a target tank mass, with the pump as a rate-limited servo) can destabilise it when it commands the rate (the
pump flow): the integrating actuator adds a pole at the origin. :func:`loop_eigenvalues` shows this before any long
simulation. It linearises the complete discrete-time loop around an equilibrium, so the plant, the actuator
dynamics, the controller states and the integration scheme are all included. :func:`compare_architectures` runs
several (controller, actuator) choices on the same plant, disturbance and integrator, and tabulates both views.

Controllers expose ``act(t, x, y, r, ydot, dt) -> command`` and their internal state as a vector
(``get_state`` / ``set_state``), which is what the closed-loop linearisation perturbs:

* :class:`PID` extends :class:`~pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.control.PIDController` with derivative on the
  measurement (or a measured rate), a derivative filter, setpoint weighting, back-calculation anti-windup and
  feed-forward;
* :class:`Cascade`: an outer controller sets the reference of an inner one;
* :class:`StateFeedback`: ``u = u_ref - K (x - x_ref)``, e.g. with gains from :func:`.tuning.lqr`.

Simulation only: nothing here has a path to real equipment.

classes.name: Plant
classes.doc:
A dynamic model for closed-loop work.

``rhs(x, u, d, t) -> dx/dt`` with ``u`` the applied actuator value (scalar) and ``d`` the disturbance (scalar or
vector). ``output`` is a state index or a callable ``x -> y``. ``rate`` is optional: a callable ``x -> dy/dt``
(a velocity or rate sensor) that a PID can use for its derivative term instead of differencing ``y``.
fields: rhs: Callable[[np.ndarray, float, Any, float], np.ndarray]

classes.name: Actuator
classes.doc:
Between the command and the plant: ``applied = actuator(command)``.

Parameters
----------
lo, hi : float
    Range of the applied value (units of the plant input).
rate : float
    Largest ``|d applied / dt|`` (plant input units per second). For an integrating actuator this limits the
    commanded rate itself.
tau : float [s]
    First-order lag of the actuator (0: none).
deadband : float
    Commands within ``+-deadband`` of the previous target (servo) or of zero (integrating) are ignored
    (command units).
delay : float [s]
    Transport delay of the command, rounded to whole steps of the simulation.
integrating : bool
    The command is the rate of the applied value (e.g. a pump flow driving a tank mass).
initial : float
    Applied value at the start (plant input units).

methods.sig: (dt: float, applied: float | None = None, command: float | None = None) -> None

methods.name: equilibrium_command
methods.doc: The command that holds ``applied`` still: the value itself for a servo, zero for an integrating one.

methods.doc: Advance one step and return the applied value.

classes.name: PID
classes.sig: (kp: float, ki: float = 0.0, kd: float = 0.0, setpoint: float = 0.0, output_limits: tuple[float, float] | None = None, bias: float = 0.0, *, derivative: str = 'measurement', filter_tau: float = 0.0, anti_windup: str = 'conditional', tracking_time: float | None = None, setpoint_weight: float = 1.0, feedforward: Callable[[float], float] | None = None)
classes.doc:
PID for real loops: ``u = bias + ff(t) + Kp (b r - y) + Ki int(e) + Kd D``, with ``e = r - y``.

Parameters
----------
kp, ki, kd : float
    Gains (command units per output unit; per output unit-second; per output unit per second).
setpoint : float
    Default reference (output units); ``act`` takes the reference of each step.
output_limits : tuple, optional
    ``(lo, hi)`` saturation of the command, with anti-windup.
bias : float
    Manual reset / feed-forward constant (command units).
derivative : {'measurement', 'error'}
    Differentiate the measurement (no derivative kick on setpoint steps) or the error. When the loop provides
    a measured rate (``ydot``), ``'measurement'`` uses it directly.
filter_tau : float [s]
    First-order filter on the derivative term (0: none).
anti_windup : {'conditional', 'back_calculation', 'none'}
    Conditional integration (the base class), back-calculation with tracking time ``tracking_time``, or none.
tracking_time : float [s], optional
    Back-calculation time constant (default ``sqrt(Ti Td)`` or ``Ti``).
setpoint_weight : float [-]
    ``b`` in the proportional term (1: plain PID; 0: I-PD, no proportional kick).
feedforward : callable, optional
    ``t -> command`` added to the output.

classes.name: Cascade
classes.sig: (outer, inner, inner_measurement: Callable[[np.ndarray], float], inner_rate: Callable[[np.ndarray], float] | None = None)
classes.doc:
Outer loop sets the reference of the inner loop.

``outer`` acts on the plant output ``y`` against the reference; its command becomes the reference of ``inner``,
which acts on ``inner_measurement(x)`` (e.g. a flow, a velocity, a valve position).
``inner_rate(x)`` optionally provides the inner rate for its derivative term.

classes.name: StateFeedback
classes.sig: (K, x_ref, u_ref: float = 0.0, ki: float = 0.0, output_limits: tuple[float, float] | None = None)
classes.doc:
``u = u_ref - K (x - x_ref)``, optionally with integral action on the output error (``ki``).

Parameters
----------
K : array_like
    Gain row (command units per state unit).
x_ref : array_like
    State the feedback regulates to (state units).
u_ref : float
    Command at ``x_ref`` (command units).
ki : float
    Integral gain on ``r - y`` (command units per output unit-second).
output_limits : tuple, optional
    Saturation of the command; the integral is frozen while saturated.

methods.name: set_equilibrium
methods.doc:
With integral action, the integral takes up the difference between ``command`` and the feedback at
``x``; without it nothing changes (``u_ref`` and ``x_ref`` define the target).

functions.name: simulate_loop
functions.sig: (plant: Plant, controller, actuator: Actuator, reference: float | Callable[[float], float], t_end: float, dt: float, disturbance: Any = 0.0, method: str = 'rk4', stop: Callable[[np.ndarray, float], str | None] | None = None, noise_std: float = 0.0, sensor_tau: float = 0.0, seed: int = 0, x0: Sequence[float] | None = None, start_at_equilibrium: bool = True, u0: float | None = None) -> dict[str, ...
functions.doc:
Simulate a closed loop with a fixed step.

At every step: measure ``y`` (with noise and an optional first-order sensor lag), let the controller compute
the command from ``y``, the reference and (when the plant has one) the measured rate, pass the command through
the actuator, and integrate the plant over ``dt`` with the applied value held.

Parameters
----------
plant : Plant
    The model.
controller : object
    ``act(t, x, y, r, ydot, dt) -> command`` (e.g. :class:`PID`, :class:`Cascade`, :class:`StateFeedback`).
actuator : Actuator
    Between the command and the plant.
reference : float or callable
    Reference of the output, constant or ``t -> r`` (output units).
t_end, dt : float [s]
    Duration and step.
disturbance : float, array or callable
    ``d`` passed to the plant, constant or ``t -> d``.
method : {'rk4', 'euler', 'sequential_euler'}
    Integrator.
stop : callable, optional
    ``(x, t) -> reason or None``: ends the run when it returns a reason (e.g. a depth limit).
noise_std : float
    Standard deviation of Gaussian measurement noise (output units).
sensor_tau : float [s]
    First-order lag of the sensor (0: none).
x0 : array_like, optional
    Initial state (default ``plant.x0``).
start_at_equilibrium : bool
    Initialise the controller bumplessly so it outputs the command that holds the actuator at ``u0``.
u0 : float, optional
    Initial applied value (default ``actuator.initial``).

Returns
-------
t : ndarray [s]
    Times of the recorded samples (``t[0] = 0``).
x : ndarray
    States (state units), one row per sample.
y : ndarray
    True outputs (output units).
applied : ndarray
    Applied actuator values (plant input units).
command : ndarray
    Controller commands (command units); ``command[k]`` acted between ``t[k]`` and ``t[k+1]``.
reference : ndarray
    References (output units).
stopped : str or None
    Reason the run ended early.
y_min, y_max : float
    Extremes of the output over the run (output units).
iae : float
    Integral of ``|r - y|`` (output units times seconds).

functions.name: loop_eigenvalues
functions.sig: (plant: Plant, controller, actuator: Actuator, x_eq: Sequence[float], u_eq: float, reference: float, dt: float, disturbance: Any = 0.0, method: str = 'rk4', t: float = 0.0, rel_step: float = 1e-06) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Stability of the complete discrete-time closed loop around an equilibrium.

The loop's state is the plant state, the actuator state and the controller state. The one-step map of
:func:`simulate_loop` is differentiated numerically at the equilibrium, so the eigenvalues include the
actuator (integrating or not, its lag and delay), the controller's integral and derivative states and the
integration scheme. Limits must be inactive at the equilibrium; rate limits are, since nothing moves there.

Parameters
----------
x_eq : array_like
    Plant equilibrium with the actuator at ``u_eq`` and the given disturbance (state units).
u_eq : float
    Applied actuator value at equilibrium (plant input units).
reference : float
    Reference at equilibrium (output units).
dt : float [s]
    Step of the loop.

Returns
-------
stable : bool
    All eigenvalues of the one-step map inside the unit circle.
spectral_radius : float [-]
    Largest eigenvalue modulus of the one-step map.
classification : str
    From :func:`.analysis.stability` on the continuous-time equivalents.
s : ndarray [1/s]
    Continuous-time equivalents ``log(z)/dt`` of the eigenvalues.
max_real : float [1/s]
    Largest real part of ``s``: positive means the loop diverges, at that e-folding rate.
doubling_time : float [s]
    ``ln 2 / max_real`` for an unstable loop (``nan`` when stable).
fixed_point_residual : float [-]
    Relative change of the loop state over one step at the equilibrium (should be ~0).
ignored_states : int
    Controller or actuator states that influence no other state (their eigenvalue is left out).

functions.name: compare_architectures
functions.sig: (plant: Plant, architectures: Mapping[str, tuple[Any, Actuator]], reference: float, t_end: float, dt: float, disturbance: Any = 0.0, method: str = 'rk4', stop: Callable[[np.ndarray, float], str | None] | None = None, x_eq: Sequence[float] | None = None, u_eq: float | None = None, d_eq: Any = 0.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run several (controller, actuator) choices on the same plant, disturbance and integrator.

Each architecture is simulated with :func:`simulate_loop` and, when ``x_eq`` and ``u_eq`` are given, analysed
with :func:`loop_eigenvalues` at the undisturbed equilibrium (``d_eq``).

Returns
-------
rows : list of dict
    Per architecture:
    ``name``, ``stable_linear`` (bool or None), ``spectral_radius`` [-], ``max_real`` [1/s],
    ``doubling_time`` [s], ``y_min`` and ``y_max`` (output units), ``final_y`` (output units),
    ``iae`` (output units times seconds), ``stopped`` (str or None) and ``t_end`` [s] reached.
runs : dict
    The full :func:`simulate_loop` result per architecture.

children.summary: Closed loops on any plant: actuators, controllers, a fixed-step simulator, and the linearised closed loop.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.control.tuning
children.doc:
Controller tuning and robustness: FOPDT identification, SIMC / IMC / Ziegler-Nichols rules, PID pole placement
for second-order plants (stable or not), LQR, tuning by closed-loop optimisation, and Monte Carlo robustness.

Rules and their sources:

* **SIMC** (Skogestad 2003, *J. Process Control* 13, 291-309):
  ``Kc = tau / (K (tau_c + theta))``, ``Ti = min(tau, 4 (tau_c + theta))``, default ``tau_c = theta``.
* **IMC-PI / IMC-PID** for FOPDT (Rivera, Morari & Skogestad 1986): PI ``Kc = tau / (K (lambda + theta))``,
  ``Ti = tau``; PID ``Kc = (tau + theta/2) / (K (lambda + theta/2))``, ``Ti = tau + theta/2``,
  ``Td = tau theta / (2 tau + theta)``.
* **Ziegler-Nichols** (1942): the ultimate-gain table (``Kc = 0.6 Ku``, ``Ti = Tu/2``, ``Td = Tu/8`` for PID) and
  the reaction-curve table (``Kc = 1.2 tau / (K theta)``, ``Ti = 2 theta``, ``Td = theta/2``).
* **Pole placement** for ``m y'' + c y' + k y = b u``: a PID with derivative on a measured rate gives the closed
  loop ``m s^3 + (c + b Kd) s^2 + (k + b Kp) s + b Ki``. Matching ``(s^2 + 2 zeta wn s + wn^2)(s + p)`` fixes the
  three gains. This holds for ``k < 0`` (a statically unstable plant, such as a submarine in depth) as well.
* **LQR**: ``scipy.linalg.solve_continuous_are`` / ``solve_discrete_are``.

functions.name: fit_fopdt
functions.sig: (t: Sequence[float], y: Sequence[float], du: float, y0: float | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Fit ``K exp(-theta s) / (tau s + 1)`` to an open-loop step response by least squares.

Returns

rmse : float
    Root-mean-square fit error (output units).

functions.name: simc_pid
functions.sig: (K: float, tau: float, theta: float, tau_c: float | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
SIMC PI rule for a FOPDT plant (Skogestad 2003).

Parameters
----------
K : float
    Plant gain (output units per input unit).
tau, theta : float [s]
    Time constant and dead time.
tau_c : float [s], optional
    Desired closed-loop time constant (default ``theta``, the "tight" setting).

Returns

ti : float [s]

functions.name: imc_pid
functions.sig: (K: float, tau: float, theta: float, lam: float | None = None, kind: str = 'pid') -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
IMC rule for a FOPDT plant (Rivera, Morari & Skogestad 1986).

Parameters

    Plant gain (output units per input unit).
tau, theta : float [s]
    Time constant and dead time.
lam : float [s], optional
    Closed-loop filter time constant (default ``max(0.25 tau, 0.8 theta)``).

    Controller form.

Returns

    Parallel-form gains.

functions.name: ultimate_gain
functions.sig: (L_unit, delay: float = 0.0, **kw) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Ultimate gain and period from the open loop at unit controller gain: ``Ku = gain margin``,
``Tu = 2 pi / w180``.

Returns
-------
ku : float
    Ultimate gain (input units per output unit).
tu : float [s]
    Ultimate period.

functions.name: ziegler_nichols
functions.sig: (kind: str = 'pid', ku: float | None = None, tu: float | None = None, K: float | None = None, tau: float | None = None, theta: float | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Ziegler-Nichols tuning from the ultimate gain (``ku``, ``tu``) or the reaction curve (``K``, ``tau``,
``theta``).

Returns
-------
kc : float
    Proportional gain (input units per output unit).
ti : float [s]
    Integral time (``inf`` for P).
td : float [s]
    Derivative time.
kp, ki, kd : float
    Parallel-form gains.

functions.name: place_pid_second_order
functions.sig: (m: float, c: float, k: float, b: float, wn: float, zeta: float = 0.7, p: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
PID gains that place the closed-loop poles of ``m y'' + c y' + k y = b u``.

With derivative on a measured rate, the closed loop is ``m s^3 + (c + b Kd) s^2 + (k + b Kp) s + b Ki``.
It is matched to ``m (s^2 + 2 zeta wn s + wn^2)(s + p)``. A negative ``k`` (statically unstable plant) is
allowed.

Parameters
----------
m : float
    Inertia (output units: kg for a position in m, or any consistent set).
c : float
    Damping of the linearised plant (same set; ``m`` per second).
k : float
    Stiffness of the linearised plant (``m`` per second squared); negative when unstable.
b : float
    Input gain (``m`` times output units per second squared per input unit).
wn : float [rad/s]
    Natural frequency of the dominant pair.
zeta : float [-]
    Damping ratio of the dominant pair.
p : float [1/s], optional
    Real integral pole (default ``wn / 4``: slow integral action that removes the offset).

Returns
-------
kp : float
    Proportional gain (input units per output unit).
ki : float
    Integral gain (input units per output unit-second).
kd : float
    Derivative gain (input units per output unit per second).
poles : ndarray [1/s]
    Closed-loop poles obtained with these gains (check against the request).

functions.name: lqr
functions.sig: (A, B, Q, R) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Continuous-time LQR: ``u = -K x`` minimising ``int (x'Qx + u'Ru) dt``.

Returns
-------
K : ndarray
    Gain (input units per state unit).
P : ndarray
    Solution of the algebraic Riccati equation.
poles : ndarray [1/s]
    Eigenvalues of ``A - B K``.

functions.name: dlqr
functions.sig: (Ad, Bd, Q, R) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Discrete-time LQR: ``u_k = -K x_k`` minimising ``sum (x'Qx + u'Ru)``.

Returns
-------
K : ndarray
    Gain (input units per state unit).
P : ndarray
    Solution of the discrete algebraic Riccati equation.
poles : ndarray [-]
    Eigenvalues of ``Ad - Bd K`` (inside the unit circle when stabilising).

functions.name: tune_by_optimization
functions.sig: (simulate: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], Mapping[str, float]], initial: Mapping[str, float], bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], objective: str = 'iae', constraints: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, maxiter: int = 60, log_scale: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Tune gains by minimising a closed-loop metric under constraints, with Nelder-Mead on a penalty.

Parameters
----------
simulate : callable
    ``gains -> metrics``: runs the closed loop with these gains and returns a dict containing ``objective`` and
    every key in ``constraints``. Unstable or stopped runs should return ``inf`` or a large value.
initial : mapping
    Starting gains.
bounds : mapping
    ``name -> (lo, hi)`` per gain.
objective : str
    Metric to minimise (e.g. 'iae', 'itae', 'energy').
constraints : mapping, optional
    ``metric -> upper bound`` (e.g. ``{'overshoot': 10, 'ms': 2.0}``).
maxiter : int
    Iterations of Nelder-Mead.
log_scale : bool
    Search in the logarithm of the gains (all bounds must then be positive).

Returns
-------
gains : dict
    Best feasible gains found (the initial gains when none improves).
metrics : dict
    Metrics of the best gains.
initial_metrics : dict
    Metrics of the initial gains.
improved : bool
    The objective decreased with all constraints met.
evaluations : int
    Closed-loop runs.

functions.name: robustness
functions.sig: (run: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], Mapping[str, Any]], ranges: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], n: int = 64, seed: int = 0, stable_key: str = 'stable', metric_keys: Sequence[str] = ()) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Monte Carlo over uncertain parameters: how often the loop stays stable and how far it strays.

Parameters
----------
run : callable
    ``params -> result``: builds and runs the loop for one parameter set; the result holds ``stable_key``
    (bool) and the metrics in ``metric_keys``.
ranges : mapping
    ``name -> (lo, hi)``, sampled uniformly (Latin hypercube).
n : int
    Samples.
seed : int
    Random seed.
metric_keys : sequence of str
    Metrics to summarise.

Returns
-------
fraction_stable : float [-]
    Share of samples with ``stable_key`` true.
samples : list of dict
    Parameters and results per sample.
worst : dict
    Per metric: the largest value and the parameters that gave it.
quantiles : dict
    Per metric: 5 %, 50 % and 95 % quantiles (metric units).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.cosimulation
pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.adapters
children.doc:
Adapters connecting pinneapple_cosim to PINNeAPPle's model and problem ecosystems.

Four adapter node types:

PINNeProblemNode
    The most powerful adapter. Wraps any model from ModelRegistry together
    with a compiled physics loss from a ProblemSpec.  The PDE is enforced
    automatically — no physics residual needs to be coded by hand.

PINNeAPPleModelNode
    Wraps any BaseModel (DeepONet, FNO, GNN, surrogate, etc.) as a co-sim
    node.  No physics loss — pure data-driven prediction.

SymbolicPDENode
    Wraps a SymbolicPDE (free-form SymPy expression) + any differentiable
    model.  The residual is compiled to autograd at runtime.

TimeSeriesCoSimNode
    Wraps a TSModelBase (LSTM, N-BEATS, TFT, FFT+LSTM, etc.) so that a
    time-series forecaster can participate in a co-simulation graph.

All adapters honour the CoSimNode step() / physics_loss() contract and
degrade gracefully (ImportError) if the required PINNeAPPle sub-package
is not available.

classes.name: PINNeProblemNode
classes.sig: (name: str, model: nn.Module, spec: Any, compiled_fn: Callable, coord_ports: List[str], field_ports: List[str], extra_input_ports: Optional[List[str]] = None, physics_weight: float = 1.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Co-sim node backed by a PINNeAPPle ProblemSpec + compiled physics loss.

The physics residual is built automatically via ``compile_problem(spec)``.
Supports any model family from ModelRegistry that accepts pointwise
coordinate inputs.

Args:
    name:            unique node name in the graph.
    model:           differentiable PyTorch model (``nn.Module``).
    spec:            ``ProblemSpec`` describing the PDE, BCs, and domain.
    compiled_fn:     pre-compiled physics loss callable
                     ``(model, y_hat, batch) -> Dict[str, Tensor]``.
    coord_ports:     input port names that carry coordinate tensors
                     (concatenated in order before the forward pass).
    field_ports:     output port names that carry field predictions
                     (split equally from the model output).
    extra_input_ports: additional input ports forwarded into the batch
                       under their own names (e.g., ``x_bc``, ``y_bc``).
    physics_weight:  scalar multiplier for the physics residual.

classes.doc:
Co-sim node whose physics residual is defined by a SymPy expression.

The ``SymbolicPDE`` is compiled to a PyTorch autograd function at
construction time.  Any differentiable model can be attached.

Usage::

    import sympy as sp
    x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
    u = sp.Function("u")
    laplace = u(x,y).diff(x,2) + u(x,y).diff(y,2)

    node = SymbolicPDENode(
        "pde_node",
        model=my_model,
        symbolic_pde=SymbolicPDE(laplace, [x,y], [u]),
        coord_ports=["x_col"],
        field_ports=["u"],
    )

classes.sig: (name: str, model: nn.Module, input_len: int, horizon: int, extra_input_ports: Optional[List[str]] = None, extra_output_ports: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Wraps a PINNeAPPle ``TSModelBase`` as a co-simulation node.

At each time step the node slides a context window forward and returns
a multi-step forecast.  This lets time-series models (LSTM, N-BEATS,
FFT+LSTM, HHT+LSTM, TFT, …) exchange information with physics solvers
inside the same co-simulation graph.

Port convention:
    Input  ``"context"`` — (1, input_len, n_features) rolling context window.
    Output ``"forecast"`` — (1, horizon,  n_features) forecast tensor.
    Output ``"context_next"`` — updated context (shift-by-one) for feedback.

Usage::

    lstm = LSTMForecaster(...)
    node = TimeSeriesCoSimNode("demand", lstm, input_len=96, horizon=24)
    graph.connect("node_a.signal", "demand.context")
    graph.connect("demand.forecast", "node_b.load")

children.name: pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.engine
children.doc:
Co-simulation engine: time-stepped execution with algebraic-loop iteration.

Execution model:
  1. ``execution_order()`` on the graph yields SCCs in topological order.
  2. Single-node SCCs execute once (no loop).
  3. Multi-node SCCs (algebraic / feedback loops) iterate with Gauss-Seidel
     or Jacobi until port values converge or ``max_iter`` is reached.
  4. The recorder captures outputs at each time step.

Differentiability:
  Torch computational graphs are preserved through every ``step()`` call by
  default.  ``CoSimTrainer`` forwards ``retain_graph`` to its ``backward()``
  call, so set ``retain_graph=True`` here if something else (a weight
  scheduler, a second loss, manual inspection) needs to walk the same
  autograd graph again after that backward pass.

Usage::

    engine = CoSimEngine(graph, recorder=recorder, loop_solver="gauss_seidel")
    engine.reset()
    engine.initialize_ports({"spring": {"x": torch.zeros(1)}})
    recorder = engine.run(T=10.0, dt=0.01)
    traj = recorder.get("mass", "x")

classes.name: CoSimEngine
classes.sig: (graph: CoSimGraph, recorder: Optional[TrajectoryRecorder] = None, loop_solver: str = 'gauss_seidel', max_iter: int = 50, tol: float = 1e-06, retain_graph: bool = False) -> None
classes.doc:
Time-stepped co-simulation engine over a ``CoSimGraph``.

Args:
    graph:        The ``CoSimGraph`` to simulate.
    recorder:     Optional ``TrajectoryRecorder``; one is created automatically
                  by ``run()`` if not provided.
    loop_solver:  ``"gauss_seidel"`` (sequential, faster convergence) or
                  ``"jacobi"`` (parallel, more faithful to true parallelism).
    max_iter:     Maximum iterations per algebraic loop per time step.
    tol:          Convergence tolerance (max absolute change across all ports).
    retain_graph: Forwarded by ``CoSimTrainer`` to ``loss.backward()``;
                  set True if the autograd graph is needed again after
                  that backward pass (increases memory usage).

methods.doc: Reset engine state and all nodes. Call before each new simulation.

methods.doc: Set initial port values before the first ``step()``.

Whether every algebraic loop in the most recent ``step()`` call

children.name: pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.graph
children.doc:
Co-simulation graph: node registry, connection management, topology analysis.

Usage::

    from pinneapple_systems.cosimulation import CoSimGraph, AnalyticalNode, PINNNode

    g = CoSimGraph()
    g.add_node(forcing_node)
    g.add_node(mass_node)
    g.connect("forcing.F", "mass.F_ext")   # "node.port" -> "node.port"
    g.connect("mass.x",    "mass.x_prev")  # feedback loop

    order = g.execution_order()   # [[forcing_node], [mass_node]] or SCC groups
    loops = g.algebraic_loops()   # [[mass_node]] if self-loop

children.name: pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.losses
children.doc:
Composite loss functions for training differentiable co-simulation graphs.

Three loss components:

DataLoss
    MSE between predicted port outputs and labelled observations.
    Keys use the dotted 'node.port' format.

PhysicsLoss
    Aggregates physics residuals from every PINNNode in the graph.
    Each PINNNode returns a scalar from ``physics_loss()``.

CouplingLoss
    Penalises inconsistencies at node interfaces: for each connection,
    checks that the source output matches the destination input value.
    Useful when the engine runs in a differentiable training loop.

CoSimLoss
    Weighted sum of the three components; returns the total scalar and a
    breakdown dict for logging.

Usage::

    criterion = CoSimLoss(data_weight=1.0, physics_weight=0.5, coupling_weight=0.1)

    total, info = criterion(
        port_values=engine.port_values,
        graph=graph,
        targets={"mass.x": x_observed, "mass.v": v_observed},
    )
    total.backward()

children.name: pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.trainer
children.doc:
CoSimTrainer — trains co-simulation graphs using PINNeAPPle's training stack.

Integrations:
  - ``TrainConfig``         hyperparameters (lr, epochs, grad_clip, device, seed, …)
  - ``WeightScheduler``     adaptive loss balancing (self-adaptive, GradNorm, NTK, …)
  - ``EarlyStopping``       patience-based early exit on val loss
  - ``ModelCheckpoint``     saves the best model weights across all nodes
  - ``CoSimLoss``           data + physics + coupling composite loss

Training loop (BPTT):
  For each epoch, the trainer unrolls ``n_unroll`` co-simulation steps while
  retaining the PyTorch computational graph.  The composite loss is accumulated
  over the rollout, then a single backward pass updates all PINN/surrogate
  parameters in the graph.

Usage::

    from pinneapple_systems.cosimulation import CoSimGraph, CoSimEngine, CoSimLoss
    from pinneapple_systems.cosimulation.trainer import CoSimTrainer
    from pinneapple_neural.trainer.trainer import TrainConfig

    trainer = CoSimTrainer(
        graph=graph,
        engine=engine,
        criterion=CoSimLoss(data_weight=1.0, physics_weight=2.0),
    )

    result = trainer.fit(
        cfg=TrainConfig(epochs=500, lr=1e-3, grad_clip=1.0),
        n_unroll=10,
        dt=0.02,
        initial_ports={"mass": {"x": torch.zeros(1,1), "v": torch.zeros(1,1)}},
        targets_fn=lambda t, pv: {"mass.x": x_ref(t)},          # optional data
        val_targets_fn=lambda t, pv: {"mass.x": x_ref_val(t)},  # optional val
    )

children.doc:
PINNeAPPle native co-simulation engine.

A graph-based, differentiable co-simulation framework with first-class
support for PyTorch models and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).

Architecture
------------
- **Nodes** — computational units with named input/output ports.
- **Connections** — directed edges between node ports.
- **CoSimGraph** — registry of nodes and connections with topology analysis
  (Tarjan SCC, condensation order for algebraic loops).
- **CoSimEngine** — time-stepped execution; handles feedback loops via
  Gauss-Seidel or Jacobi iteration.
- **TrajectoryRecorder** — logs port values over time for analysis/plotting.
- **CoSimLoss** — composite weighted loss (data + physics + coupling).

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_systems.cosimulation import (
        CoSimGraph, CoSimEngine, TrajectoryRecorder,
        AnalyticalNode, PINNNode,
        CoSimLoss,
    )

    # 1. Build graph
    graph = CoSimGraph()
    graph.add_node(forcing_node).add_node(mass_node)
    graph.connect("forcing.F", "mass.F_ext")
    graph.connect("mass.x",    "mass.x_prev")   # feedback loop

    # 2. Simulate
    recorder = TrajectoryRecorder().watch("mass", "x").watch("mass", "v")
    engine = CoSimEngine(graph, recorder=recorder)
    engine.reset()
    engine.run(T=10.0, dt=0.01)

    # 3. Plot
    traj = recorder.get("mass", "x")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    plt.plot(traj.times, traj.values)

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.benchmark
children.doc:
The twin benchmark (#57): the same rigour for twins that a surrogate gets, measured on one case.

A surrogate benchmark reports an error. A twin is judged on six other things as well, and this module measures them
on the same case, with the protocol written down and a results table at the end:

**state error** -- how far the estimate is from the plant, against the plant's own truth: RMSE of the outlet
temperature, the slow parameter's error at the end of the run, NIS against its chi-square band, NEES over independent
plants, and the *persistence* baseline (estimate the next reading with the previous one). A twin that cannot beat
persistence has not earned the filter.

**latency** -- the hard constraint of a real-time twin, ``T_inference <= T_data_input``
(:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.realtime_pipeline` states it and enforces it): the per-reading cost of
forecast + innovation + analysis at the case's ensemble size, its 95th percentile, and the share of readings that
would overrun the data period. The *recovery* path is timed separately, because a recalibration runs an inverse
workflow over the alarm window: what matters is whether it fits inside the window it collects
(``recalibration_window * dt``) or arrives after the fact.

**robustness to noise** -- the plant's readings are made 0.5x .. 4x noisier than the twin was told
(``sensor_std``), which is the commissioning error that actually happens: RMSE ratio against the nominal case, mean
NIS and whether it stays inside its band.

**robustness to sensor failure** -- four failure modes on the two-sensor channel, each injected into a simulated
record: *dropout* (a fraction of readings missing at random), *outage* (a contiguous block missing on one sensor),
*stuck* (a sensor repeating its last value) and *bias* (a step offset). For each: the state RMSE during the failure
against the healthy baseline, whether the twin raised anything, and how many readings it took; a twin that keeps a
finite, sane estimate through a dead sensor and *says* it lost it is the deliverable -- one that silently
interpolates is not.

**anomaly detection** -- spikes injected at known steps: detection rate, detection delay and false alarms per 100
readings, over several seeds.

**remaining useful life** -- a wear scenario with a known failure time (the wall conductance ramping to a stated
threshold): the twin's estimate of the parameter is the health indicator, ``estimate_rul``
(:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.prognostics`) extrapolates it, and the RUL error is reported at 40 %, 60 % and
80 % of life, with the share inside a stated +-30 % band (the PHM alpha-lambda idea, at the checkpoints stated rather
than as a cone over every lambda).

**decision** -- not only the error: the action the twin's estimate would drive. Each reading is classified into
*safe* / *warn* / *stop* by the outlet temperature against the case's limits, once from the twin's estimate and once
from the truth, and the disagreement is priced by a documented cost matrix (a missed stop is 100, a false stop 1, a
missed warning 10, a false warning 1). The result is the agreement rate, the cost of the twin's actions, the cost of
a perfect-information operator (0) and the cost of never acting -- the number an operations manager actually asks
for. :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.decision` holds the same idea for design surrogates (``flip_rate``, ``regret``): it
compares *designs* pairwise, and a twin has no pairwise designs, so the decision here is the action confusion at a
stated limit, priced.

Protocol
--------
Fixed seeds per scenario, the plant's true parameters stated (a twin is never commissioned exactly), the sensor noise
and the thresholds the twin is told stated in the protocol block of the result, and every number reproducible from
``seed``. ``quick=True`` (the default) keeps each run to a couple of hundred readings and 80 members -- the table is
then a few seconds; ``quick=False`` multiplies the readings, the members and the seeds, which is what a published
number should be measured at.

The case defaults to :func:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.workflow.heated_channel` (two temperature sensors around
a fouling wall conductance), because sensor failure needs more than one output to be interesting; any built-in model
or ``module:function`` can be passed instead, and the sections that need two sensors say so when it has one.

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.benchmark import list_benchmark, twin_benchmark

    r = twin_benchmark()                       # the heated channel, quick sizes
    print(list_benchmark(r))                   # the results table, as markdown
    r["sections"]["decision"]["cost"]["twin"]   # one section's numbers, as measured

Scope: nothing here is a truth it does not have. Every scenario is a simulated plant, so every number is scored
against a known truth and the result says ``synthetic``; a twin on a real record is scored by
:func:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.end_to_end.end_to_end_twin` and its drift verdict instead.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.conditioning
children.doc:
Causal, sample-by-sample telemetry conditioning for production digital twins.

``signal_reconstruction`` cleans a signal *after the fact* (FFT, SSA, wavelets, interpolation over
the whole history). A running twin cannot wait for the future: every reading must be conditioned
the moment it arrives, before it reaches the model or the state estimator. This module does that,
causally, per signal, with settings that depend on what the signal is (a thermocouple is slow and
smooth, a pressure transmitter fast and spiky, a valve command must not be filtered at all).

Pipeline per reading (each step flags what it did, nothing is changed silently):

1. **range check**: outside ``valid_range`` -> treated as missing (``out_of_range``).
2. **outlier rejection**: Hampel test made causal. A plain median of *past* readings lags a
   trending signal by half a window and flags good readings, so the reading is compared with a
   one-step prediction instead: last accepted value + median of the recent rates of change x dt.
   Scale: 1.4826 * MAD of those rates x dt, floored by the median |rate| x dt. Beyond
   ``hampel_k`` scales -> replaced by the prediction (``outlier``). Spikes are short: after
   ``max_consecutive_outliers`` rejections in a row the reading is accepted (a real step change
   in the process, ``level_shift``) and the rate history restarts.
3. **rate limit**: change per second capped at ``max_rate`` (``rate_limited``).
4. **low-pass**: first-order filter with time constant ``tau_s``; the gain uses the actual
   time step (``alpha = 1 - exp(-dt / tau)``), so irregular sampling is handled correctly.
5. **gaps**: ``fill(t)`` when no reading arrives: holds the last value up to ``max_gap_s``
   (``gap_filled``), then returns NaN (``stale``) so downstream code knows the sensor is gone.

Motivation: R. Belbachir, "a deployable industrial AI pipeline begins before the model" (2026,
see ``ROADMAP.md`` §11). Methods: Hampel identifier (Hampel, J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 69 (1974) 383;
Pearson, "Outliers in process modeling and identification", IEEE TCST 10(1) (2002) 55-63) and
the first-order low-pass filter.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.cooled_part
children.doc:
A 3-D thermal digital twin of a part cooled by internal passages (a battery cold plate, a cooled mould, a cold
plate under power electronics), built from the part's geometry file.

    grid = voxelize_part("plate.stl", pitch=(0.01, 0.004, 0.002), unit="m")
    model = CooledPart(grid, h=2500.0, heat_flux=2000.0 / 0.06, T_in=25.0)          # W/m2 on the loaded face
    plant = CooledPart(voxelize_part("plate.stl", pitch=(0.005, 0.002, 0.001)), h=2500.0, heat_flux=..., T_in=25.0)
    rec = simulate_readings(plant, sensors, t_end=900, dt=1.0, noise=0.05, fault={"passage": 2, "t": 400, ...})
    out = run_twin(model, rec, sensors)               # field, coefficients with bands, alarms, checks

**Geometry.** :func:`voxelize_part` puts the file on a box grid (the pitch may differ per axis; the file's length
unit is stated by the caller: STL stores none). A cell is solid when its centre is inside the closed surface (ray
parity along the last axis). The coolant passages are the void regions of the bounding box that cross it along the
flow axis without touching its side faces; every solid face on a passage is a wall of that passage.

**Physics** (constant properties, SI units, temperatures in degC)::

    rho c dT/dt = div(k grad T)              in the solid
    -k dT/dn = h_p (T - T_in)                on the walls of passage p
    -k dT/dn = -q''                          on the loaded face (the face of the bounding box at the top of
                                              ``load_axis``: where the cells sit), adiabatic elsewhere

The coolant is taken at its inlet temperature along the whole passage (no heating along the flow): a stated
simplification, good when the coolant's rise is small next to the wall-to-coolant difference. Time stepping is
implicit (backward Euler), with the walls at their nominal coefficients in the matrix, factorised once, and the
departure of each coefficient from nominal (a clogging passage) taken explicitly. Conduction conserves energy, so
at steady state with nominal coefficients the heat removed by the walls equals the heat put in (the test checks it).

**Twin.** :func:`run_twin` is a stochastic ensemble Kalman filter with perturbed observations (Evensen 2009,
*Data Assimilation*, ch. 9), written in ensemble space so no state-by-state matrix is formed (``TwinRuntime``'s
filter holds dense covariances, which a 3-D field does not fit). The members step a POD-Galerkin reduction of the
full model (:class:`ReducedPart`), so the filter keeps up with the sensors. The state is the field plus
``log h_p`` of every passage, the coefficients as random walks: a passage that clogs loses its coefficient, and
the filter follows it.
An alarm is raised when a passage's coefficient stays below ``alarm_fraction`` of its nominal value, with its upper
2-sigma band below too, for ``alarm_samples`` samples in a row.

**Replay.** Without live data, :func:`simulate_readings` makes a recording from a *plant*: the same physics on a
finer grid (so the twin is not checked on its own discretisation), a blockage of one passage at a stated time and
Gaussian sensor noise. The recording says ``simulated: True``; the twin's checks on it are a replay of a known
fault, not a measurement of the real part.

methods.doc: Heat put into the part [W].

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (T: np.ndarray, h: np.ndarray, dt: float, load: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Advance ``T`` (n,) or (n, m) [degC] by ``dt`` [s] with coefficients ``h`` (P,) or (P, m) [W/(m2 K)];
``load`` scales the heat flux. Backward Euler with the walls at their nominal coefficients in the matrix
(factorised once per ``dt``) and the difference ``h - h_nominal`` taken explicitly: exact when ``h`` is
nominal, first order otherwise, and stable for ``h`` up to about twice nominal at any ``dt``.

methods.doc: The steady field (marched in time until it stops changing by ``tol`` degC per step).

classes.name: ReducedPart
classes.sig: (full: CooledPart, *, dt_snap: float = 5.0, t_snap: float | None = None, fractions: Sequence[float] = (0.2, 0.6), loads: Sequence[float] = (1.0,), energy: float = 1 - 1e-09, max_modes: int = 80)
classes.doc:
A POD-Galerkin reduced model of a :class:`CooledPart` (Holmes, Lumley & Berkooz, *Turbulence, Coherent
Structures, Dynamical Systems and Symmetry*, 1996, ch. 3): the field ``T = T_in + Phi a`` with ``r`` modes taken
from snapshots of the full model (warm-up at nominal coefficients, and with each passage's coefficient at
``fractions`` of nominal), and the full model's backward-Euler step projected on them. The departure of each
coefficient from nominal enters through one ``r x r`` matrix per passage, so an ensemble of a few dozen
members steps in microseconds instead of a sparse solve per member.

``energy``: the fraction of the snapshots' energy the modes keep; ``max_modes`` caps ``r``.

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (a: np.ndarray, h: np.ndarray, dt: float, load: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Advance the coordinates ``a`` (r, m) by ``dt`` [s] with coefficients ``h`` (P, m).

methods.doc: Temperature [degC] of the cells from coordinates ``a`` (r,) or (r, m).
