functions.name: run_twin
functions.sig: (model: CooledPart, rec: Mapping[str, Any], *, members: int = 32, h_spread: float = 0.3, q_log_h: float = 0.01, q_T: float = 0.002, inflation: float = 1.01, alarm_fraction: float = 0.7, alarm_samples: int = 5, burn_in: float = 0.2, reduced: ReducedPart | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Keep the model in step with the recording ``rec`` (``t``, ``y``, ``sensors``, ``noise``; ``load``

Parameters

rec : dict
    As :func:`simulate_readings` returns, or the same keys from a live or recorded source.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.end_to_end
children.doc:
The twin end to end on a real sensor stream (#84): one call that takes readings from where they actually come
from, runs the standard workflow (:func:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.workflow.digital_twin_workflow`) over them
and then asks the question a twin with real sensors has to answer after it is commissioned -- *is it still fitted to
the plant it is watching?* -- through :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.drift`.

Where the readings come from
----------------------------
Nothing here invents a sensor. The sources are, and each result carries its provenance in ``origin``:

``"simulated"``
    The library's own simulated plant (``simulate_plant``): process noise, a known parameter drift and an injected
    sensor spike. It is **synthetic** and the origin says so; it exists so that every check can be scored against a
    truth.
``"usgs"``
    A **real** public gauge: ``https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv/`` (USGS Water Services, U.S. Government work,
    public domain, no key). Discharge of site 01646500, Potomac River near Washington, DC, every 5-15 min, fetched at
    run time and never stored in this repository (that is the rule :mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.usgs`
    already follows). The twin is the linear reservoir (:func:`linear_reservoir`), the baseflow-recession model of
    hydrograph analysis, whose slow parameter is the recession constant ``k``.
``"synthetic_river"``
    A baseflow recession generated by ``recession.synthetic_recession`` with the same shape as the gauge record, for
    running without a network. It is **synthetic** and labelled so in ``origin``; it is not a stand-in for a
    measurement and its numbers are not evidence about any river.
``"record"``
    Arrays you pass (``record=``, columns ``t``, the model's inputs and outputs, optional ``dt`` and ``origin``): a
    CSV replay, an MQTT/OPC-UA/REST adapter (``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream``), or a fixture read from
    disk.

What the twin does with them
----------------------------
The workflow's ensemble Kalman filter of the states and log parameters, its NIS / NEES consistency, anomaly flags,
the two-sided CUSUM with recalibration through the inverse workflow, the forecast with its interval and the
what-if runs -- and it carries a reading that did not arrive as a **gap** (the members keep forecasting, nothing is
assimilated, a recalibration window containing a gap is refused) instead of filling it in. Real provisional feeds
drop readings, and a gauge that stops reporting is itself a fact the twin should keep rather than interpolate.

Then :func:`twin_drift_check` asks the question the checks a committed twin already had cannot answer -- *is it
still fitted to the plant it is watching?* It keeps the first part of the record as the validation baseline,
calibrates the drift thresholds on a second held-out part
(:meth:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.drift.DriftMonitor.calibrate`) and measures the rest as the deployment window,
each window earning a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.drift.RetrainDecision`: STABLE / REVIEW / RETRAIN, with the
reason written down. It runs in **innovation space** (:class:`ResidualModel`), because a twin tracks: its states and
its predictions are supposed to leave the validated range as the plant moves, and what must not move is the
distribution of what it failed to predict.

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.end_to_end import end_to_end_twin, usgs_record

    r = end_to_end_twin(source="usgs", out_dir="out/river")      # a real gauge, live
    r["origin"]["site_name"], r["origin"]["url"]                 # where the readings came from
    r["summary"], r["drift"]["verdict"], r["drift"]["reason"]     # what the twin saw, and whether it aged

    record = usgs_record()                                       # the readings alone, with their provenance
    r = end_to_end_twin(source="record", record=record)          # the same twin over saved arrays

Scope: the drift check runs on the model's first output (the channel's upstream thermocouple, the gauge's
discharge), on the innovations the filter itself reported. It measures distribution shift, not the cause of it: a
river that rises and a gauge that drifted both look like drift, and the workflow's own anomaly flags are what
separate a single spike from a level change.

classes.name: ResidualModel
classes.doc:
The twin's next normalised innovation, as the model the drift monitor watches.

A consistent filter predicts its own next innovation as **zero** with **unit** spread: ``z = v / sqrt(diag S)``
is standard normal by construction when the ensemble covariance and the sensor variance are right, whatever the
plant's operating point is doing. That is the whole reason the drift check runs here and not on the readings: a
twin *tracks* a plant whose level moves by design (a river receding, a channel heating up), so its states and its
predictions are supposed to leave the validated range; what must not move is the distribution of what it failed
to predict. Windows are compared on ``z`` (input drift: a bias or a variance change), on ``|z|`` (error drift,
the twin's health) and on the joint gate of the last innovations (envelope: the structure changed).

functions.name: usgs_record
functions.sig: (site_id: str = USGS_SITE, period: str = USGS_PERIOD, *, parameter_cd: str | None = None, fill_gaps: bool = True, fetch = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A USGS gauge as the twin's record: ``{"t", "dt", "Q_base", "Q", "origin"}``, ``dt`` in hours.

The discharge is downloaded from the USGS Water Services instantaneous-values API (public domain, no key) at run
time. ``Q_base`` -- the inflow the linear reservoir recedes towards -- is **not** measured by this gauge, so it
is held at zero: the twin extrapolates the recession, and a rise of the river is a departure it flags, not an
inflow it pretends to know. Readings that did not arrive (provisional feeds drop values, and USGS removes the
ones that fail its own checks) become ``NaN`` on the regular grid when ``fill_gaps`` -- the workflow carries them
as gaps -- and are skipped otherwise. ``fetch`` overrides the downloader (``usgs.fetch_iv`` by default), for a
recorded payload in a test.

functions.name: synthetic_river_record
functions.sig: (q0: float = 2000.0, k_per_hour: float = 0.0035, hours: float = 120.0, step_minutes: float = 5.0, noise: float = 0.01, seed: int = 0, bump_at_hour: float | None = None, bump: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A **synthetic** baseflow recession on the same grid as :func:`usgs_record`, for running without a network.

The origin says ``"synthetic"`` and stays attached to every result built from it: these numbers are not a
measurement and say nothing about any river. ``bump_at_hour`` / ``bump`` add a runoff step, which is what a real
gauge does after rain and what the recession-only twin sees as a departure.

functions.name: river_model
functions.sig: (record: Mapping[str, Any], *, sensor_std: float | None = None, process_std: float | None = None) -> StateSpaceModel
functions.doc:
The linear reservoir **commissioned** on the first half of a river record, as the twin's model.

Commissioning is system identification, not assumption, and every number below is measured on the record:

* ``k`` -- the recession constant from :func:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.recession.fit_recession` (a window
  that is not receding gives a non-positive slope: it is floored at 1e-5 1/h rather than negated).
* ``sensor_std`` -- the *resolution* of the feed: the smallest step between two distinct reported values, over
  ``sqrt(12)`` (a value rounded to a grid of that step has that standard deviation). A USGS gauge reports
  discharge from a rating curve, so its values land on a grid -- 30 ft3/s on the Potomac record this was built
  against -- and the per-sample reading uncertainty is not published; the grid is what the record itself shows.
* ``process_std`` -- the one-step residual of the fitted recession, from the *measured* previous reading: how far
  the river actually moves away from the forecast between two samples, which is what the model cannot explain and
  therefore what its process noise has to carry. On a quantised feed that residual holds the whole scatter (a
  value is reported on a grid, and consecutive readings repeat exactly, so the grid error cannot be separated
  out): the twin then carries a slightly conservative budget, which its NIS check reports rather than hides.
  When the record states its own reading noise (``known_sensor_rel``: a fixture whose generator knows it) and
  that noise is independent sample to sample, its contribution ``(1 + a^2) r^2`` is removed first -- with the
  exception of a robust estimator, which is no use here anyway: most consecutive values are identical, so the
  median absolute deviation is exactly zero.

The twin then runs *unassisted* on the second half, which is what the checks and the drift verdict judge. Both
noise levels can be overridden; neither is a gauge figure and neither is claimed to be one.

functions.name: twin_drift_check
functions.sig: (flow: Mapping[str, Any], model: StateSpaceModel, *, split: Sequence[float] = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2), quantile: float = 0.99, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Has the twin aged? Its normalised innovations measured against the validation window, window by window.

The record is cut into a baseline (the split's first part, the validation stand-in), a calibration part (a
*second* held-out part, from which the null distribution of every statistic is drawn) and a deployment part (the
last one, measured in windows of the calibrated size). Each live window is one
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.drift.DriftReport` on :class:`ResidualModel`: the innovation distribution, the
residual magnitude, the domain gate, against limits calibrated at the stated quantile, and the
STABLE / REVIEW / RETRAIN decision with its reason. A bias the filter cannot absorb is a mean shift of ``z``; a
sensor that went noisy is a variance change; a plant that changed behaviour is a heavier tail. None of them
needs the operating point to stand still.

Returns the thresholds, every window's verdict and alarms, and the last window's decision; ``status`` is
``"ok"`` or ``"not_run"`` with the reason (a record too short to hold ten calibration windows is reported, not
guessed at). ``model`` is the twin's model, carried for the reader; the statistic does not need it.

functions.name: end_to_end_twin
functions.sig: (*, source: str = 'simulated', model: Any = None, model_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, record: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, site_id: str = USGS_SITE, period: str = USGS_PERIOD, fetch = None, n_steps: int = 300, dt: float = 1.0, members: int = 200, horizon: int = 60, drift: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, spike: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, plant_params: Mapping[str, float] | ...
functions.doc:
The twin end to end over one source, with its provenance and the drift verdict on what it produced.

``source`` is one of :data:`SOURCES`. The result is the workflow's own record (traces, events, checks, forecast,
what-if, dashboard path) plus ``origin`` (where the readings came from, with the USGS citation or the word
synthetic), ``record`` (the arrays that were fed, so a run can be replayed) and ``drift`` (the trust module's
verdict). The workflow's checks that need a truth stay ``inconclusive`` on a real record, and the result says so
-- nothing is scored against a truth that does not exist.

children.summary: The twin end to end on a real sensor stream (#84): one call that takes readings from where they actually come from, runs the standard workflow ...

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io
pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.mqtt_broker
children.doc:
A small embedded MQTT 3.1.1 broker for demos, tests and single-asset edge deployments.

Implements the part of MQTT 3.1.1 (OASIS standard, 2014) a sensor gateway and a twin need: CONNECT/CONNACK,
PUBLISH with QoS 0 and 1 (PUBACK), retained messages, SUBSCRIBE/SUBACK and UNSUBSCRIBE/UNSUBACK with ``+`` and
``#`` wildcards, PINGREQ/PINGRESP and DISCONNECT. Messages are delivered to subscribers at QoS 0. There is no
persistence, no QoS 2, no will messages and no TLS: put a production broker (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ) in front of
real equipment and point :class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream.MQTTStream` at it instead.

Optional username/password: when both are set, CONNECT packets with other credentials get return code 4.

>>> broker = MQTTBroker(port=0).start()      # port 0: any free port
>>> broker.port > 0
True
>>> broker.stop()

classes.name: MQTTBroker
classes.sig: (host: str = '127.0.0.1', port: int = 1883, username: str | None = None, password: str | None = None, max_packet: int = 256 * 1024)
classes.doc: Run with :meth:`start` (background thread with its own event loop) and :meth:`stop`.

methods.doc: Send ``payload`` to every subscriber of ``topic`` (call from the broker's loop).

methods.name: publish

methods.doc: Publish from the hosting process (thread-safe), as if a client had sent it.

functions.sig: (filt: str, topic: str) -> bool
functions.doc: MQTT topic-filter matching (``+`` one level, ``#`` the rest; ``$`` topics need an explicit first level).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.sensors
children.doc:
Sensor management for digital twins.

A ``SensorRegistry`` keeps track of sensor positions, calibration offsets,
and expected field mappings.  Each ``Sensor`` converts a raw reading into a
calibrated ``Observation``.

classes.name: Sensor
classes.doc:
Represents a single physical sensor.

Parameters
----------
sensor_id : str
    Unique identifier (e.g. "pressure_01").
coords : dict
    Spatial position {"x": ..., "y": ..., "z": ...} (subset allowed).
field_names : list[str]
    Names of the physical fields this sensor measures.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream
children.doc:
Real-time data stream adapters for digital twins.

Provides adapters for multiple data sources:
- ``FileWatchStream``: polls a JSON/CSV/Parquet file for new rows
- ``MQTTStream``: subscribes to an MQTT broker (requires paho-mqtt)
- ``HTTPPollStream``: periodically polls a REST endpoint
- ``KafkaStream``: reads from Apache Kafka (requires kafka-python)
- ``OPCUAStream``: polls an OPC-UA server's tags (requires asyncua)
- ``ModbusStream``: polls a Modbus TCP server's holding registers (requires pymodbus)
- ``MockStream``: synthetic stream for testing/simulation

All streams emit ``Observation`` objects to a shared queue consumed by
the ``DigitalTwin.update_loop``.

classes.name: BaseStream
classes.sig: (sensor_id: str, field_names: List[str]) -> None
classes.doc: Abstract base class for all data stream adapters.

classes.sig: (path: str, sensor_id: str, field_names: List[str], *, poll_interval: float = 1.0, format: str = 'jsonl') -> None
classes.doc:
Polls a JSON-lines file (or CSV/Parquet) for new rows.

Each row must have fields matching ``field_names`` and optionally
"timestamp", "x", "y", "z" columns for spatial context.

Parameters
----------
path : str | Path      path to the data file
poll_interval : float  seconds between file checks
format : str           "jsonl" | "csv" | "parquet"

classes.doc:
Subscribes to an MQTT topic and emits Observations.

Requires ``paho-mqtt``: pip install paho-mqtt

Message payload must be JSON with keys matching ``field_names``.

classes.doc:
Periodically polls a REST endpoint (GET) and emits Observations.

The response must be JSON with keys matching ``field_names``.

classes.doc:

classes.name: OPCUAStream
classes.sig: (server_url: str, node_ids: Dict[str, str], sensor_id: str, field_names: List[str], *, poll_interval: float = 1.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Polls an OPC-UA server for real-time tag values.

Requires ``asyncua``: pip install asyncua

OPC-UA is a pull (polled) protocol at the level this class uses it
(reading each node's current value on an interval) -- unlike
MQTT/Kafka, there is no server-push subscription used here, so
``poll_interval`` directly controls how fresh the emitted
``Observation``s are. (A real OPC-UA subscription -- server pushes
on value change -- is possible via ``asyncua``'s subscription API
but adds real complexity, e.g. a running event loop and a
datachange callback, for a benefit -- lower latency -- this
polling-based digital twin update loop does not need, since
``DigitalTwin`` itself already runs its own fixed-interval update
loop on top of this.)

Parameters
----------
server_url : e.g. ``"opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840/freeopcua/server/"``
node_ids : maps ``field_name -> a real OPC-UA NodeId string``
    (e.g. ``"ns=2;s=Temperature"`` or ``"ns=2;i=2"``) -- the caller
    must know the real node ids on the target server (browse the
    server's address space to find them; this class does not guess
    or browse for a matching node by name).

classes.name: ModbusStream
classes.sig: (host: str, port: int, register_map: Dict[str, 'tuple[int, float]'], sensor_id: str, field_names: List[str], *, poll_interval: float = 1.0, device_id: int = 1) -> None
classes.doc:
Polls a Modbus TCP server's holding registers for real-time values.

Requires ``pymodbus``: pip install pymodbus

Like :class:`OPCUAStream`, this is polling-based -- Modbus itself is
a request/response protocol with no native push/subscribe mechanism,
so polling is the only option, not a design shortcut taken here.

Parameters
----------
host, port : the Modbus TCP server's address (standard Modbus TCP
    port is 502; many real devices and simulators instead expose a
    non-privileged port such as 5020/5502 in test/dev setups).
register_map : maps ``field_name -> (register_address, scale)`` --
    ``scale`` converts the raw 16-bit unsigned integer register
    value to a real physical float (e.g. a register storing
    millidegrees needs ``scale=0.001``). Every field is read as ONE
    holding register (count=1) -- multi-register (32-bit/float)
    values are not supported by this class.
device_id : the Modbus unit/device id (also called "slave id" in
    older Modbus terminology) -- 1 by default, matching the most
    common single-device setup.

classes.name: MockStream
classes.sig: (sensor_id: str, field_names: List[str], generator_fn: Callable[[float], Dict[str, float]], *, tick_interval: float = 0.1, coords: Optional[Dict[str, float]] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Synthetic data stream for testing.

A ``generator_fn(t)`` is called at each tick and should return
``{field_name: value}`` for the simulated sensor.

other parameters of US stream gauges every 5-15 minutes.

    https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv/?format=json&sites=<SITE>&parameterCd=<CODE>&period=<ISO 8601 duration>

Parameter codes: ``00060`` discharge (ft^3/s), ``00065`` gage height (ft). USGS data are U.S. Government works in the
public domain (https://www.usgs.gov/information-policy-and-instructions/copyrights-and-credits); they are downloaded

in-process cache (``cache_ttl_s``, default 90 s) avoids re-querying on rapid reloads.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library
pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.base
children.doc:
The contract every system in the Digital Twin Library honours.

A twin in this library is a *reference model*: a deterministic, physically interpretable
reduced model of an engineering system, written so that three things can be checked without
anyone's opinion — its conservation laws, the invariants that follow from its own equations,
and the domain where it stops being valid.

Why a reference model and not a surrogate
-----------------------------------------
A trained surrogate is only as good as the solver output behind it, and the solver is only
as good as the case it was given. A reference model closes the loop the other way: it is
cheap enough to run in a test suite, it states its own assumptions, and it produces the
numbers a surrogate would later be trained on. Every twin here is the *first rung* of the
fidelity ladder the Digital Twin Library issues describe — 0D now, 1D/2D/3D and a trained
surrogate later, on top of data this model generates.

What is deliberately not here
-----------------------------
No telemetry, no state estimation, no streaming. Those live in
:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin` (the runtime) and
:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product` (the commissioning layer, whose
:class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.spec.TwinSpec` can wrap a model written
here). This package only answers: *given these inputs, what does the physics say, and does
it balance?*

The three checks a result carries
---------------------------------
``balances``
    Conservation laws with both sides computed independently — carbon in versus carbon out,
    energy in versus energy stored plus lost. A residual above the tolerance fails the run.
``checks``
    Invariants that follow from the equations themselves and must hold for *any* parameter
    set (a recovery that cannot exceed 100 %, an equilibrium conversion that rises with
    pressure, a landing that cannot use more propellant than it carries).
``not_verified``
    The honesty list: what this model cannot say, written by the author of the model rather
    than discovered by the user. It is printed by the examples and stored in the JSON.

classes.name: LibraryError
classes.doc: The twin cannot be built or run as asked.

classes.name: ParameterError
classes.doc: A parameter is missing, out of its declared range, or not a finite number.

classes.name: BalanceFailed
classes.doc: A conservation law did not close. Raised only when a caller asks for it.

classes.name: Parameter
classes.doc:
One input of a reference model: its unit, its range, and what it means.

``lo``/``hi`` are the range in which the model's own equations are the right physics —
not merely where the arithmetic survives. A hydrostatic line model is valid at 50 bar and
arithmetic at 5000 bar; the difference is a phase change the model does not carry, so the
range stops first. Values outside the range raise unless the caller passes
``strict=False`` to :meth:`ReferenceModel.simulate`, which is how an extrapolation study
is run deliberately and recorded as such.

methods.name: check
methods.doc: Return ``value`` as a float, refusing what the model cannot mean.

classes.name: Quantity
classes.doc: A number, its unit, and the sentence that says how it was obtained.

classes.name: Balance
classes.doc:
One conservation law, with both sides computed from independent input routes.

``inflow`` and ``outflow`` are not two halves of the same sum — that would close by
construction and prove nothing. For the blast furnace, for instance, the carbon entering
is weight times assay, while the carbon leaving is read back out of the top-gas
composition and the metal's carbon content; they agree only if the stoichiometry is right.

methods.name: residual
methods.doc: Relative residual, against ``scale`` when the two sides are near zero.

classes.name: Check
classes.doc: An invariant of the model, asserted rather than measured.

classes.name: TwinRun
classes.doc: Everything one run of a reference model produces, in a form that outlives the session.

methods.name: balanced
methods.doc: Every conservation law closed within its own tolerance.

methods.name: ok
methods.doc: The run is usable: every balance closed and every invariant held.

methods.name: value
methods.doc: The numeric value of one output, raising a clear error if it was not produced.

methods.name: require
methods.doc: Raise :class:`BalanceFailed` unless the run passed. The chainable form of ``assert run.ok``.

methods.name: series_json
methods.doc: The time series, kept apart from the summary so a run's JSON stays readable.

methods.name: report
methods.doc: One screen: the outputs, the balances, the invariants and what was not checked.

classes.name: ReferenceModel
classes.doc:
Base class for a system in the library.

A subclass declares ``slug``, ``title``, ``physics``, ``parameters`` (a mapping of
:class:`Parameter`), its ``assumptions``, ``limits`` and ``sources``, and implements
:meth:`_run`, returning a :class:`TwinRun`. It must not implement its own validation of
parameters or its own JSON: that is this class's job, so that every twin in the library
behaves the same way.

The dependencies between parameters are the one thing a declaration cannot express
(``pressure_outlet`` must stay below ``pressure_reservoir``), so :meth:`_validate` exists
for those and raises :class:`ParameterError` with the offending pair named.

methods.name: defaults
methods.doc: Every parameter at its declared default — the reproducible scenario.

methods.name: simulate
methods.sig: (values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, strict: bool = True, **kwargs) -> TwinRun
methods.doc: Validate the inputs, run the model, and stamp the result with its provenance.

functions.name: relative_error
functions.sig: (computed: float, reference: float) -> float
functions.doc: ``|computed - reference| / |reference|``, safe at a zero reference.

functions.name: close
functions.sig: (name: str, inflow: float, outflow: float, unit: str, *, tolerance: float = BALANCE_TOLERANCE, detail: str = '', scale: float | None = None) -> Balance
functions.doc: Build a :class:`Balance` from two independently computed totals.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.blast_furnace
children.doc:
A blast furnace: what goes in, what comes out, how hot the raceway runs and how much carbon it costs.

What is modelled
----------------
One tonne of hot metal, on a 0D basis: the burden (ore, coke, injected coal, flux), the hot blast
and the top gas. The two balances that a furnace actually obeys — carbon and oxygen — are solved
together, so the top-gas composition and the degree of direct reduction are *answers*, not inputs:
give the furnace more coke and less blast and it returns a richer CO and a cooler raceway, exactly
as a furnace does.

The raceway is solved separately for its adiabatic flame temperature (RAFT): the carbon burnt at
the tuyeres, the blast's sensible heat and the endothermic decomposition of the blast humidity
against the heat capacity of the gas leaving the raceway. That number is the one an operator
watches, because it decides whether the hearth stays hot enough to tap.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``iron``   the iron in the burden against the iron in the metal and in the slag
``carbon`` the carbon from coke, coal and flux against the carbon in the top gas and in the metal
``oxygen`` the oxygen from the blast, the ore and the flux against the oxygen in the top gas
``mass``   everything charged against everything tapped, blown over and carried out as gas —
           computed from molar masses, so it is independent of the algebra above
``energy`` the raceway heat release against the sensible heat of the gas leaving it, at the
           flame temperature the solver found

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
A single control volume at steady state: no shaft profile, no temperature distribution up the
stack, no burden descent, no cohesive zone, no recirculation of alkalis. The raceway is treated
as adiabatic with constant heat capacities. Direct reduction is derived from the oxygen balance,
not from the wustite equilibrium, so the model does not predict a furnace that is kinetically
limited. Slag is a mass and a basicity, not a chemistry: no sulphur, no desulphurisation, no
viscosity. It is a stoichiometry and heat balance for a trade study, never a furnace setpoint.

classes.name: BlastFurnace
classes.doc: One tonne of hot metal, its burden, its blast and its top gas.

functions.name: top_gas
functions.sig: (*, carbon_in: float, oxygen_in: float, flux_carbon: float, flux_oxygen: float, ore_oxygen: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Top gas and the degree of direct reduction, from the carbon and oxygen balances.

Two equations, two unknowns::

    CO + CO2 = carbon available in the gas
    CO + 2 CO2 = oxygen available in the gas

The oxygen that the ore gives up leaves as CO (when carbon takes it directly, in the shaft)
or as CO2 (when CO from the raceway takes it), and the split is reported as the degree of
direct reduction — the fraction of the ore's oxygen that carbon removed itself.

functions.name: raceway_flame_temperature
functions.sig: (*, carbon_burnt: float, o2_blast: float, h2o_blast: float, n2_blast: float, blast_temperature: float, ambient: float = 298.15) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Adiabatic flame temperature of the raceway (K), and the heat that goes into it.

Heat in: the carbon burning to CO at the tuyeres plus the sensible heat of the blast.
Heat out: the same gas raised from ambient to the flame temperature. The humidity is not
inert — it decomposes into H2 and CO and takes 131.3 kJ per mole with it, which is why a wet
blast runs cold. Solved in closed form because the heat capacities are taken as constant.

children.summary: A blast furnace: what goes in, what comes out, how hot the raceway runs and how much carbon it costs.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.chemical_plant
children.doc:
A chemical plant: an equilibrium reactor, a recycle loop, a feed/effluent exchanger and a flash.

What is modelled
----------------
A synthesis loop of the shape every methanol, ammonia or dimethyl-ether plant has: fresh make-up
gas at the stoichiometric ratio, a recycle compressor returning what the reactor did not convert,
a feed/effluent exchanger that preheats the reactor inlet against its own outlet, an adiabatic
equilibrium reactor, a cooler and a flash that drops the product and sends the rest back.

The reaction is written generically as ``A + 2 B <-> C`` in the gas phase, with the enthalpy and
entropy of reaction as inputs. That is deliberate: the model is about the *loop*, the balances
and the coupling between equilibrium, temperature and pressure, and it must be usable for any
synthesis with that stoichiometry by changing two numbers and citing where they came from. The
defaults are an illustrative exothermic synthesis and are labelled as such.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``atoms_A``  the A that enters in the make-up against the A in the product, the purge and the
             recycle inventory (which does not change at steady state)
``atoms_B``  the same for B
``energy``   the heat the reaction releases against the heat the exchanger recovers and the
             cooler removes

The invariants are the ones that make the loop trustworthy: the equilibrium constant is the
exponential of the Gibbs energy and follows van't Hoff, conversion rises with pressure and falls
with temperature, and the inert purge is what keeps the loop from drowning in what does not react.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
Constant enthalpy and entropy of reaction over the temperature range (no Cp integration), ideal
gas, no kinetics — the reactor is at equilibrium, which is the optimistic bound. The flash is
perfect: the product leaves pure and no gas dissolves in it. Compressor work, pressure drop and
catalyst deactivation are outside the model.

classes.name: ChemicalPlant
classes.doc: A synthesis loop closed by a recycle compressor.

functions.name: equilibrium_constant
functions.sig: (temperature: float, delta_h: float, delta_s: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Dimensionless K at ``temperature`` from ``dG = dH - T dS``.

``K = exp(-dG/RT)`` with the standard state at one bar. The stoichiometry is fixed to
``A + 2 B -> C``, so K multiplies two bar of B: the pressure dependence of the conversion
comes from here and nowhere else.

functions.name: reactor_outlet
functions.sig: (moles: Mapping[str, float], *, inlet_temperature: float, pressure: float, delta_h: float, delta_s: float, heat_capacity: float, iterations: int = 400, damping: float = 0.35) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
An adiabatic equilibrium reactor: conversion and outlet temperature solved together.

The two are coupled the hard way — the conversion sets the heat released, the heat released
sets the temperature, and the temperature sets the conversion through K. A damped fixed
point finds the same answer every time; the residual is returned so a caller can see how
well it converged rather than trusting the iteration.

children.summary: A chemical plant: an equilibrium reactor, a recycle loop, a feed/effluent exchanger and a flash.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.compression_station
children.doc:
A gas compression station: a multistage machine, its intercoolers, its power and its fuel.

What is modelled
----------------
A station that lifts gas from a suction pressure to a discharge pressure in one or more stages,
cooling it back to a set temperature between stages. Each stage is an adiabatic polytropic
compression, so the discharge temperature follows from the ratio and the polytropic efficiency,
and the shaft work follows from the temperature rise — for an adiabatic machine every joule of
shaft work ends up in the gas.

The two answers a station is actually sized on are both here: how the total ratio should be split
between stages (equal ratios, when the intercoolers bring the gas back to the same temperature,
and the model *proves* it by minimising the work numerically rather than asserting it), and what
that costs in shaft power and fuel.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``mass``    what the station takes in against what it delivers
``energy``  the polytropic shaft work of every stage against the enthalpy the gas took, stage by
            stage, with the integral of ``v dp`` along the path computed numerically instead of
            trusting the closed form twice
``cooling`` what the intercoolers and aftercooler remove against what the gas gives up

The invariants are the ones that make the machine trustworthy: the isentropic efficiency cannot
exceed one, splitting the ratio over more stages cannot cost more work, and equal ratios are the
minimum of the split.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
Ideal gas with constant cp and gamma: no real-gas departure, so a dense or rich gas is off. One
polytropic efficiency for the whole map, no speed lines, no fouling, no driver curve beyond a
single efficiency, and no mechanical losses. Surge is a declared minimum inlet flow from the
vendor's map, not something this model predicts. It sizes a station; it does not select a machine.

classes.name: CompressionStation
classes.doc: A multistage compressor station with intercooling.

functions.name: polytropic_exponent
functions.sig: (gamma: float, polytropic_efficiency: float) -> float
functions.doc: ``m = (gamma - 1) / (gamma eta_p)`` — the exponent in ``T2 = T1 r^m``.

functions.name: stage_discharge_temperature
functions.sig: (*, suction_temperature: float, ratio: float, gamma: float, polytropic_efficiency: float) -> float
functions.doc: Discharge temperature of one stage (K).

functions.name: stage_work
functions.sig: (*, mass_flow: float, suction_temperature: float, ratio: float, gamma: float, heat_capacity: float, polytropic_efficiency: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Shaft power of one stage (W): ``m_dot cp (T2 - T1)``, the enthalpy the gas took.

An adiabatic compressor has nowhere else to put its shaft work, which is why this is the
power and not merely a proxy for it.

functions.name: split_ratios
functions.sig: (total_ratio: float, stages: int, *, fractions: tuple[float, ...] | None = None) -> list[float]
functions.doc: The per-stage ratios: equal by default, or a declared split whose product is the total.

children.summary: A gas compression station: a multistage machine, its intercoolers, its power and its fuel.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.data_center
children.doc:
A data centre: the room's heat, the air that carries it, the chillers and the PUE it all adds up to.

What is modelled
----------------
A hall of IT load, cooled by air, with a chilled-water plant behind it. The airflow the hall is
designed for fixes the supply-to-return temperature rise; the chilled water carries the same heat
away; and the chillers make that chilled water against the ambient wet bulb, with an economiser that
does the job for fans and pumps alone whenever the wet bulb is low enough.

The number the industry is judged on is the **PUE**, and this model decomposes it rather than
assuming it: IT, the chillers, the air handlers, the pumps, the UPS and PDU losses and the rest of
the facility each appear with their own term, and the run reports both the design-point PUE and the
annual one, which is lower because the economiser takes hours off the chillers.

Why there is one balance and not four
-------------------------------------
In a data centre every watt that enters leaves as heat, inside the same fence: the first law is a
tautology, and a model that dressed it up as two independent routes would be marking its own
homework. The balance here is therefore a **completeness** check, and it is the one that fails when
a PUE is wrong: the electricity summed component by component has to equal the load the cooling
plant actually moves plus the cooling plant's own power. A forgotten fan or a UPS loss missing from
the cooling load shows up as a residual, which is exactly how it shows up in a real audit.

The invariants are what an engineer checks: the chiller cannot beat Carnot, the air temperature rise
has to sit in the band the equipment tolerates, the economiser hours cannot exceed the hours the
ambient allows, and the PUE cannot be below one.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
No CFD: the hall is one well-mixed volume, so hot spots, bypass and recirculation are invisible —
which is the whole reason a data-centre airflow study exists. No part-load chiller map, no thermal
storage, no liquid cooling, no humidity control and therefore no water model. It sizes a plant; it
does not certify a hall.

classes.name: DataCentre
classes.doc: An air-cooled data hall and its chilled-water plant: airflow, chiller, PUE and annual energy.

children.summary: A data centre: the room's heat, the air that carries it, the chillers and the PUE it all adds up to.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.desalination
children.doc:
A seawater reverse-osmosis plant: recovery, osmotic pressure, specific energy and the salt balance.

What is modelled
----------------
A single-stage RO train. The feed is split into permeate and brine by a declared recovery; the
brine therefore carries all the salt the permeate left behind, which fixes its concentration and,
through van't Hoff, its osmotic pressure. The pump has to exceed that pressure to make water at
all, and what it costs per cubic metre is the whole economics of a desalination plant.

The two numbers a project is judged on are both outputs: the **specific energy** in kWh per cubic
metre of permeate (2-4 kWh/m3 for seawater, against a thermodynamic floor near 1 kWh/m3), and the
**permeate salinity** the membrane's rejection leaves behind. The floor is computed here as an
integral, not quoted, and every run is checked against it.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``water``   feed against permeate plus brine
``salt``    the salt entering against the salt leaving, with the brine concentration *derived* from
            that balance rather than assumed — the two routes are the atom balance and van't Hoff
``energy``  the net shaft power against the specific energy times the permeate flow, with the
            pressure-exchanger recovery taken off the brine side

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
One salt, fully dissociated, ideal solution: van't Hoff is linear in concentration, so a brine above
about 70 g/L is outside what this model can say. No concentration polarisation, no membrane
fouling or ageing, no flux decline, no temperature correction beyond the ideal-gas R T. The net
driving pressure is an input, not a consequence of a membrane area and a permeability. It sizes a
train; it does not design a membrane.

classes.name: DesalinationPlant
classes.doc: A seawater RO train: recovery, osmotic pressure and what a cubic metre costs in electricity.

functions.name: osmotic_pressure
functions.sig: (*, concentration: float, temperature: float) -> float
functions.doc: van't Hoff: ``pi = i c R T`` (Pa), with ``concentration`` in mol/m3.

functions.name: minimum_specific_energy
functions.sig: (*, feed_osmotic_pressure: float, recovery: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The reversible work of separating permeate from feed, per m3 of permeate (J/m3).

Water is drawn off against a brine that gets more concentrated as it goes: at the moment the
fraction ``x`` of the feed has been taken, the osmotic pressure is ``pi_f / (1 - x)``. The
integral of that from zero to the recovery is ``pi_f ln(1/(1-r)) / r`` per cubic metre, which is
the floor no membrane, no energy-recovery device and no operating pressure can beat.

children.summary: A seawater reverse-osmosis plant: recovery, osmotic pressure, specific energy and the salt balance.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.fpso
children.doc:
FPSO and subsea production: reservoir inflow, line hydraulics, cooling and separation.

The system, as this model sees it
---------------------------------
A single subsea well drains a tank reservoir through a tubing, a flowline on the seabed and
a riser to the FPSO. On board, the production stream is split into stabilised oil (export),
gas (export or flare) and produced water. The model is 0D for the reservoir and 1D along the
line: pressure and temperature are integrated along it, so the wellhead pressure is an answer
rather than an input, and the operating point is where the inflow performance of the
reservoir crosses the outflow performance of the line.

What makes it a twin rather than a spreadsheet
----------------------------------------------
* The three rates (oil, gas, water) and the operating point are solved together: the inflow
  depends on the bottom-hole pressure, which depends on the line drop, which depends on the
  rates. ``q`` is found by bisection on a monotone residual.
* Reservoir pressure declines as it is drained (compressibility tank model), so the well
  declines on its own and the run reports the recovery factor at the end of the campaign.
* Everything is in SI (m, s, K, Pa, kg). The oilfield units an engineer will want (bar,
  m3/d, degC) are derived outputs, never inputs.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``oil``    stock-tank oil implied by the tank pressure decline (``Vp ct dp / Bo``) against
           the oil integrated from the rates — two routes through the same physics, which
           agree only if the depletion equation and the volume factors are consistent
``gas``    produced gas against the export plus flare split (accounting identity)
``lift``   the solved bottom-hole pressure against ``p_sep + hydrostatic + friction``
``energy`` the enthalpy the stream gave up against the heat flux integrated along the
           line — two different closed forms of the same temperature equation

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
No-slip homogeneous multiphase flow with one mixture density and one friction factor:
slugging, liquid holdup and terrain effects are not represented. The temperature model uses
a constant overall heat-transfer coefficient and a constant Joule-Thomson coefficient in the
liquid region. Hydrate and wax are *screening* comparisons against a temperature the user
supplies for their own fluid — this model does not predict a hydrate curve, and it must
never be read as a flow-assurance design.

classes.name: FPSOSubsea
classes.doc: One well, one flowline, one FPSO. See the module docstring for what is modelled.

functions.name: vogel_qmax
functions.sig: (productivity_index: float, reservoir_pressure: float, exponent: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The rate at zero bottom-hole pressure for ``q/qmax = 1 - (1-a)x - a x^2``.

Written so that ``a = 0`` is the straight-line productivity index and ``a = 0.8`` is
Vogel's solution-gas-drive curve. The maximum follows from matching the slope at
``x = 1``: ``f'(1) = -(1+a)``, so ``qmax = J p_r / (1 + a)``.

functions.name: ipr_rate
functions.sig: (bottom_hole_pressure: float, productivity_index: float, reservoir_pressure: float, exponent: float) -> float
functions.doc: Inflow performance: stock-tank oil rate (m3/s) of one well at a bottom-hole pressure.

functions.name: line_pressure_drop
functions.sig: (*, oil_rate: float, gor: float, water_cut: float, oil_density: float, gas_specific_gravity: float, diameter: float, length: float, rise: float, pressure: float, temperature_k: float, oil_viscosity: float, formation_volume_factor: float = 1.0, roughness: float = 4.6e-05) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Frictional and hydrostatic drop of the mixed stream over a line, at its inlet state.

The two components are reported separately because they answer different questions: the
hydrostatic part is set by the riser and cannot be engineered away, the friction part is
what a larger line buys. The mixture is homogeneous no-slip — in-situ volume fractions
from the formation volume factors, then one density, one viscosity, one velocity.

functions.name: solve_operating_point
functions.sig: (*, separator_pressure: float, productivity_index: float, reservoir_pressure: float, exponent: float, tubing: Mapping[str, float], line: Mapping[str, float], tolerance: float = 0.001) -> tuple[float, float, dict[str, float], dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
Solve inflow = outflow by bisection on the bottom-hole pressure.

The outflow curve is the two lifts in series — the tubing from the reservoir up to the
tree, then the flowline and riser to the separator — and the inflow curve is the IPR.
The residual is monotone: a lower bottom-hole pressure means more inflow and less lift, so
it changes sign exactly once between the separator pressure and the reservoir pressure.
Returns ``(rate, p_wf, tubing_drop, line_drop)``.

children.summary: FPSO and subsea production: reservoir inflow, line hydraulics, cooling and separation.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.green_hydrogen
children.doc:
A green hydrogen plant: an electrolyser stack, its water, its oxygen and what it costs per kilogram.

What is modelled
----------------
A stack of ``n`` cells in series, each held at a cell voltage, taking a current density over a cell
area. Faraday's law fixes the hydrogen: two electrons per molecule, so the charge that passes at
the electrodes *is* the gas produced. The cell voltage fixes the rest: below the thermoneutral
voltage the stack absorbs heat, above it the stack rejects the difference as heat, and the ratio of
the reversible voltage to the cell voltage is the efficiency.

Three quantities decide whether a plant is credible, and all three are outputs here: the specific
energy per kilogram (the number a purchase order quotes), the fraction of the electricity that
leaves as hydrogen rather than as heat, and the water and oxygen that move with it.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``electricity``  the stack power asked for against the power the cell count and current actually draw
``energy``       electricity in against hydrogen's higher heating value plus the heat the stack
                 rejects, with the heat taken from the overpotential and the hydrogen from the
                 molar enthalpy of formation — two routes, not one equation written twice
``water``        the water the stoichiometry demands against the mass of hydrogen and oxygen that
                 actually leaves: ``H2O -> H2 + 1/2 O2`` conserves mass, so the two must agree
``oxygen``       the oxygen from the hydrogen's mass ratio against the oxygen from the charge

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
A single cell voltage for the whole stack: no activation, ohmic and concentration overpotentials
as a function of current density, so there is no polarisation curve and no part-load behaviour.
No degradation, no membrane crossover beyond the declared faradaic efficiency, no stack thermal
model — the heat is an energy-balance remainder, not a temperature. Balance of plant is one
declared fraction. It sizes a plant; it does not select an electrolyser.

classes.name: GreenHydrogenPlant
classes.doc: An electrolyser stack, its water, its oxygen and its specific energy.

functions.name: reversible_voltage
functions.sig: (temperature: float = 298.15) -> float
functions.doc:
``dG/(2F)``: the minimum cell voltage that can split water at all (V).

``dG = 237.2 kJ/mol`` for liquid water at 25 degC is the standard value; the temperature
dependence is not carried, because the twin declares one stack temperature by construction.

functions.name: thermoneutral_voltage
functions.sig: () -> float
functions.doc: ``dH/(2F)``: above this voltage the stack rejects heat instead of absorbing it (V).

functions.name: hydrogen_from_charge
functions.sig: (*, current: float, cells: int | float, faradaic_efficiency: float) -> float
functions.doc: Hydrogen produced by a series stack (kg/s): ``n I eta / (2F)`` moles per second.

children.summary: A green hydrogen plant: an electrolyser stack, its water, its oxygen and what it costs per kilogram.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.lunar_base
children.doc:
A lunar base: solar power through the night, a thermal balance, and the life-support loop.

What is modelled
----------------
A crewed outpost at the lunar equator, sized for one thing above all: surviving the night.
The Moon turns once in a synodic month, so the night is fourteen and three-quarter Earth days
long, and everything here follows from that number. The array area comes from the energy the
day has to hand over to the storage; the storage comes from the load the night has to carry;
the radiator comes from what the habitat has to reject; the oxygen comes from the crew and
from the regolith the crew can process.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``energy``  what the arrays deliver over a lunar day against what the load, the storage losses
            and the night discharge take out
``oxygen``  what the regolith plant produces in a lunar day against what the crew breathes
``water``   what the recycling loop returns plus the makeup against what the crew consumes

The checks are the invariants a sizing study must respect: the storage never goes negative,
the arrays do not have to carry the night, the radiator area is finite and positive, and the
night length agrees with the synodic month it was derived from.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
Constant solar constant and a flat equatorial site: no horizon, no dust deposition, no solar
incidence beyond a cosine, no eclipse by terrain. The thermal model is a single radiative
node — no conduction into the regolith, no multilayer insulation detail, no radiator
degradation. Oxygen from regolith is stoichiometric yield only: no reactor efficiency, no
power demand of the plant. This is a sizing model for a trade study, not a design.

classes.name: LunarBase
classes.doc: A lunar outpost sized by its night.

functions.name: night_factor
functions.sig: () -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: Day and night length of the equatorial Moon (h), from the synodic month.

functions.name: regolith_oxygen_yield
functions.sig: (oxygen_rich_fraction: float) -> float
functions.doc:
kg of oxygen extractable per kg of regolith, from the FeO it carries.

The route assumed is the one every lunar oxygen study starts from: reduce the ferrous iron
(FeO -> Fe + 1/2 O2) and take the oxygen. Per kilogram of a regolith whose FeO mass
fraction is ``f``, the oxygen is ``f * M(O) / M(FeO)`` — 0.2226 kg O2 per kg FeO, so a
regolith with 15 % FeO gives 3.3 % of its mass as oxygen. Ilmenite and pyroclastic deposits
do better; this is the conservative number a sizing study should use.

children.summary: A lunar base: solar power through the night, a thermal balance, and the life-support loop.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.pipeline_network
children.doc:
A gas transmission network: segments, compressor stations, and the linepack between them.

What is modelled
----------------
A buried gas line between two points, cut into segments by compressor stations. The flow is
isothermal and compressible, so a segment obeys the classic relation

    p1^2 - p2^2 = f (L / D) (m_dot^2 R T) / A^2

with the Darcy factor from Colebrook-White. Given the delivery pressure and the throughput the
model marches the line *backwards* to the inlet and solves the common pressure ratio the
stations have to deliver; from that it answers the questions a line is actually operated on: how
much power the stations draw, how hot the gas leaves each of them, how much of it is stored in
the pipe at that moment, and whether the ratios stay inside what a machine can do.

The linepack is the state that makes this a twin rather than a sizing calculation: the mass
sitting in the pipe is what a dispatcher trades against a nomination, and it is computed here
two ways — the closed-form integral of ``p(x)`` over the segment and a sum over the same profile.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``mass``      what enters the line against what is delivered, at steady state
``energy``    the shaft power from the polytropic relation against the enthalpy the gas took:
              an adiabatic compressor puts every joule of shaft work into the gas
``linepack``  the closed-form integral of the density profile against a quadrature of it

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
Isothermal, ideal gas with one mean temperature and a constant compressibility factor: no
terrain, no elevation profile, no transient packing, no real-gas departure. Compressors are a
single polytropic efficiency, with no map, no surge line and no fouling. Linepack is the
steady-state inventory, not what a line can release in an hour.

This is the second rung of the Digital Twin Library ladder for pipelines: the FPSO twin models
one subsea flowline with multiphase flow, this one a network with stations and a storage state,
and the 1-D transient solver in :mod:`pinneapple_systems.process_components.pipe_network_1d`
is what a transient study would use next.

classes.name: PipelineNetwork
classes.doc: A gas line cut into segments by compressor stations.

functions.name: segment_pressure_square_drop
functions.sig: (*, mass_flow: float, length: float, diameter: float, friction_factor: float, temperature: float, specific_gas_constant: float) -> float
functions.doc:
``p1^2 - p2^2`` for isothermal compressible flow in a pipe (Pa^2).

Momentum balance of an ideal gas at constant temperature: ``p dp = -(f m_dot^2 R T /
(2 D A^2)) dx``, integrated over the length. The friction factor is evaluated by the caller
at the mean condition, which is the only closure the correlation needs.

functions.name: linepack_of_segment
functions.sig: (*, p_upstream: float, p_downstream: float, length: float, diameter: float, specific_gas_constant: float, temperature: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Mass stored in one segment (kg), from the exact integral of the isothermal profile.

``p(x)^2`` is linear along the segment, so ``integral p dx = (2/3) (p1^3 - p2^3) / (p1^2 -
p2^2)`` and the mass is ``A/(R T)`` times that — the number a dispatcher calls linepack.

functions.name: compressor_discharge
functions.sig: (*, suction_temperature: float, pressure_ratio: float, gamma: float, polytropic_efficiency: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Discharge temperature of a polytropic compression (K).

``T2 = T1 PR^((gamma-1)/(gamma eta_p))``: the efficiency sits in the exponent, and it is the
*polytropic* one, which is why a real machine's discharge temperature is higher than the
isentropic endpoint.

children.summary: A gas transmission network: segments, compressor stations, and the linepack between them.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.refrigeration
children.doc:
An industrial refrigeration plant: a vapour-compression cycle, its COP and the Carnot wall it cannot pass.

What is modelled
----------------
An ammonia plant on the four-point cycle every refrigeration engineer draws: evaporate at the
load temperature, compress to the condensing pressure, condense against the cooling medium, and
throttle back. Saturation pressures come from Antoine's correlation for ammonia and the latent heat
from Watson's, both anchored on the normal boiling point, so the cycle is built from correlations
that can each be checked against published data instead of from a table lookahead.

Two numbers decide whether a plant is worth building, and both are outputs: the **coefficient of
performance**, and how far it sits below the **Carnot COP** between the same two temperatures. The
gap is not an opinion — it is the second-law efficiency, and it is what an energy audit asks about.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``energy``  the compressor's work by two routes: the enthalpy rise the isentropic efficiency
            produces, and the integral of ``v dp`` along the same path, computed numerically
``duty``    the first law round the loop (evaporator plus compressor equals condenser) against the
            condenser's own enthalpy route — desuperheat plus the latent heat at the condensing
            temperature. The residual is the property model talking, not the plant: Watson's latent
            heat and a constant liquid specific heat are not exactly consistent, and the balance
            reports how much that costs (a few per cent) instead of hiding it.

The invariants are the thermodynamic ones: no plant beats Carnot, the second-law efficiency stays in
the band real machines occupy, the discharge temperature stays inside what a compressor survives, and
the evaporator has to sit below the load it serves.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
One refrigerant (ammonia), one pressure level, no subcooling, no superheat beyond the compressor's
own discharge, no oil, no pressure drops, and a single isentropic efficiency. The property model is
Antoine plus Watson plus constant specific heats, which is accurate enough to size a plant and not
accurate enough to replace a property database. It does not select a compressor.

classes.name: RefrigerationPlant
classes.doc: An ammonia vapour-compression plant: pressures, the cycle, COP and the Carnot gap.

functions.name: saturation_pressure
functions.sig: (temperature: float) -> float
functions.doc: Antoine's saturation pressure of ammonia at ``temperature`` (K), in Pa.

functions.name: saturation_temperature
functions.sig: (pressure: float) -> float
functions.doc: The inverse of :func:`saturation_pressure`: the temperature at which ammonia boils (K).

functions.name: latent_heat
functions.sig: (temperature: float) -> float
functions.doc: Watson's latent heat of ammonia at ``temperature`` (J/kg), anchored at the normal boiling point.

functions.name: carnot_cop
functions.sig: (*, evaporating_temperature: float, condensing_temperature: float) -> float
functions.doc: ``T_evap / (T_cond - T_evap)`` — the ceiling every real cycle works under.

children.summary: An industrial refrigeration plant: a vapour-compression cycle, its COP and the Carnot wall it cannot pass.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.registry
children.doc:
The registry: every twin in the library, by slug, with its fidelity and what it answers.

This is the discoverability half of the shared-twin-specification issue (#1802): a catalogue a
reader can print, a ``build``/``run`` pair that is the whole surface, and a ladder that records what
each system is today and what the next rung above it is meant to be.

It lives in its own module so that :mod:`.scenarios` can name twins without importing the package
that imports it — a registry that can only be reached through the package it registers is a
circular import waiting for the first module that needs to enumerate it.

classes.name: TwinEntry
classes.sig: (model: type[ReferenceModel], *, fidelity: str = '0D/1D', status: str = 'reference model') -> None
classes.doc: One row of the catalogue: what the system is, what it solves, and what it does not.

functions.name: catalogue
functions.sig: () -> list[TwinEntry]
functions.doc: Every system in the library, in slug order, with its fidelity and status.

functions.name: build
functions.sig: (slug: str) -> ReferenceModel
functions.doc: Instantiate one system by slug (the model is stateless; this is for ``describe``).

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (slug: str, values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, strict: bool = True, **kwargs) -> TwinRun
functions.doc: Run one system: ``run("fpso_subsea", production_days=30)``.

functions.name: describe
functions.sig: (slug: str) -> str
functions.doc: The parameter table, assumptions, limits and sources of one system, as text.

functions.name: compare
functions.sig: (slugs: list[str] | None = None, *, values: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc: Run several systems on their declared defaults and tabulate the verdict of each.

children.summary: The registry: every twin in the library, by slug, with its fidelity and what it answers.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.reusable_booster
children.doc:
A reusable booster: ascent, turnaround, entry and a powered landing, in one trajectory.

What is modelled
----------------
The first stage of a two-stage launcher, flown as a point mass in a plane: a vertical rise
that turns over into a gravity turn up to main engine cutoff, an immediate boostback burn, a
coast to apogee, a ballistic descent with an entry burn, and a landing burn that brings the
stage to rest at the ground. Thrust follows the ambient pressure between its sea-level and
vacuum ratings, drag uses an exponential atmosphere and a constant drag coefficient, and
gravity falls off with altitude.

The question the model answers is the one a recovery engineer actually asks: *how much of the
propellant has to be held back for the way home, and does the stage still close?* The
boostback is not an input — the horizontal velocity it removes is solved by bisection so that
the stage lands where it took off.

The conservation laws it checks
-------------------------------
``mass``      propellant integrated from the mass flow against the tank difference
``momentum``  the acceleration integrated along the path against the endpoint velocity
``energy``    the specific power integrated along the path against the change in kinetic plus
              potential energy

The last two are the ones that catch a bad integrator or a sign error in the drag: a path
integral against a difference of state functions only agrees when the equations being solved
are the ones the model believes it is solving.

Limits, stated rather than discovered
-------------------------------------
Three degrees of freedom, not six: attitude is the thrust direction by assumption, so angle of
attack, base moments, control authority and structural loads are not modelled. The atmosphere
is exponential, not a standard table; drag is a constant coefficient; wind, gusts and the
second stage are absent. A real recovery has to be flown in a 6-DOF simulator, and this
model's answer is a budget, not a clearance.

classes.name: ReusableBooster
classes.doc: A reusable first stage flown from the pad back to the ground.

functions.name: atmosphere
functions.sig: (altitude: float) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
Exponential atmosphere: density and pressure at an altitude (m).

Two lines instead of a standard table, and the reason is stated where it matters: over
0 to 70 km an isothermal fit is within a factor of about two on density. That moves the
drag loss by tens of metres per second — which the model reports as its own output, so the
size of the approximation can be judged instead of hiding inside a coefficient.

functions.name: flight
functions.sig: (p: Mapping[str, float], *, boostback_delta_v: float | None = None, record: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Fly the whole mission and return the budget, the losses and (optionally) the path.

``boostback_delta_v`` is the horizontal velocity the return burn takes out, in m/s. The
solver in :meth:`ReusableBooster._run` iterates on it: the burn is commanded in velocity
rather than in propellant, because downrange distance is monotone in the velocity removed
and badly conditioned in the mass spent.

The integrator is written in plain floats on purpose. This function is called a few dozen
times by the solver below, and an RK4 over thousands of steps with NumPy scalars spends all
its time in call overhead.

children.summary: A reusable booster: ascent, turnaround, entry and a powered landing, in one trajectory.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library.scenarios
children.doc:
Named scenarios, the manifest they roll up to, and the status of every twin.

Why a scenario is a first-class object
--------------------------------------
A parameter set that says something is worth keeping. "The well after two years of decline",
"the furnace on high pulverised coal", "the hall in a cold climate" are the cases a study is
actually about, and retyping them as keyword arguments is how two people end up comparing two
different runs and calling it a disagreement.

A :class:`Scenario` is a slug, a name, a handful of parameter overrides and a line saying where
the numbers came from. It runs through the same :meth:`ReferenceModel.simulate` as anything else,
so a scenario can never bypass the range checks, and it saves to JSON so a scenario can be sent to
somebody.

Scenarios that are meant to fail
--------------------------------
Four of the eleven cases below trip an invariant on purpose: a 3:1 ratio in a single compression
stage discharges at 143 degC, a 69 K lift in a single-stage ammonia machine discharges above 150
degC, a heavier booster runs out of landing propellant, and one cold-climate data hall has an
economiser that costs more than the chiller it replaces. Those are **findings**, not failures of
the library: the model is doing its job by refusing the case. They carry ``expect="finding"``, and
:func:`check` is strict in both directions — a finding that stops being reported has changed the
physics, which is a regression just as much as a passing case that starts failing.

The manifest
------------
:func:`manifest` is the registry's status page as data: every twin, its fidelity, its named
scenarios, and — for each — the verdict, the worst balance residual against its own tolerance and
the parameter that was deliberately extrapolated. It is what a CI job reads and what a reviewer
looks at instead of eleven terminal scrollbacks.

What this is not
----------------
This is the *registry* half of the shared-twin-specification issue (#1802): discoverability, named
scenarios and result status. The typed unit algebra, the component graph with ports, the solver
adapter protocol, the cross-fidelity consistency checks and the VeriPhysics applicability gate are
**not** here, and the issue is not closed by this module. What is here is the part the library can
carry today without pretending.

classes.name: Scenario
classes.doc: A named parameter set: what it is, what it changes, and where the numbers came from.

methods.name: name
methods.doc: ``<twin>/<scenario>``: unique in the registry and readable in a report.

methods.name: run
methods.doc: Run the twin with this scenario's overrides applied to its declared defaults.

functions.name: scenario_names
functions.sig: (slug: str | None = None) -> list[str]
functions.doc: Every registered scenario, or the ones of one twin, in name order.

functions.name: run_scenario
functions.sig: (name: str, *, strict: bool = True) -> TwinRun
functions.doc: Run a scenario by name: ``run_scenario("pipeline_network/low_delivery_pressure")``.

functions.name: manifest
functions.sig: (*, include_defaults: bool = True, include_scenarios: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The registry's status page as data: every twin, its scenarios and the verdict of each run.

A run that fails is recorded and *not* raised: a manifest is a report on the library, and a
library with a red entry is exactly what it exists to show. Use :func:`check` to turn the
manifest into an exit code.

functions.name: check
functions.sig: () -> list[str]
functions.doc:
Every reason the manifest is not green, as sentences. Empty means the library is green.

Strict in both directions: a case that had to pass and did not is a problem, and a case that was
meant to report a finding and now passes is one too — the second is how a regression shows up if
the physics somehow becomes more permissive than the operating case allows.

functions.name: save_scenarios
functions.sig: (path: str | Path, scenarios: list[Scenario] | None = None) -> Path
functions.doc: Write scenarios to JSON, so a case can be handed to somebody else.

functions.name: load_scenarios
functions.sig: (path: str | Path) -> dict[str, Scenario]
functions.doc: Read scenarios from JSON, rejecting anything the library would refuse to run.

children.summary: Named scenarios, the manifest they roll up to, and the status of every twin.

children.doc:
The Digital Twin Library: reference models of engineering systems, one per domain.

What this package is
--------------------
Each module here is a *reference model* of a real system written to be read, run and checked
in seconds: FPSO and subsea production, a blast furnace, a chemical plant, a reusable
booster, a lunar base, a gas pipeline network, a compression station, a green hydrogen plant, a
desalination train, an industrial refrigeration plant and a data centre. They share :class:`~.base.ReferenceModel`, so every one of them takes
SI parameters with declared ranges, returns a machine-readable :class:`~.base.TwinRun` with
its conservation balances and its invariants, and states the limits of its own physics.

Where a twin goes after this
----------------------------
The fidelity ladder of the Digital Twin Library issues is 0D -> 1D -> 2D/3D -> trained
surrogate -> commissioning. This package is the bottom rung, and it is the rung the others
need: a model cheap enough to run in CI is also the model that generates the solver data a
surrogate is trained on, and the one a
:class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.spec.TwinSpec` can wrap to be commissioned
against measured history.

Use
---
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.library import catalogue, run, describe
>>> [entry.slug for entry in catalogue()]
['blast_furnace', 'chemical_plant', 'compression_station', 'data_center_cooling',

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.monitoring
pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.monitoring.anomaly
children.doc:
Anomaly detection for digital twins.

Compares model predictions against real-time observations and flags
deviations beyond configurable thresholds.

Algorithms available
--------------------
- ThresholdDetector   : simple upper/lower band check
- ZScoreDetector      : rolling z-score against a baseline window
- MahalanobisDetector : multivariate Mahalanobis distance (covariance-aware)
- ResidualDetector    : checks innovation residuals from the Kalman filter

classes.name: AnomalyEvent
classes.doc: Records a detected anomaly.

classes.name: ThresholdDetector
classes.sig: (thresholds: Dict[str, float], rel_thresholds: Optional[Dict[str, float]] = None, eps: float = 1e-08) -> None
classes.doc:
Simple threshold-based anomaly detector.

Flags observations where |obs - pred| > threshold (absolute) or
|obs - pred| / (|pred| + eps) > rel_threshold (relative).

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (timestamp: float, sensor_id: str, observed: Dict[str, float], predicted: Dict[str, float]) -> List[AnomalyEvent]

classes.name: ZScoreDetector
classes.sig: (z_threshold: float = 3.0, window_size: int = 100, min_samples: int = 10) -> None
classes.doc:
Rolling z-score anomaly detector.

Maintains a window of residuals (obs - pred) and flags when
the current residual exceeds z_threshold standard deviations
from the window mean.

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (timestamp: float, sensor_id: str, observed: Dict[str, float], predicted: Dict[str, float]) -> List[AnomalyEvent]

classes.name: MahalanobisDetector
classes.sig: (threshold: float = 3.0, field_order: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Multivariate Mahalanobis distance anomaly detector.

Uses the state covariance P from the Kalman filter to compute
the Mahalanobis distance of the innovation vector:
    d = sqrt( delta^T P^{-1} delta )

Thresholds can be set using chi-squared quantiles.

methods.name: update_covariance
methods.doc: Update the covariance (and its field ordering) used by `check`.

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (timestamp: float, sensor_id: str, observed: Dict[str, float], predicted: Dict[str, float]) -> List[AnomalyEvent]
methods.doc:
Adapt the common per-sensor `(observed, predicted)` interface to the
vector Mahalanobis check.

methods.name: check_vector
methods.sig: (timestamp: float, delta: np.ndarray, covariance: np.ndarray, *, sensor_id: str = 'system', field_name: str = 'state') -> Optional[AnomalyEvent]
methods.doc: Check a residual vector delta against covariance.

classes.name: ResidualDetector
classes.sig: (z_threshold: float = 3.0, window_size: int = 100, min_samples: int = 10) -> None
classes.doc:
Checks the innovation residuals produced by the assimilation filter.

Unlike `ThresholdDetector`/`ZScoreDetector`, which recompute a residual
as ``obs - pred`` from scratch, this detector consumes the innovation
(observation-minus-background, ``y - h(x_pred)``) that the EKF/EnKF
already computes on every `step()` — i.e. `SystemState.residuals` — and
flags entries that stray far from their own rolling distribution.  This
catches filter divergence and sensor drift that a simple obs-vs-pred
comparison would miss once the filter has started fusing bad data.

methods.name: check_residuals
methods.sig: (timestamp: float, residuals: Dict[str, float], *, sensor_id: str = 'system') -> List[AnomalyEvent]
methods.doc: Check a {field_name: innovation} dict, e.g. `SystemState.residuals`.

classes.name: AnomalyMonitor
classes.sig: () -> None
classes.doc:
Composite anomaly monitor that runs multiple detectors in sequence.

Usage
-----
>>> monitor = AnomalyMonitor()
>>> monitor.add_detector(ThresholdDetector({"p": 500.0}))
>>> monitor.add_detector(ZScoreDetector(z_threshold=3.0))
>>> events = monitor.check(ts, "sensor_01", obs, pred)

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.pipe_loop.benchmark
children.doc:
Controlled test cases with a known answer, and the confusion matrix of the diagnosis.

``make_cases`` draws scenarios of four kinds (seeded): healthy operation, a partial obstruction in one pipe (process
changed), a drifting or noisy sensor (sensor wrong), the plant driven outside the twin's training envelope (model
outside its domain). Fault onset, size, location and the operating history are random per case. The diagnoser is
calibrated on separate healthy runs (other seeds), then every case is diagnosed at its end; the matrix counts true
kind (rows) against diagnosed kind (columns), and the location / sensor / input is scored separately.

functions.sig: (n_per_kind: int = 20, seed: int = 0) -> list[Scenario]

functions.doc:
Fit the twin's fast model, calibrate the diagnoser on healthy runs, diagnose every controlled case and
return the confusion matrix, isolation scores, false alarms, delays and timings.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.pipe_loop.diagnose
children.doc:
How the twin knows it is wrong: physics residuals, a fast model, a Kalman filter and its domain of validity.

Three independent sources of evidence at every step:

1. **Physics residuals** (:class:`Residuals`), from the readings alone: mass balance at the tee; Darcy-Weisbach /
   Colebrook flow of each pipe from its measured pressure drop vs its flow meter; the pump curve; each valve's
   orifice law; the heater energy balance; each branch's heat loss. Each residual involves a few sensors and
   components, so a fault moves the residual vector in its own *direction* (the derivative of the residuals with
   respect to that fault). A biased sensor moves every residual it appears in; an obstruction in pipe B moves only
   the Darcy residual of pipe B (mass and energy still balance).
2. **The fast model** (:class:`Surrogate`): a POD + Gaussian-process surrogate of the ten readings over the operating
   envelope it was trained on, with its predictive standard deviation; its innovations say "the plant does not do
   what I predict".
3. **The domain of validity**: the inputs against the training envelope (normalised excess outside the box) and
   the Gaussian-process spread; plus the quasi-steady validity of the model for valve moves.

A Kalman filter (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman.ExtendedKalmanFilter`) tracks an extra loss
coefficient per pipe (random walk) from the measured pressure drops and flows, so a process change comes with its
size and uncertainty.

:class:`Diagnoser` turns the evidence into one of four answers -- normal, process changed (which pipe), sensor wrong
(which sensor, bias or noise), model outside its domain (which input) -- with thresholds calibrated on healthy runs
(:meth:`Diagnoser.calibrate`), and says what it needs next: inspect the pipe, recalibrate the sensor, or run the
reference simulation at the new operating point (and add it to the model).
