children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.pipe_loop.plant
children.doc:
The plant: a pumped, heated water loop with an elbow and a T junction, and its reference simulator.

    reservoir -> pump (speed n) -> heater (duty Qh) -> pipe A (with a 90° elbow) -> T junction
                                                          |-> branch B (pipe, valve uB) -> tank at z_B
                                                          '-> branch C (pipe, valve uC) -> tank at z_C

Quasi-steady hydraulics (operator moves are slow against the acoustic time 2L/a, see :func:`quasi_steady_valid`):
pump head ``H = n^2 H0 - k_p Q^2`` (affinity laws), Darcy-Weisbach pipes with the Colebrook friction factor
(``pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pipe_flow``), minor losses of the elbow, the tee and the valves (``K_v(u) = K_v0 /
u^2``); the junction head and the two branch flows are solved by Newton each time step. Energy: the heater raises the
water by ``Qh / (m cp)``; each branch loses heat to the room through ``UA`` (``T_out = T_room + (T_A - T_room)
exp(-UA / (m cp))``).

Ten sensors (pressures in bar gauge, flows in m3/h, temperatures in °C) with Gaussian noise; faults are injected on
the *truth* (a partial obstruction: extra loss coefficient in a pipe) or on the *readings* (a sensor bias drift, a
noisier sensor), so every test case has a known answer.

Water properties: White, *Fluid Mechanics* 7th ed., Table A.1 (density, viscosity, 0-100 °C).

3-D control-room scene of the loop: pipes coloured by pressure, a transparent elbow with its velocity profile,
the T junction, valves, tanks, the pump and the sensors coloured by the twin's verdict, frame by frame.

The layout is schematic (lengths not to scale, labelled in the report); every colour comes from a solve or from the
diagnosis:

* pipe walls: the reference pressure along each pipe, linear between its end pressures (uniform Darcy gradient of a
  constant-diameter pipe), per frame;

  CFD solution) scaled by the bulk velocity of pipe A;
* sensor markers: 0 = consistent, 1 = flagged by the diagnosis at that frame (the isolated sensor, the obstructed
  pipe's sensors, or every model-predicted sensor when the twin is outside its domain).

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product
pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.assimilation
children.doc:
The twin's estimator: an ensemble Kalman filter over the state the model cannot know.

The baseline model predicts the world as designed. The twin's job is the other half: find
the value of the *latent* state — the fouling resistance, the wall thickness, an instrument
bias — for which the model reproduces what the sensors are actually reading. That value is
what an operator can act on, and it is never in the model.

Model inputs
------------
The model is evaluated as ``model(X, theta)`` where each row of ``X`` is
``[coordinate…, driver…]``: the sensor's fixed position, then the driver values of the
current frame (inlet temperature, mass flow, ambient). Carrying the drivers in the input
matrix is what lets one twin cover an operating envelope instead of one steady point. A
driver missing from a frame is forward-filled and counted in :attr:`LatentStateTwin.n_driver_gaps`,
because silently reusing a stale flow would bias the estimate without a trace.

The filter is the platform's :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman.EnsembleKalmanFilter`
with a persistence transition and the model itself as the observation operator, so every
assimilated sensor contributes one equation and the latent state is over-determined when
there are more sensors than unknowns — the condition for an estimate to mean anything.

Uncertainty
-----------
The 95 % band comes from the *ensemble spread* around each predicted sensor value. It is a
band on the twin's state, not a prediction interval for a change of regime: if the plant
starts failing in a way the model cannot express, the band stays tight and wrong. Only the
held-out coverage in the backtest detects that, which is why the spec requires a holdout.

classes.doc: One analysis instant: the latent state, its spread, and the innovation.

classes.name: LatentStateTwin
classes.sig: (model: Callable[..., Any], spec: TwinSpec, *, n_ens: int = 64, inflation: float = 1.02, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Estimates the latent state of one asset from a spec and the model behind it.

Parameters
----------
model :
    ``model(X, theta) -> {field: array}``. A model that takes only ``X`` is wrapped in
    :class:`~.model.BiasModel`; see :func:`~.model.ensure_twin_model`.
spec :
    The :class:`~.spec.TwinSpec`. It supplies the sensor layout, the units, the sensor
    noise used for ``R``, which sensors are held out, and which are drivers.
n_ens, inflation, seed :
    Passed to the filter. The seed makes a commissioning run reproducible.

Notes
-----
Latent dimension: one entry per field declared ``kind="parameter"`` when the spec has
any, otherwise one bias per predicted field. The two are different instruments — a
parameter is a physical quantity you can report; a bias absorbs everything, including
model error, and hides it.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.commission
children.doc:
Commissioning: the two gates a twin passes before it is allowed to run.

**Preflight** reads the spec and the plant history and refuses the twin if the contract is
not checkable — a unit mismatch, an unobservable field, a channel stuck at a constant, a
history that never visited the operating range. These are cheap checks that catch the
failures which otherwise cost a month: a °C/°F mix-up produces a twin that tracks perfectly
and is wrong by 1.8×.

**Backtest** replays the history through the twin and measures it against the sensors that
were never assimilated. It answers the only two questions that matter: how far the twin is
from reality, and whether its own uncertainty band contains reality. The second one catches
the twin that is right on average and confidently wrong where it counts.

Neither gate proves the twin will hold for a regime the history never saw. That is why
:func:`backtest` reports the window it used and :mod:`~.runner` lists it under
``unverified``.

functions.name: read_timestamp
functions.sig: (frame: Frame) -> float
functions.doc: The frame's timestamp, under any of the conventional keys.

functions.name: read_readings
functions.sig: (frame: Frame, spec: TwinSpec) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: The sensor values present in a frame, ignoring keys that are not sensors.

functions.name: preflight
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, history: Sequence[Frame]) -> CheckReport
functions.doc:
Check that this twin can be commissioned at all, before spending a backtest on it.

Returns a :class:`~.evidence.CheckReport`. A single ``FAIL`` blocks commissioning;
``WARN`` items are reported and carried into the evidence so nobody can say later that
they were not told.

functions.name: backtest
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, model: Callable[..., Any], history: Sequence[Frame], *, n_ens: int = 64, inflation: float = 1.02, seed: int = 0, warmup_steps: int = 0, calibrate_fraction: float = 0.5) -> TrackingReport
functions.doc:
Replay the history through the twin and measure it against the held-out sensors.

``warmup_steps`` frames are assimilated but excluded from the metrics — use it to let the
latent state converge before scoring, and say so when you report the number.

``calibrate_fraction`` splits the scored window in two, in time. The band the filter
produces is a band on its *state*; it does not include the instrument noise of the
assimilated channels, which propagates into the estimate and is the dominant error term on
a clean process. Commissioning therefore measures a single multiplicative band scale on
the **first** part and reports coverage on the **second**, later part — an out-of-sample
check, not a band fitted to the data it is scored on. Set it to 0 to report the raw
ensemble band instead, and it is recorded either way.

children.summary: Commissioning: the two gates a twin passes before it is allowed to run.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.evidence
children.doc:
The evidence a twin has to produce to be trusted, and the shapes it is filed in.

Two rules run through this module.

**A number carries its source.** Every metric knows how many comparisons produced it and
over which window, because "RMSE 0.4 °C" means nothing without "on 1184 held-out
observations over 19.7 h".

**What was not checked is listed.** :class:`TwinEvidence` carries an ``unverified`` list
next to its metrics. A report that only shows what passed is a brochure, not evidence.

Nothing here computes physics: these are containers plus honest formatting. The numbers
come from :mod:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.commission`.

classes.name: CheckItem
classes.doc:
One line of a preflight checklist.

``why`` says what goes wrong if it is ignored; ``fix`` says what to change. A checklist
that only says "invalid" pushes the diagnosis back to the reader.

classes.name: CheckReport
classes.doc: An ordered checklist with a verdict: any ``FAIL`` blocks commissioning.

methods.name: add
methods.sig: (check_id: str, status: str, title: str, **kw) -> CheckItem

classes.name: FieldMetrics
classes.doc:
Agreement between the twin and reality, on observations it never assimilated.

``rmse_frac`` and ``bias_frac`` are divided by the field's declared span so the gate
means the same thing across quantities. ``coverage`` is the fraction of held-out
observations inside the twin's own 95 % band: the honesty check. A twin can have a low
RMSE and a poor coverage at the same time — right on average, wrong where it counts.

classes.name: TrackingReport
classes.doc: Per-field tracking metrics plus the gate verdict and the alarm lead times.

classes.name: TwinEvidence
classes.doc: Everything a commissioned twin produces, in one file, keyed by the spec digest.

methods.name: commissioned
methods.doc: A twin is commissioned only if preflight passed *and* tracking cleared its gates.

methods.name: render
methods.doc: A plain-text report: what passed, what the tracking error is, what was skipped.

children.summary: The evidence a twin has to produce to be trusted, and the shapes it is filed in.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.model
children.doc:
What a model must accept to be run as a twin, and an adapter so existing surrogates fit.

The contract is one signature::

    model(X, theta) -> {field_name: array of shape (n,)}

where ``X`` is ``(n, n_coords)`` in the column order the spec declares, and ``theta`` is the
latent state the twin is estimating — the fouling resistance, the wall thickness, the bias.

Passing ``theta`` down to the model is what makes a twin more than a plot: the model has to
be able to *reproduce the observed world* for some value of the latent state, and the filter
finds that value. A surrogate that ignores ``theta`` still works as a twin, but it can only
be corrected on its outputs, not its inputs — which is why :class:`BiasModel` exists.

Limits
------
Nothing here validates that the model is physically right. If the model cannot express how
the latent state changes the outputs, the filter will converge to a plausible wrong answer
and report a tight band around it. Check the backtest against held-out sensors before
believing the band.

classes.name: TwinModelError
classes.doc: The model does not honour the twin contract.

classes.name: BiasModel
classes.sig: (model: Callable[[np.ndarray], Any], field_names: Sequence[str]) -> None
classes.doc:
Wrap a plain ``model(X)`` so it satisfies the twin contract with an output bias.

The latent state is one additive offset per field, in field units. This is the cheapest
honest correction: it fixes a model that is *right in shape, wrong in level* (a sensor
drift, a fouled surface, an off-calibration). It cannot fix a model whose error depends
on the operating point — for that, give the model its own ``theta``.

Parameters
----------
model :
    Callable ``model(X) -> dict | array`` with the signature surrogates already use.
field_names :
    The fields the twin predicts, in order.

functions.name: as_array_dict
functions.sig: (out: Any, field_names: Sequence[str]) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Normalise a model output to ``{field: (n,) float32}``.

Accepts a dict, a 2-D array, or a 1-D array for a single-field twin — the three shapes
surrogates in this library already return.

functions.name: ensure_twin_model
functions.sig: (model: Callable[..., Any], field_names: Sequence[str], n_latent: int) -> Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray], dict[str, np.ndarray]]

children.summary: What a model must accept to be run as a twin, and an adapter so existing surrogates fit.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.policy
children.doc:
What the twin does when it stops agreeing with the plant.

A twin that only draws a line is a dashboard. A twin that knows it has drifted is a product:
the operator needs to be told *before* the prediction is worthless, and the system needs a
defined thing to do about it.

The signal is **band consistency**, not raw error. The filter's own 95 % band is the twin's
claim about itself; when held-out measurements fall outside it far more often than 5 % of the
time, the twin's claim is false and no threshold on the error would have said so — the error
can be within tolerance while the band is a lie.

The ladder
----------
``NORMAL``      the band contains reality at the declared rate.
``WATCH``       consistency has been off for ``max_sustained`` steps; keep running, tell someone.
``ALARM``       consistency broke hard; the estimate is not to be used for decisions.
``RECALIBRATE`` the state has been unusable for ``recalibrate_after`` steps; re-run
                commissioning on recent data before trusting it again.

Limits
------
This detects that the twin is wrong, not why. A fouled surface, a drifting instrument and a
genuinely new operating regime all look the same here; only a human or a second model can
tell them apart. The policy therefore never silently retrains — it states the mode and stops.

classes.name: DriftPolicy
classes.doc:
Thresholds for the consistency ladder.

``target_coverage`` should match the band the estimator produces (0.90 for a 90 %
interval, 0.95 for 95 %). ``hard_break`` is the coverage that ends the argument: below it
the twin is not mildly off, it is describing a different machine.

classes.name: DriftMonitor
classes.doc:
Rolling consistency of the twin's band, converted into a mode with hysteresis.

Feed it one boolean per step per held-out sensor — ``in_band`` — and read
:attr:`mode`. Every transition is appended to :attr:`decisions` so the evidence file says
what the twin thought of itself, and when.

methods.name: observe
methods.sig: (in_band: Sequence[bool], *, t: float | None = None) -> TwinMode
methods.doc: Record one instant's band consistency and return the resulting mode.

children.summary: What the twin does when it stops agreeing with the plant.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.runner
children.doc:
The product surface: one call to commission a twin, one to run it, one to file the evidence.

Everything else in :mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product` is a part. This module is
the thing a project uses::

    spec = TwinSpec.from_yaml("exchanger.yaml")
    evidence = commission(spec, model, plant_history)      # preflight + backtest + report
    if evidence.commissioned:                              # gates cleared
        run = run_live(spec, model, streaming_frames, evidence=evidence)
        run.final_mode                                      # NORMAL | WATCH | ALARM | RECALIBRATE

``commission`` is deterministic for a given ``seed``, so a client can re-run it and get the
same number. That is the whole point of shipping the evidence file with the twin.

classes.name: RunResult
classes.doc: What happened while the twin ran.

functions.name: commission
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, model: Callable[..., Any], history: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], *, n_ens: int = 64, inflation: float = 1.02, seed: int = 0, warmup_steps: int = 0, calibrate_fraction: float = 0.5, notes: str = '') -> TwinEvidence
functions.doc:
Run both gates and return the evidence file.

The backtest only runs when the preflight passes: replaying a twin whose sensors are
mislabelled produces a number that is worse than no number, because it looks like data.

``warmup_steps`` frames are assimilated but excluded from the metrics, letting the latent
state converge. The count is recorded in the evidence so the window is never implicit.

functions.name: run_live
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, model: Callable[..., Any], frames: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], *, n_ens: int = 64, inflation: float = 1.02, seed: int = 0, policy: DriftPolicy | None = None, evidence: TwinEvidence | None = None, theta0: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> RunResult
functions.doc:
Assimilate a run of frames, monitor consistency, and record what the twin decided.

Frames without a held-out reading still move the state; they simply contribute no
consistency observation. That is the common case on line, where the reference instrument
is a monthly lab sample.

When ``evidence`` is supplied its ``decisions`` are updated in place, so the same file
that commissioned the twin also carries its on-line behaviour. Pass ``theta0`` — normally
``evidence.initial_state`` — so the twin starts from the state commissioning converged to
instead of a cold prior.

functions.name: describe
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, latent: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]], fields: Mapping[str, float] | None = None)
functions.doc:
Describe the twin for the industry standards the platform already speaks.

Returns a :class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.standards.TwinDescription`, which
``to_aas`` (AAS / IDTA), ``to_dtdl``, ``to_ngsi_ld`` and ``to_ditto_thing`` turn into the
corresponding document, and which ``OpcUaTwinServer`` serves over OPC UA.

Estimated parameters go out as ``parameter`` properties with their standard deviation in
the description; the field estimates go out as ``state``. Sensor identifiers are not
published directly because the standards require identifier-safe names and plant tags
contain dashes — the twin's *outputs* are what a platform consumes.

functions.name: export_scene
functions.sig: (spec: TwinSpec, frames: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], folder: str, *, mesh: Any = None, field_on_mesh: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None, times: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Write a ``pinneapple_twin3d`` scene for this twin: sensors with measured series and envelopes.

The geometry is the asset's, so it is supplied rather than invented: pass ``mesh`` (a
trimesh object) and ``field_on_mesh`` (name -> per-vertex values per time step) to see a
field painted on it. Without a mesh, a wireframe box is drawn around the instrument layout
so the viewer has something to open — it marks the extent of the measurements, it is not
the machine, and the scene title says so.

Sensor coordinates must be 3-D for the viewer; anything else is padded with zeros and the
scene records that in its title, rather than silently pretending to a position.

children.summary: The product surface: one call to commission a twin, one to run it, one to file the evidence.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product.spec
children.doc:
The twin contract: what a digital twin is asked to deliver, signed before it runs.

A ``TwinSpec`` is the artifact a client and an engineer agree on *before* commissioning:
which quantities the twin estimates, which sensors measure them and in which units, which
model is behind it and the accuracy it claims, and — the important part — the
:class:`AcceptanceGates` that decide whether the twin is allowed to go live.

Without gates, "the twin works" is an opinion. With them it is a number that either
clears a threshold or does not, and the spec digest records which revision was accepted.

Limits
------
The spec does not validate the physics; it validates that a claim exists and can be
falsified. A spec whose gates are too loose will commission a bad twin honestly — set the
gates from the engineering requirement (the temperature the process may not exceed, the
thickness that forces a stop), not from what the model already achieves.

classes.name: SpecError
classes.doc: The spec is not usable: a missing claim, a contradiction, an unobservable field.

classes.name: FieldSpec
classes.doc:
One quantity the twin estimates.

``kind``
    ``state`` — an unmeasured quantity the twin must infer (fouling resistance,
    wall thickness, reaction extent). These are what a twin is *for*.
    ``parameter`` — a design/configuration value the twin carries but does not infer.
    ``telemetry`` — a measured quantity the twin predicts so it can be compared.

``alarm_above`` / ``alarm_below``
    The engineering limit for this field. When present, commissioning measures how far
    *ahead* of the measured crossing the twin raised its own alarm — the only number
    that makes a twin worth running.

methods.name: span
methods.doc: Physical span (hi − lo), the denominator that makes errors comparable.

classes.name: SensorSpec
classes.doc:
A measurement available to the twin, with the envelope that makes it checkable.

``driver``
    Marks the channel as an *input* to the model rather than something the twin
    predicts: the inlet temperature, the mass flow, the ambient. Drivers are appended to
    the model input matrix after the coordinates, in declaration order, and their values
    change every frame — which is what lets one twin cover a whole operating envelope
    instead of a single steady point. A driver needs no ``field``.

``at``
    Coordinates where the model is evaluated to compare against this sensor. A twin
    that cannot say *where* it is predicting cannot be compared to a thermocouple.

``holdout``
    Marks the sensor as ground truth for commissioning: it is never assimilated, only
    compared. Without at least one holdout, a backtest measures nothing but how well
    the filter fits the data it was fed.

``max_gap_s``
    The longest silence accepted from this channel. Longer gaps fail preflight, because
    a twin that stops hearing a sensor keeps predicting confidently.

classes.name: ModelSpec
classes.doc:
The model behind the twin, and the accuracy it claims.

``accuracy_floor``
    The absolute error, in field units, that the model's author claims on unseen
    operating points. Commissioning reports it next to the measured tracking error so
    an improvement (or a regression) is visible instead of assumed.

classes.name: AcceptanceGates
classes.doc:
The thresholds that decide whether a twin goes live.

Errors are expressed as a fraction of the field span so a gate means the same thing on
a 5 °C and a 500 °C process. ``min_coverage`` is the fraction of *held-out* observations
that must fall inside the twin's own 95 % band — the check that catches a confident twin
that is confidently wrong.

classes.name: TwinSpec
classes.doc:
A complete, checkable definition of one digital twin.

Build it directly, from a dict, or from YAML::

    spec = TwinSpec.from_yaml("twin.yaml")
    report = commission(spec, history, model)
    if not report.passed:
        ...   # the reasons are in report.items, each with a suggested fix

methods.name: input_names
methods.doc: Model input columns, in order: coordinates, then drivers as declared.

methods.name: sensors_for
methods.sig: (field_name: str, *, holdout: bool | None = None) -> tuple[SensorSpec, ...]

methods.name: digest
methods.doc: Stable SHA-256 of the spec, short form. Name this in every report you file.

methods.name: from_yaml
methods.doc: Load from YAML. PyYAML is imported here only, so the rest of the module is stdlib.

methods.name: with_gates
methods.doc: Return a copy with new gates. Editing a gate is a decision; it gets a new digest.

children.summary: The twin contract: what a digital twin is asked to deliver, signed before it runs.

children.doc:
The closed digital-twin product: spec, commissioning, live run, evidence, drift policy.

``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin`` is the runtime — streams, filters, monitors. This
package turns it into a product with a lifecycle, entry criteria and an artifact to hand over:

=============================  ============================================================
stage                          what it produces
=============================  ============================================================
:mod:`.spec`                   :class:`TwinSpec` — the contract, with acceptance gates and a
                               digest recorded in every later artifact
:mod:`.model`                  the model contract (``model(X, theta)``) and
                               :class:`BiasModel` so an existing surrogate fits
:mod:`.assimilation`           :class:`LatentStateTwin` — EnKF over the state the model
                               cannot know
:mod:`.commission`             preflight checklist + held-out backtest
:mod:`.evidence`               :class:`TwinEvidence` — one JSON file: what passed, the
                               tracking numbers with their sources, and what was not checked
:mod:`.policy`                 :class:`DriftMonitor` — NORMAL → WATCH → ALARM → RECALIBRATE
:mod:`.runner`                 :func:`commission`, :func:`run_live`, :func:`export_scene`,
                               :func:`describe` (AAS / DTDL / NGSI-LD / Ditto / OPC UA)
=============================  ============================================================

Relationship to the runtime
---------------------------
``pinneapple_systems.operations`` (the library behind ``apps/twin_runtime``) is the **runtime**:
models, EnKF, forecasts, alerts, storage, MQTT/REST/OPC UA. This package is the
**commissioning layer** it does not have: a signable contract, a preflight that can refuse, a
held-out backtest against acceptance gates, and filed evidence. Use them together — commission
here, run there — or use this layer alone with any ``model(X, theta)``.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product import TwinSpec, commission, run_live
>>> spec = TwinSpec.from_yaml("exchanger.yaml")
>>> evidence = commission(spec, model, history)
>>> evidence.commissioned
True
>>> result = run_live(spec, model, frames, evidence=evidence)
>>> evidence.save("twin_evidence.json")
children.summary: The closed digital-twin product: spec, commissioning, live run, evidence, drift policy.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.prognostics
children.doc:
Predictive maintenance: trend-based Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation.

This module adds a prognostics capability on top of the digital twin's
existing *diagnostic* signals — the anomaly severity scores produced by
``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.monitoring.anomaly`` (``ThresholdDetector``,
``ZScoreDetector``, ``MahalanobisDetector``, ``ResidualDetector``) and the
rolling state/observation history kept by ``DigitalTwin``/``SystemState``.
Every one of those detectors already emits a scalar ``AnomalyEvent.score``
per timestep where *higher = more anomalous* (see ``monitoring/anomaly.py``);
this module treats that scalar score (or any other user-supplied scalar
"health indicator") as a **degradation indicator time series** and fits a
trend to it in order to extrapolate forward to a failure threshold.

Technique: trend-based / regression-based RUL estimation
----------------------------------------------------------
Given a scalar health/degradation indicator ``h(t)`` sampled at times
``t``, we fit a parametric degradation *path* model and extrapolate it
forward to the time ``t*`` at which it crosses a user-specified
``failure_threshold``. Remaining useful life is then::

    RUL = t* - t_now

Two standard degradation-path models are supported:

- ``"linear"``:      ``h(t) = a + b*t``
- ``"exponential"``: ``h(t) = h0 * exp(k*t)``, fit by ordinary least
  squares on ``ln(h(t)) = ln(h0) + k*t``. The exponential form is the
  textbook model for many wear / fatigue-crack-growth / corrosion
  degradation processes, where the *rate* of degradation grows
  proportionally to the current damage level.

Both cases reduce, after an optional log-transform, to fitting a straight
line ``y = a + b*t`` by OLS and solving for the crossing time
``t* = (y_threshold - a) / b``. This is the same "general path model"
approach to trend-based RUL used throughout the prognostics-and-health-
management (PHM) literature — see e.g.:

    Coble, J. & Hines, J.W., "Applying the General Path Model to
    Estimation of Remaining Useful Life," International Journal of
    Prognostics and Health Management, 2011.

    Meeker, W.Q. & Escobar, L.A., "Statistical Methods for Reliability
    Data," Wiley, 1998 (Ch. 13, degradation/general-path models,
    including the log-linear treatment of exponential degradation).

Uncertainty quantification
---------------------------
The OLS fit yields a parameter covariance matrix for ``(a, b)``. We
propagate that covariance to the crossing time ``t*`` via the **delta
method**: treating ``t* = g(a, b) = (y_threshold - a) / b`` as a smooth
function of the (asymptotically normal) regression coefficients,

    Var(t*) ~= grad(g)^T * Cov(a, b) * grad(g)

with ``grad(g) = (-1/b, -t*/b)``. A two-sided prediction interval for
``t*`` (and hence for RUL) is then ``t* +/- c * sqrt(Var(t*))`` where
``c`` is the Student-t critical value at ``dof = n - 2`` (via SciPy if
available) or, as a documented fallback when SciPy is not importable, the
corresponding standard-normal critical value.

**Limitations, stated explicitly**: the delta method is a first-order
(linearized) approximation — for the exponential model applied to a ratio
of two correlated Gaussian parameters this is not the exact fiducial
interval one would get from e.g. Fieller's theorem, and for very small
samples or near-zero slopes the linearization can understate the true
tail width. This module does not silently pretend otherwise: fit quality
(R^2 in the fitted, i.e. possibly log-transformed, space) and sample size
are both surfaced in ``RULEstimate``, and ``is_extrapolation_reliable``
is set to ``False`` whenever the fit is poor, the sample is small, the
trend has no discernible slope, or the fitted trend does not actually
point toward the failure threshold in the future — precisely so callers
do not over-trust a bad extrapolation.

Usage
-----
Standalone, from plain arrays::

    >>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.prognostics import estimate_rul
    >>> rul = estimate_rul(health_scores, timestamps, failure_threshold=10.0,
    ...                     model="linear", confidence_level=0.90)
    >>> rul.estimated_rul, rul.rul_confidence_interval, rul.is_extrapolation_reliable

Driven by a live ``DigitalTwin``'s accumulated anomaly-detector history::

    >>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.prognostics import estimate_rul_from_twin
    >>> rul = estimate_rul_from_twin(twin, failure_threshold=10.0, detector="zscore")

This module only *consumes* ``AnomalyEvent``/``SystemState`` objects; it
does not modify anomaly detection or state-tracking logic.

classes.name: HealthIndicatorHistory
classes.doc:
A scalar health/degradation-indicator time series.

Light wrapper so `estimate_rul` can be driven either from plain
arrays (`HealthIndicatorHistory.from_arrays`) or from a live
`DigitalTwin`'s accumulated anomaly-detector event history
(`HealthIndicatorHistory.from_twin`), without requiring a separate
data pipeline.

Attributes
----------
timestamps : np.ndarray, shape (N,)
    Monotonically increasing sample times (any consistent time unit).
values : np.ndarray, shape (N,)
    The scalar health/degradation indicator at each timestamp. For
    anomaly-detector-sourced series this is `AnomalyEvent.score`
    (higher = more anomalous / less healthy, per `monitoring/anomaly.py`).
source : str
    Free-form provenance label (e.g. "custom", "digital_twin.anomaly_monitor").

methods.name: from_arrays
methods.sig: (timestamps: Union[Sequence[float], np.ndarray], values: Union[Sequence[float], np.ndarray], source: str = 'custom') -> 'HealthIndicatorHistory'

methods.name: from_twin
methods.sig: (twin: Any, *, detector: Optional[str] = None, sensor_id: Optional[str] = None, field_name: Optional[str] = None, n: Optional[int] = None) -> 'HealthIndicatorHistory'
methods.doc: Build a health-indicator series from a live `DigitalTwin`.

classes.name: RULEstimate
classes.doc:
Result of a trend-based Remaining Useful Life estimation.

Attributes
----------
estimated_rul : float
    Point estimate of remaining useful life (`failure_time_estimate -
    current_time`), in the same time unit as the input timestamps.
    Can be negative if the fitted trend indicates the health indicator
    has *already* crossed `failure_threshold` as of `current_time`, or
    `float('inf')` if the fitted trend has no slope toward the
    threshold (see `reliability_reasons`).
rul_confidence_interval : (float, float)
    Two-sided `confidence_level` interval on `estimated_rul`, from
    delta-method propagation of the trend fit's parameter covariance
    (see module docstring for the method and its limitations).
failure_time_estimate : float
    Absolute time at which the fitted trend crosses `failure_threshold`.
degradation_model_used : str
    `"linear"` or `"exponential"`.
fit_quality : float
    R^2 of the OLS fit, in the space it was actually fit (i.e. for the
    exponential model, R^2 of the log-linear fit `ln(h)` vs `t`).
is_extrapolation_reliable : bool
    `False` whenever the extrapolation should not be trusted at face
    value: too few points, poor fit quality, a degenerate/no-slope
    trend, a non-finite confidence interval, or a trend that does not
    point toward the failure threshold in the future. See
    `reliability_reasons` for exactly which check(s) failed.
current_time, current_health : float
    The reference time/health level the RUL is measured from.
failure_threshold, confidence_level : float
    Echoed inputs, for convenience.
n_points : int
    Number of (timestamp, health) samples the trend was fit on.
trend_params : dict
    Fitted parameters: `{"a":, "b":}` for linear (`h = a + b*t`), or
    `{"h0":, "k":, "ln_h0":}` for exponential (`h = h0*exp(k*t)`).
reliability_reasons : list[str]
    Human-readable reasons behind `is_extrapolation_reliable` (empty
    when reliable).
metadata : dict
    Extra diagnostic info (dof, standard error, critical value, etc).

functions.name: estimate_rul
functions.sig: (health_indicator_series: Union[Sequence[float], np.ndarray, HealthIndicatorHistory], timestamps: Optional[Union[Sequence[float], np.ndarray]] = None, failure_threshold: Optional[float] = None, model: str = 'linear', confidence_level: float = 0.9, *, current_time: Optional[float] = None, min_points: int = 4, r2_reliable_threshold: float = 0.7) -> RULEstimate
functions.doc:
Trend-based Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation.

Fits a degradation trend to a scalar health/degradation-indicator time
series and extrapolates to the time it crosses `failure_threshold`.
See the module docstring for the underlying method (general-path-model
trend fitting) and its uncertainty propagation (delta method).

Parameters
----------
health_indicator_series : array-like or HealthIndicatorHistory
    The scalar health indicator at each sample time (e.g. anomaly
    severity scores — higher = less healthy — from
    `monitoring/anomaly.py`, or any other user-supplied scalar signal
    that trends toward a known failure threshold). May be a
    `HealthIndicatorHistory`, in which case `timestamps` is ignored.
timestamps : array-like, optional
    Sample times matching `health_indicator_series`. Required unless
    `health_indicator_series` is a `HealthIndicatorHistory`.
failure_threshold : float
    The health-indicator value that defines failure.
model : {"linear", "exponential"}
    Degradation path model. `"linear"`: h(t) = a + b*t. `"exponential"`:
    h(t) = h0*exp(k*t) (requires all health values > 0), the standard
    model for wear/fatigue/corrosion-type degradation.
confidence_level : float
    Two-sided confidence level for `rul_confidence_interval`, e.g. 0.90.
current_time : float, optional
    Reference "now" to measure RUL from. Defaults to the last
    (largest) timestamp in the series.
min_points : int
    Minimum number of samples required to consider the extrapolation
    reliable (the fit itself only requires >= 2 points, but very short
    series fail the `is_extrapolation_reliable` check).
r2_reliable_threshold : float
    Minimum fit R^2 (in the fitted space) to consider the
    extrapolation reliable.

Returns
-------
RULEstimate

Convenience wrapper: estimate RUL directly from a live `DigitalTwin`.

Pulls the health-indicator series from the twin's accumulated
`AnomalyEvent` history (`twin.anomaly_monitor.all_events`, i.e. exactly
the anomaly severity scores the twin has already been computing — see
`HealthIndicatorHistory.from_twin`) and forwards to `estimate_rul`.

This is optional polish on top of the standalone, array-based
`estimate_rul`, which remains the mandatory core API and works without
any live `DigitalTwin` at all.

Parameters
----------
twin : DigitalTwin
    A live (or previously-run) digital twin whose `anomaly_monitor`
    has accumulated `AnomalyEvent`s.
failure_threshold : float
    Health-indicator (anomaly score) value that defines failure.
detector, sensor_id, field_name : str, optional
    Filters passed through to `HealthIndicatorHistory.from_twin`.
n : int, optional
    Keep only the most recent `n` matching anomaly events.
model, confidence_level, **kwargs
    Forwarded to `estimate_rul`.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.realtime_pipeline
children.doc:
Real-time inference pipeline for digital twins.

Enforces the hard constraint:  T_inference ≤ T_data_input

When a model takes longer to run than the data arrival period the pipeline
can:
  - ``"warn"``    — log a latency warning but continue
  - ``"skip"``    — drop the current frame and keep up
  - ``"throttle"``— reduce the inference grid to bring latency back under budget
  - ``"raise"``   — raise LatencyBudgetExceeded

Throughput and latency are tracked via an exponential moving average.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.realtime_pipeline import RealtimePipeline
>>> pipeline = RealtimePipeline(model, data_period=0.1, field_names=["u", "v"])
>>> pipeline.start()
>>> pipeline.push({"u": 1.2, "v": 0.0}, timestamp=time.time())
>>> state = pipeline.latest_state()
>>> pipeline.stop()

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.recession
children.doc:
A river digital twin from baseflow recession: calibrate on the recent past of a gauge, forecast the present, flag
a sustained departure.

Baseflow recession (the exponential "master recession curve" of hydrograph analysis; Linsley, Kohler & Paulhus,
*Hydrology for Engineers*, 3rd ed., ch. 7; Tallaksen 1995, J. Hydrol. 165, 349-370)::

    Q(t) = Q0 exp(-k (t - t0))

``fit_recession`` calibrates Q0 and k by least squares on ln Q = ln Q0 - k t (``numpy.polyfit``) and returns R^2
and the residual mean and standard deviation in flow units. ``detect_divergence`` flags the first run of readings
whose residual (actual - forecast) stays more than ``n_sigma`` calibration-residual standard deviations above or
below the calibration-residual mean for at least ``sustained_minutes`` of reading time; a single noisy reading is
not flagged.

``run_twin`` is the whole pipeline on a series (timestamps, values): split into a calibration window (the
``calibration_hours`` before the last ``comparison_hours``) and a comparison window (the last ``comparison_hours``),
calibrate, forecast, compare, and give a verdict:

* ``DIVERGENCE_DETECTED`` - a sustained departure in the comparison window;
* ``MATCHES_FORECAST`` - the calibration window was receding (k > epsilon) and the present follows the forecast;
* ``NO_CLEAN_RECESSION`` - the calibration window was not receding, so the model does not apply (said, not forced).

Scope: one exponential reservoir; no rainfall input, no routing, no rating-curve change. A poor calibration R^2 means
the gauge is not in a recession regime and the forecast should not be trusted; the result carries R^2 for that.

functions.sig: (q0: float, k_per_hour: float, hours: float | np.ndarray) -> float | np.ndarray
functions.doc: Q0 exp(-k t), t in hours since t0.

functions.name: fit_recession
functions.sig: (hours: Sequence[float], values: Sequence[float]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Least-squares Q0, k on the log-linearised recession; ``hours`` is re-based to its first sample (``t0_hours``).

functions.name: forecast
functions.sig: (calibration: dict[str, float], hours: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The calibrated curve at ``hours`` (same axis as the fit).

functions.name: detect_divergence
functions.sig: (hours: Sequence[float], actual: Sequence[float], predicted: Sequence[float], residual_mean: float, residual_std: float, n_sigma: float = N_SIGMA, sustained_minutes: float = SUSTAINED_MINUTES) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: First sustained excursion of ``actual - predicted`` beyond ``residual_mean +- n_sigma * residual_std``.

functions.name: run_twin

functions.doc:
Calibrate, forecast and compare one discharge series (and, optionally, fit the gage height the same way for
the water level now vs forecast). Raises ``ValueError`` when the series is too short to calibrate.

Returns the series, calibration (``q0``, ``k_per_hour``, ``r_squared``, residual statistics, window), forecast,
comparison window, detection, verdict, the half-life ln 2 / k and ``water_level`` (``None`` without a usable
gage-height series).

functions.doc:
A synthetic gauge record for tests and offline demos: an exponential recession with multiplicative noise and an
optional step increase ``bump`` (fraction) from ``bump_at_hour`` on. Timestamps start 2026-01-01 UTC.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.signal_reconstruction
children.doc:
Signal reconstruction from incoming data streams.

Provides methods to reconstruct continuous, clean signals from the sparse,
noisy observations arriving via digital twin streams.  All methods operate
on the ``Observation`` objects accumulated by ``DigitalTwin._last_observations``.

Methods
-------
spectral     : FFT-based — fit dominant harmonics and extrapolate/interpolate
ssa          : Singular Spectrum Analysis — decompose + keep dominant components
wavelet      : Wavelet soft-thresholding denoising + reconstruction
interpolate  : Scipy-based gap-filling (linear, cubic, PCHIP)
model_based  : Use the twin's physics model to fill gaps in space or time

All methods return ``ReconstructionResult`` containing the reconstructed
signal, timestamps, and quality metrics.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin import DigitalTwin
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.signal_reconstruction import SignalReconstructor

>>> twin = DigitalTwin(model, ["u", "v"])
>>> rec = SignalReconstructor(twin)

>>> # Reconstruct sensor 'inlet' field 'u' using SSA
>>> result = rec.reconstruct("inlet", "u", method="ssa")
>>> result.signal          # np.ndarray — reconstructed signal
>>> result.timestamps      # np.ndarray — corresponding times
>>> result.quality         # dict with SNR, RMSE vs raw, etc.

children.doc:
Digital-twin interoperability: describe a PINNeAPPle twin once and publish it in the open standards industry
platforms read.

=============================  ==========================================================================
standard                       what it is, and the function here
=============================  ==========================================================================
Asset Administration Shell     Industrie 4.0 / IDTA (IEC 63278): the asset's shell with submodels (identification,
(AAS, metamodel v3)            technical data, operational data, simulation models). :func:`to_aas` builds it
                               with the Eclipse BaSyx Python SDK and returns its JSON
DTDL v3                        Digital Twins Definition Language (Azure Digital Twins, also read by other
                               platforms): an Interface with Properties, Telemetry and Relationships. :func:`to_dtdl`
NGSI-LD                        ETSI context-information standard (FIWARE Orion-LD and others): an entity with
                               Property / Relationship attributes. :func:`to_ngsi_ld`
Eclipse Ditto                  open-source twin service: a Thing with attributes and features. :func:`to_ditto_thing`
OPC UA                         IEC 62541, the shop-floor protocol: :class:`OpcUaTwinServer` serves the twin's
                               values live (asyncua) so SCADA, MES and OPC UA clients read and subscribe to them
=============================  ==========================================================================

A :class:`TwinDescription` holds the asset (id, name, type), its parameters, live telemetry with units, the models
behind the twin and their physical validity (from :mod:`pinneapple_physics.physics_audit`: assumption status,
compatibility, the probable failure cause), so the trust layer travels with the twin into every standard.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.twin
children.doc:
Core DigitalTwin class.

A DigitalTwin wraps a trained surrogate model (PINN, GNN, DeepONet, etc.),
manages real-time data streams, performs data assimilation, detects
anomalies, and maintains a live state estimate of the physical system.

Architecture
------------
    Sensors/Streams  -->  ObsQueue  -->  update_loop()
                                             |
                                    assimilation (EKF/EnKF)
                                             |
                                    model prediction
                                             |
                                    anomaly monitoring
                                             |
                                    SystemState (current estimate)

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin import DigitalTwin
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io import MockStream
>>> import torch

>>> # Load a trained model
>>> model = torch.load("my_pinn.pt")

>>> # Create digital twin
>>> dt = DigitalTwin(model, field_names=["u", "v", "p"])

>>> # Add a mock sensor stream
>>> stream = MockStream(
...     sensor_id="inlet_probe",
...     field_names=["u", "v"],
...     generator_fn=lambda t: {"u": 1.0 + 0.05 * np.sin(t), "v": 0.0},
...     coords={"x": 0.0, "y": 0.5},
... )
>>> dt.add_stream(stream)
>>> dt.start()        # begin update loop
>>> # ... use dt.state to access current estimate
>>> dt.stop()

children.name: pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.workflow
children.doc:
The standard digital-twin workflow (#1193): a model, a data source, assimilation of the states and the slow
parameters, monitoring (filter consistency, drift, anomalies), recalibration through the inverse workflow, a
forecast with intervals, what-if runs and a dashboard page.

**Model.** A :class:`StateSpaceModel`: states, slow parameters, known inputs and measured outputs, with a batched
step ``x' = step(x, u, theta, dt)`` and an observation ``y = observe(x, theta)``. Any library solver, formulated
model, surrogate or zoo model wraps into one by writing those two functions; the built-ins are :func:`thermal_plant`
(a lumped heated body, exact zero-order-hold discretisation of ``C dT/dt = Q - UA (T - T_amb)``),
:func:`heated_channel` (two temperature sensors around a fouling wall conductance: the case of the twin benchmark,
where one sensor can be lost) and :func:`linear_reservoir` (the baseflow recession a river gauge follows).

**Data.** A simulated plant (the same model, with process noise, a known parameter drift and an injected sensor
spike: the truth is known, so every check can be scored), a CSV replay (columns ``t``, the inputs, the outputs), or
arrays (``{"t": [...], <input>: [...], <output>: [...]}``) from a live adapter (MQTT, OPC-UA, REST, a public gauge:
:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream`, the ``twin.connect`` node). A reading that did not arrive is
carried as a gap, never filled in: the members keep forecasting, nothing is assimilated, the drift chart does not
move, and a recalibration window that contains a gap is refused rather than fitted.

**Assimilation.** An ensemble Kalman filter of the states augmented with the logarithms of the slow parameters,
which follow a random walk (positive parameters, slow drift tracked): the deterministic ensemble transform analysis
(:func:`etkf_analysis`, default) or the stochastic one with perturbed observations (Burgers et al. 1998, through
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman.enkf_analysis`).

**Monitoring.**

* Innovation statistics. The normalised innovation squared ``NIS_k = v' S^-1 v`` (``S`` from the forecast ensemble
  plus the sensor variance) of a consistent filter is chi-square with ``m`` degrees of freedom, so the mean over
  ``n`` steps must sit inside the two-sided 95 % band ``chi2_{0.025, 0.975}(n m) / n`` (Bar-Shalom, Li &
  Kirubarajan 2001, *Estimation with Applications to Tracking and Navigation*, sec. 5.4). With a known truth the
  normalised estimation error squared (NEES) of the augmented state (states and log parameters: what the filter
  estimates) is tested over ``nees_runs`` independent simulated plants (estimation errors, unlike innovations, are
  correlated in time, so one run's time average is not chi-square): :func:`nees_monte_carlo`.
* Anomalies. A reading whose normalised innovation exceeds ``anomaly_z`` (default 4: two-sided p = 6e-5 per reading)
  is flagged and not assimilated (innovation gating); ``persist`` such readings in a row are a level change, not
  an outlier, and are assimilated again (the CUSUM sees every reading, its value clipped at ``anomaly_z``).
* Drift. A two-sided Page CUSUM (Page 1954, *Biometrika* 41:100) of the normalised innovations, reference ``k`` and
  threshold ``h``; its in-control average run length (Siegmund 1985 approximation) is reported, so the false-alarm
  rate is stated. An alarm triggers a **recalibration** through
  :func:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.workflow.inverse_workflow` on the next ``recalibration_window``
  readings (the slow parameters and the initial states of the window estimated, with identifiability, intervals and
  its own checks); the filter restarts from the recalibrated parameters (their interval as prior spread) and from the states that
  the recalibrated run reaches at the window's end. A recalibration whose fit fails (the model does not fit the
  window at the stated sensor noise, or the parameters are not identifiable) is refused and stated.

**Outputs.** A forecast of the outputs ``horizon`` steps ahead with the 90 % interval (members propagated with their
process noise and sensor noise), scored against the withheld future when the truth is known; what-if runs (the inputs
scaled or replaced) with the interval of each output's peak; a self-contained HTML dashboard.

classes.name: StateSpaceModel
classes.doc:
A discrete-time model for the twin. ``step(x (N, nx), u (nu,), theta (N, np), dt) -> (N, nx)`` and
``observe(x (N, nx), theta (N, np)) -> (N, ny)`` are batched over ensemble members.

classes.sig: (model: StateSpaceModel, *, members: int = 200, param_walk: float = 0.0002, param_spread: float = 0.1, x0: Sequence[float] | None = None, x0_std: Sequence[float] | None = None, inflation: float = 1.0, scheme: str = 'etkf', seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
Stochastic EnKF of ``[states, log(params)]``. One :meth:`step` per reading: forecast, innovation statistics,
gating, analysis.

methods.name: reset
methods.sig: (values: Sequence[float], std_log: Sequence[float], x: Sequence[float] | None = None, x_std: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> None
methods.doc: Restart the members at parameters ``values`` (log-normal spread ``std_log``) and, given, states ``x``.

methods.name: innovation
methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
``v``, ``S``, the NIS and the normalised innovations of one reading. ``mask`` selects the sensors that
reported (a lost, frozen or rejected reading is left out instead of being invented); the returned ``mean``
and ``std`` cover those sensors only.

methods.name: analyse
methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, hx: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray | None = None) -> None

functions.name: thermal_plant
functions.sig: (C: float = 20000.0, T_amb: float = 20.0, UA: float = 50.0) -> StateSpaceModel
functions.doc:
Lumped heated body (a tank, a casting, a cooled housing): ``C dT/dt = Q - UA (T - T_amb)``, ``C`` in J/K,
``UA`` in W/K, ``Q`` in W. Exact discretisation for ``Q`` held over the step:
``T' = T_inf + (T - T_inf) exp(-UA dt / C)`` with ``T_inf = T_amb + Q / UA``.

functions.name: heated_channel
functions.sig: (C1: float = 1200.0, C2: float = 2400.0, H: float = 40.0, UA: float = 3.0, T_amb: float = 20.0, Q_nominal: float = 1500.0) -> StateSpaceModel
functions.doc:
A heated channel with two temperature sensors (#57's twin case): an upstream node taking the heater power and
a downstream node losing heat to the ambient, coupled by the wall conductance ``H``::

    C1 dT1/dt = Q - UA (T1 - T_amb) - H (T1 - T2)
    C2 dT2/dt =            H (T1 - T2) - UA (T2 - T_amb)

``H`` is the slow parameter (fouling of the channel walls lowers it). Two outputs, so a reading can be lost,
frozen or biased on one sensor and the other still reports: the case the twin benchmark scores. Explicit Euler,
the smallest time constant being ``C1 / (UA + H)`` = 28 s against ``dt`` = 1 s.

functions.name: linear_reservoir
functions.sig: (k_per_hour: float = 0.0035, q_reference: float = 1000.0, sensor_std: float | None = None, process_std: float | None = None) -> StateSpaceModel
functions.doc:
A linear reservoir (first-order storage; the baseflow-recession model of hydrograph analysis)::

    dQ/dt = -k (Q - Q_base)      exactly:  Q' = Q_base + (Q - Q_base) exp(-k dt)

``k`` (1/h) is the slow parameter and ``Q_base`` the known inflow, so the twin assimilates a river gauge
(:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.usgs`) with the same filter, alarms and recalibration as the thermal
cases. ``dt`` is in hours. The reading uncertainty of a gauge is not published per sample, so ``sensor_std``
is a stated assumption (2 % of ``q_reference`` by default), not a measurement: the benchmark's noise sweep
shows what it changes. The process noise is small (0.05 % per step) because the unmeasured inflow varies over
hours, not samples; a twin that cannot fit the recession shows it as a NIS above its band, which is the honest
reading of a model that does not describe the river.

functions.name: resolve_model
functions.sig: (model: str | StateSpaceModel | Callable[..., StateSpaceModel], model_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> StateSpaceModel
functions.doc: A model by name (:data:`MODELS`), a ``module:function`` returning a :class:`StateSpaceModel`, or one.

functions.name: square_wave
functions.sig: (n: int, dt: float, low: float, high: float, period: float) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: simulate_plant
functions.sig: (model: StateSpaceModel, *, n_steps: int = 400, dt: float = 5.0, inputs: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None, drift: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, spike: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, horizon: int = 0, plant_params: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A simulated sensor stream of ``model`` with its process and sensor noise; the plant's parameters are
``plant_params`` (default: the model's nominal values; a twin is never commissioned exactly). ``drift``: ``{param, at (step),
to (value), ramp (steps, 0: a step change)}``; ``spike``: ``{at, size (in sensor sigmas)}``. ``horizon`` more
steps are simulated and withheld (the future the forecast is scored on). Returns the record and the truth.

functions.name: read_csv_record
functions.sig: (path: str, model: StateSpaceModel) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: CSV replay: columns ``t``, the model's inputs and outputs (a header row).

functions.name: chi2_band_total
functions.sig: (dof_total: int, n: int, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
Two-sided band of the mean of ``n`` readings whose normalised innovation squares add up to a chi-square with
``dof_total`` degrees of freedom: the general case, when some readings carry fewer sensors than others (the sum
of independent NIS is chi-square with the summed degrees of freedom, and the mean over ``n`` readings is that
divided by ``n``).

functions.name: chi2_band
functions.sig: (dof: int, n: int, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: Two-sided band of the mean of ``n`` independent chi-square(dof) values.

functions.name: cusum_arl0
functions.sig: (k: float, h: float) -> float
functions.doc:
In-control average run length of a two-sided CUSUM of N(0, 1) values (Siegmund 1985 approximation of each
one-sided chart, combined as 1/ARL = 1/ARL+ + 1/ARL-).

functions.name: etkf_analysis
functions.sig: (ens: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, hx: np.ndarray, r_var: np.ndarray, *, inflation: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Ensemble transform Kalman filter analysis (Bishop, Etherton & Majumdar 2001; the symmetric square root of
Hunt, Kostelich & Szunyogh 2007, *Physica D* 230:112): deterministic, so the analysis spread carries no
perturbed-observation sampling noise. ``ens`` (N, n), ``hx`` (N, m), independent sensor variances ``r_var``.

functions.name: nees_monte_carlo
functions.sig: (model: StateSpaceModel, plant_params: Mapping[str, float], U: np.ndarray, dt: float, *, runs: int = 20, members: int = 200, param_walk: float = 0.0002, burn: int = 20, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
NEES consistency over independent plants (Bar-Shalom et al. 2001, sec. 5.4.2): ``runs`` plants with fresh
noise and the inputs ``U``; at each step the NEES averaged over the runs is chi-square(runs * d) / runs. Returns
the fraction of the steps inside the two-sided 95 % band (about 95 % for a consistent filter).

functions.name: recalibrate
functions.sig: (model: StateSpaceModel, U: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, dt: float, *, x_start: Sequence[float], theta_start: Sequence[float], bootstrap: int = 30, n_recovery: int = 8, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The inverse workflow on one window of readings: the slow parameters and the window's initial states.

functions.sig: (*, model: str | StateSpaceModel = 'thermal_plant', model_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, source: str = 'simulated', data: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, csv_path: str | None = None, n_steps: int = 400, dt: float = 5.0, drift: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, spike: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, plant_params: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, members: int = 200, param_walk: float...
functions.doc:
Run the twin over the record; returns the traces, the events, the recalibrations, the forecast, the what-if
runs and the checks (``pass`` / ``fail`` / ``inconclusive``; the truth-scored ones only on a simulated plant).

functions.name: write_dashboard
functions.sig: (r: Mapping[str, Any], out_dir: str) -> str
functions.doc:
A self-contained HTML page: measured output with the twin's band, the parameter with its 90 % band (and the
truth), NIS with its band, the CUSUM with its threshold, the forecast and the what-if table, the checks.

children.doc:
pinneapple_digital_twin — Digital twins built on top of pinneapple surrogate models.

Key capabilities
----------------
- Wrap any trained model (PINN, GNN, DeepONet, FNO, …) as a digital twin.
- Ingest real-time sensor data from MQTT, Kafka, REST APIs, files, or mocks.
- Fuse predictions with observations using Kalman-family filters (EKF, EnKF).
- Detect anomalies via threshold, z-score, and Mahalanobis distance checks.
- Maintain rolling history of state estimates.
- Callback hooks for custom monitoring / dashboards.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin import DigitalTwin, build_digital_twin
>>> from pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io import MockStream
>>> import numpy as np

>>> model = ...  # your trained surrogate model
>>> dt = build_digital_twin(model, field_names=["u", "v", "p"])
>>> stream = MockStream(
...     "inlet", ["u", "v"],
...     lambda t: {"u": 1.0 + 0.1 * np.sin(t), "v": 0.0},
...     coords={"x": 0.0, "y": 0.5},
... )
>>> dt.add_stream(stream)
>>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
>>> y = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
>>> xx, yy = np.meshgrid(x, y)
>>> dt.set_domain_coords({"x": xx.ravel(), "y": yy.ravel()})
>>> with dt:
...     import time; time.sleep(5)   # twin runs for 5 s
... print(dt.state.fields["u"].mean())

children.name: pinneapple_systems.excitation
children.doc:
Actuator excitation signals for system identification and surrogate training (numpy).

Every ``shape_*`` function maps normalised time ``tau`` in ``[0, 1]`` (an array) to a signal in ``[0, 1]``;
:func:`actuator_series` scales one to ``[lo, hi]`` and optionally rate-limits it with :func:`rate_limit`.
Random shapes take an ``rng`` (``numpy.random.Generator``) so a seed reproduces the signal.

Families: step, ramp, sinusoid, piecewise constant (random staircase), PRBS (pseudo-random binary sequence),
linear chirp, sawtooth, smoothed random walk, Gaussian bumps and an amplitude-modulated two-tone. Persistently
exciting inputs (PRBS, chirp/swept sine) are the standard identification signals of Ljung, *System Identification:
Theory for the User*, 2nd ed., Prentice Hall (1999), ch. 13.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_systems.excitation import actuator_series
    >>> u = actuator_series("prbs", 500, lo=0.75, hi=1.25, seed=3, dwell=0.05)
    >>> set(np.unique(u)) <= {0.75, 1.25}
    True

functions.name: shape_step
functions.doc: Unit step at ``tau = t0``.

functions.name: shape_ramp
functions.doc: Linear ramp from 0 at ``tau = 0`` to 1 at ``tau = t1``, then held.

functions.name: shape_sinusoid
functions.sig: (tau, freq = 2.0, phase = 0.0, **_)
functions.doc: ``0.5 + 0.5 sin(2 pi freq tau + phase)`` (``freq`` in cycles per unit ``tau``).

functions.name: shape_piecewise_constant
functions.sig: (tau, rng = None, n_seg = 5, **_)
functions.doc: Random staircase: ``n_seg`` levels ~ U(0, 1) between sorted random edges in ``[0.05, 0.95]``.

functions.name: shape_prbs
functions.sig: (tau, rng = None, dwell = 0.08, **_)
functions.doc:
Pseudo-random binary sequence in ``{0, 1}``.

The clock period is ``hold = max(1, round(dwell * len(tau)))`` samples; at every clock tick (sample index a
multiple of ``hold``) the level is redrawn by an independent fair coin flip, so it can only change on the clock.

functions.name: shape_chirp
functions.doc:
Linear chirp ``0.5 + 0.5 sin(phi)``, instantaneous frequency ``f0 + (f1 - f0) tau`` (cycles per unit tau).

Equals ``0.5 + 0.5 * scipy.signal.chirp(tau, f0, 1, f1, method="linear", phi=-90)``.

functions.name: shape_sawtooth
functions.doc: Rising sawtooth ``(freq * tau) mod 1``.

functions.name: shape_smoothed_random_walk
functions.sig: (tau, rng = None, **_)
functions.doc: Gaussian random walk smoothed by a 15-sample moving average, rescaled to ``[0, 1]``.

functions.name: shape_gaussian_bumps
functions.sig: (tau, rng = None, n_bumps = 4, width = 0.05, **_)
functions.doc: Sum of ``n_bumps`` Gaussians (centres ~ U(0.1, 0.9), amplitudes ~ U(0.5, 1), std ``width``), peak-normalised.

functions.name: shape_am_two_tone
functions.sig: (tau, f_carrier = 5.0, f_mod = 0.7, **_)
functions.doc: Amplitude modulation: ``(0.5 + 0.5 sin 2 pi f_carrier tau) (0.5 + 0.5 sin 2 pi f_mod tau)``.

functions.name: rate_limit
functions.sig: (series: np.ndarray, tau_steps: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
First-order low-pass ``y[i] = y[i-1] + (x[i] - y[i-1]) / tau_steps`` (time constant ``tau_steps`` samples).

Models an actuator lag: the output moves at most ``|x[i] - y[i-1]| / tau_steps`` per sample and never
overshoots the input range. ``tau_steps <= 1`` returns the input unchanged.

functions.name: actuator_series
functions.sig: (shape: str | Callable[..., np.ndarray], n_steps: int, *, lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0, seed: int = 0, rate_limit_steps: float = 0, **kwargs) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Sample one excitation on ``n_steps`` uniform points of ``tau`` in ``[0, 1]``, scaled to ``[lo, hi]``.

``shape`` is a key of :data:`SHAPES` or a callable ``f(tau, rng=..., **kwargs) -> [0, 1]``; ``seed`` seeds the
``rng`` of the random families; ``rate_limit_steps > 1`` applies :func:`rate_limit`. Returns ``(n_steps,)`` float64.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.operations
pinneapple_systems.operations.anomaly
children.doc:
Physics anomaly detection on sensor time series: statistics, time-series models, conservation balances and
physical-model residuals, fused into events with severities and verifiable explanations.

Four families of detectors, all calibrated on a window the user declares normal (never on the data being judged):

``statistical``   per sensor, robust z-score of the value and of its rate of change against the normal window
                  (median / MAD; Rousseeuw & Croux 1993);
``timeseries``    per sensor, an autoregressive model AR(p) of the first difference fitted on the normal window;
                  one-step residuals feed a two-sided CUSUM (Page 1954) that catches slow drifts;
``balance``       conservation laws written as formulas over the columns (:class:`BalanceRule`): over a trailing
                  window ``W``, ``[Acc(t) - Acc(t - W)] / W - mean(inflow - outflow)``; a broken balance says *which*
                  law failed and *by how much* in its own units;
``model``         a physical reference model with ``step(x, v)`` (e.g. the lumped tank or a reduced model) predicts
                  each state one step ahead from the measured state and inputs; the windowed prediction error is the
                  residual.

A sample is flagged when a detector's score (residual / its normal-window spread) exceeds ``threshold``; flags
closer than ``merge_gap`` samples are merged into events, events shorter than ``min_samples`` are dropped.

:func:`fault_benchmark` builds labelled runs of the heated tank with known faults and :func:`score_events`
reports point-wise and event-wise precision / recall, false alarms and detection delays.

classes.name: BalanceRule
classes.doc:
A conservation law over the columns: ``d(accumulation)/dt = inflow - outflow``.

Each field is a formula over column names and ``constants`` (``+ - * / **``, ``sqrt``, ``exp``, ``log``, ...,
evaluated safely, no Python ``eval``). ``units`` names the units of the rate (e.g. ``m3/s``, ``W``).

classes.name: DetectorConfig
classes.doc: What to run and how strict to be. ``normal_until`` (time, same units as ``t``) ends the normal window.

methods.name: from_dict
methods.doc: Build from a JSON object (balances as a list of objects); unknown keys are an error.

classes.name: Channel
classes.doc: One detector output: a residual series, its normal-window centre/spread and score = (r - centre) / spread.

classes.name: LabelledInterval
classes.doc: A labelled abnormal interval ``[start, end)`` read from data (same interface as a plant ``Fault``).

functions.name: tank_balance_rules
functions.sig: () -> list[BalanceRule]
functions.doc: Mass and energy balances of the heated tank (:mod:`pinneapple_systems.operations.plant`).

functions.name: tank_constants
functions.sig: (p: TankParams | None = None) -> dict[str, float]

functions.name: windowed_balance
functions.sig: (t, acc, net_in, w: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``[acc(t_k) - acc(t_{k-w})] / (t_k - t_{k-w}) - (trapezoid mean of net_in over the same interval)``.

functions.name: severity_of
functions.sig: (ratio: float) -> str
functions.doc: Severity from the peak score / threshold ratio: < 2 low, < 4 medium, < 8 high, else critical.

functions.name: detect
functions.sig: (data, config: DetectorConfig, model = None, model_states: Sequence[str] = (), model_inputs: Sequence[str] = ()) -> DetectionResult
functions.doc: Run the configured detectors on ``data`` (DataFrame or dict of columns with ``t``).

functions.name: benchmark_faults
functions.sig: (t0: float = 7200.0) -> list[Fault]
functions.doc:
The faults of :func:`fault_benchmark`, after a fault-free first ``t0`` seconds (the calibration window).
Magnitudes are small on purpose (a few percent of the nominal flows and powers).

functions.name: fault_benchmark
functions.sig: (seed: int = 0, t0: float = 7200.0, dt: float = 10.0) -> tuple[dict[str, np.ndarray], list[Fault]]
functions.doc:
One labelled run: ``t0`` s of normal operation, then the six faults of :func:`benchmark_faults` separated by
normal periods. Different ``seed`` = different operating profile and noise (a held-out run).

functions.name: intervals_from_labels
functions.sig: (t, labels) -> list[LabelledInterval]
functions.doc:
Contiguous runs of a label column: empty, ``0``, ``normal`` or ``false`` mean normal, anything else names
the anomaly. Each run ends at the next sample's time.

functions.name: score_events
functions.sig: (result: DetectionResult, faults: Sequence[Fault], grace: float = 600.0, evaluate_from: float | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Point-wise and event-wise scores against the true fault intervals.

Point-wise: a sample is positive when a fault is active; predictions are the flagged samples. Event-wise: a
fault is detected when an event overlaps ``[start, end + grace]`` (the grace covers windowed detectors that
lag); an event overlapping no fault (with grace) is a false alarm. Only samples after ``evaluate_from``
(default: the end of the calibration window) count.

functions.name: run_benchmark
functions.sig: (seeds: Sequence[int] = (101, 102, 103), methods_sets: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] | None = None, window: int = 12, threshold: float = 5.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Score each detector family alone and all together on held-out labelled runs (one per seed). The
calibration window of every run is its own fault-free first two hours; thresholds are never tuned on the
faulty part. Returns per-method aggregate scores (sums of TP/FP/FN over runs) and per-run details.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.operations.control
children.doc:
Physics-based control of the heated tank: model predictive control against PID and rule-based baselines, in
closed loop on the same simulated plant, in simulation / recommendation mode only.

Controllers (all expose ``act(t, reading, estimate) -> (u, info)``):

``PIDBaseline``        two decoupled loops (level -> pump flow, temperature -> heater power) with feed-forward
                       bias, saturation and anti-windup (:class:`~pinneapple_systems.component_modeling.control.PIDController`);
``RuleBasedBaseline``  what many plants run today: hysteresis bands that switch the pump between two rates and the
                       heater between off and a high power;
``LinearMPC``          successive linearisation of the tank's balances at every step, zero-order-hold
                       discretisation (matrix exponential), a quadratic program over the horizon solved with SLSQP
                       (hard actuator and rate limits, soft output constraints);
``NonlinearMPC``       the full nonlinear balances over the horizon: CasADi + IPOPT with multiple shooting when
                       CasADi is installed, otherwise single shooting with SciPy's SLSQP and batched finite-difference
                       gradients. ``model=`` may be any model with ``step(x, v)`` -- e.g. a reduced-order surrogate --
                       which then runs through the SciPy path.

The MPCs act on the state estimated by a :class:`~pinneapple_systems.operations.twin.TwinRuntime` (ensemble Kalman
filter with an unaccounted outflow and a heater efficiency in the state), which is what makes them offset-free
under unmeasured disturbances. :func:`run_closed_loop` simulates one controller on a :class:`ControlScenario` and
:func:`compare_controllers` runs several on identical scenarios (same noise, same disturbances) and tabulates
tracking error, constraint violations, energy, actuator travel and solve time.

There is deliberately no path from these controllers to real equipment: :func:`recommend` returns proposed actions
and their predicted consequences for a person to review.

classes.name: ControlSpec
classes.doc:
Objectives, constraints and actuator limits.

``setpoints`` is a list of ``(time, h_ref, T_ref)`` steps. Tracking errors are normalised by ``h_scale`` and
``T_scale``; ``w_energy`` prices heater power (per unit of ``Q / Q_max`` and step), ``w_move`` actuator moves.
Output constraints are soft (penalty ``w_constraint`` per normalised violation squared) so that a disturbance
beyond the actuators' reach degrades gracefully instead of making the problem infeasible.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.operations.exchanger
children.doc:
A counterflow water/water heat exchanger with fouling — the plant a twin is built for.

The model is the exchanger's own effectiveness-NTU solution. What it cannot know is the
fouling resistance: it is not an input anybody measures, it builds up over months, and it is
the number that decides when the exchanger is cleaned. That makes the exchanger the reference
asset for the twin commissioning layer in
:mod:`pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.product`, where the fouling resistance is the latent
state the ensemble Kalman filter has to recover.

Two callables, deliberately different:

* :func:`exchanger_model` is what a twin is given — ``model(X, theta)``, the clean rating plus
  the fouling resistance in ``theta``;
* :func:`plant_outlets` is the plant — the model plus a few percent of flow-dependent UA that
  the model does not know. Without that gap a twin would be right by construction and the
  coverage check would mean nothing.

:func:`generate_history` produces a deterministic, clearly synthetic plant history so the
commissioning layer can be exercised end to end without an exchanger. The fouling trajectory
is an asymptotic (Kern-Seaton style) curve and the constants are ordinary engineering values
for a shell-and-tube water exchanger — this is not a lab dataset.

``X`` columns, in the order the spec declares: ``position, T_hi, T_ci, m_h, m_c``.
``theta[0]`` is the fouling resistance in m2 K/W.

``LiveTwin`` wires the pieces the twin app needs and nothing else:

* a source -- the built-in simulated heated tank publishing JSON readings to an MQTT topic (through the embedded
  broker or an external one), REST pushes (:meth:`LiveTwin.push`), or an OPC UA server polled by
  :class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream.OPCUAStream` (experimental, needs ``asyncua``);
* a consumer thread that subscribes with :class:`~pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.io.stream.MQTTStream` and feeds
  every reading to the twin, which writes its history to a :class:`~.twin.TwinStore`.

Simulated time runs ``speed`` times faster than the wall clock so a demo shows an hour of plant in a minute.
:func:`replay` runs the same twin over a recorded table (CSV / Parquet / JSON) in one go.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.operations.plant
children.doc:
Heated buffer tank: a lumped (0-D) plant with a mass and an energy balance, its sensors and its faults.

One plant shared by the operations tools (digital twin runtime, physics anomaly detection, physics-based
control), so a twin's state estimate, an anomaly detector's balances and a controller's model all describe the
same equations and can be checked against each other.

Model (states ``h`` liquid level [m], ``T`` liquid temperature [degC]; inputs ``q_in`` pump inflow [m3/s],
``Q`` heater power [W]; disturbances ``T_in`` inlet temperature, ``T_amb`` ambient temperature, ``q_leak`` an
unmeasured outflow)::

    q_out        = k_out * sqrt(h)                                   (gravity drain through a fixed valve)
    A dh/dt      = q_in - q_out - q_leak                             (mass balance, constant density)
    A h dT/dt    = q_in (T_in - T) + (eta Q - UA (T - T_amb)) / (rho cp)
                                                                      (energy balance, perfectly mixed)

The energy equation is the product rule applied to ``d(rho cp A h T)/dt = rho cp (q_in T_in - (q_out + q_leak) T)
+ eta Q - UA (T - T_amb)`` with the mass balance substituted, so both balances in their conservative form hold
exactly for a fault-free plant; :func:`mass_balance_residual` and :func:`energy_balance_residual` evaluate them
from measured signals.

Faults (each with a start and end time) change the *plant* or the *sensors*, never the equations used by the
detectors: ``leak`` (unmeasured outflow), ``heater`` (efficiency ``eta`` drops), ``sensor_bias`` (a constant
offset on one sensor), ``sensor_drift`` (a ramp on one sensor), ``stuck_sensor`` (a sensor freezes) and ``valve``
(the drain valve partially closes: ``k_out`` scaled).

than the measured power says), a leak makes it equal to ``-rho cp q_leak T``.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.operations.rom
children.doc:
Operator inference with inputs: a discrete-time polynomial reduced model fitted by ridge regression.

``pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.OperatorInference`` learns autonomous latent dynamics. Operating assets
are driven by inputs (pumps, heaters, valves) and disturbances, so this variant adds them (Peherstorfer & Willcox
2016, "Data-driven operator inference for nonintrusive projection-based model reduction", CMAME 306, sec. 3.3)::

    x_{k+1} = x_k + dt * ( c + A x_k + H (x_k (x) x_k) + B v_k + N (x_k (x) v_k) )

with ``v = [inputs, disturbances]``, all variables scaled to zero mean / unit spread on the training data.
The model is a few matrices: it serialises to JSON, runs in microseconds and is what the digital twin and the
controller can use as a surrogate of an expensive plant model.

Validation is part of the fit: :func:`fit_controlled_opinf` holds out whole trajectories (not random samples)
and reports one-step and full-rollout errors on them, plus the training box of every variable.

classes.doc: A fitted model; build it with :func:`fit_controlled_opinf` or :meth:`from_dict`.

methods.doc: One step of ``dt`` seconds from state(s) ``x`` (n,) or (N, n) with inputs ``v`` (m,) or (N, m).

methods.doc: The same step on CasADi symbols (column vectors), for optimisation with IPOPT.

functions.doc:
Fit on all but the last ``holdout`` trajectories and validate on those.

Each trajectory is a dict of equally spaced columns (spacing ``dt``) containing ``state_names`` and
``input_names``. The returned model's ``validation`` holds, per state, the one-step and rollout RMSE on the
held-out trajectories (absolute, and relative to the state's spread), and ``bounds`` the training box.

functions.doc:
One-step residual standard deviation per state on ``trajectories`` (use held-out ones): the process noise
a filter running this model should assume.
