Refit ``name`` (its first grid configuration) on data whose labels end before ``event_start`` and forecast
from ``origins`` (for an event inside the development period, e.g. 1997/98, so no forecast uses a model that saw
it). Returns the forecasts and the fitted model's description.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab
pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.base
children.doc:
Common interface of the forecasters in :mod:`pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab`.

A forecaster sees a :class:`SeriesData` (the observed array, which column is the target, the sampling step) and
makes direct multi-horizon forecasts from *origins*: a forecast from origin ``t`` may use ``obs[: t + 1]`` only and
predicts the target at ``t + h`` for every ``h`` in ``horizons``.

``fit(data, train_origins, val_origins, horizons)`` receives the origins of the training samples and of the
validation block. The labels of a training origin reach ``t + max(horizons)``, so the data a forecaster may use for
fitting end at ``train_end(train_origins, horizons)``; models fitted on a contiguous segment (physical models,
ARIMA, filters) use exactly that segment, window models use the samples. The validation block is used for early
stopping and to calibrate the predictive spread (:meth:`Forecaster.calibrate`): a point forecaster gets a Gaussian
predictive distribution whose standard deviation at each horizon is the root-mean-square error on the validation
block. Nothing after the validation block is ever passed to ``fit``.

classes.name: SeriesData
classes.doc: Observed series (T, d), the forecast target column, the sampling step and free-form metadata.

classes.name: Forecast
classes.doc:
Predictive distribution at (origin, horizon): a mean, and either a Gaussian ``std`` or ``samples``
(members, origins, horizons).

methods.name: coverage
methods.doc: Per-horizon fraction of targets inside the central ``level`` interval.

classes.name: Forecaster
classes.doc: Base class: subclasses implement :meth:`_fit` and :meth:`_predict_mean` (or override :meth:`predict`).

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (data: SeriesData, train_origins, val_origins = None, horizons: Sequence[int] = (1,)) -> Forecaster

methods.name: calibrate
methods.doc: Gaussian spread per horizon = RMSE on ``origins`` (the validation block when there is one).

functions.name: train_end
functions.sig: (train_origins, horizons) -> int
functions.doc: Exclusive end index of the data that a fit on these origins may use.

functions.name: forecast_origins
functions.sig: (lo: int, hi: int, horizons, *, stride: int = 1, min_history: int = 0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Origins t with lo <= t, t >= min_history - 1 and t + max(h) < hi, every ``stride`` samples.

functions.name: targets_at
functions.sig: (data: SeriesData, origins, horizons) -> np.ndarray

children.summary: Common interface of the forecasters in pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.baselines
children.doc:
Baselines every other forecaster must beat: persistence, climatology, AR(p), ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and
for (near-)periodic series the seasonal-naive forecast and a phase-aligned mean cycle.

classes.name: Persistence
classes.doc: y_{t+h} = y_t (the random-walk forecast).

classes.name: Climatology
classes.doc: y_{t+h} = mean of the training segment, spread = its standard deviation.

classes.name: ARForecaster
classes.sig: (max_order: int = 20, criterion: str = 'aic', difference: bool = False)
classes.doc: Least-squares AR(p) on the target, order by AIC up to ``max_order``, iterated to each horizon.

classes.name: ARIMAForecaster
classes.sig: (p: Sequence[int] = (0, 1, 2), d: Sequence[int] = (0, 1), q: Sequence[int] = (0, 1), max_fit_length: int = 2000)
classes.doc:
ARIMA(p, d, q) (statsmodels SARIMAX), order by AIC over a small grid on the training segment; forecasts
from every origin with the fitted parameters fixed, through the Kalman filter state at that origin (so a
forecast uses data up to its origin only). The Gaussian predictive variance comes from the state space.

classes.name: ExponentialSmoothing
classes.doc:
Simple exponential smoothing l_t = alpha y_t + (1 - alpha) l_{t-1}, flat forecast l_t; alpha minimises the
one-step squared error on the training segment.

classes.name: SeasonalNaive
classes.sig: (period: float | None = None)
classes.doc:
y_{t+h} = y_{t+h-kP} with k = ceil(h / P): the value one period (or the fewest whole periods) before the
target. ``period`` in samples; by default the dominant period of the training segment (rounded to an integer
number of samples).

classes.name: PhaseClimatology
classes.sig: (period: float | None = None, fit_cycles: float = 1.0)
classes.doc:
The mean cycle, aligned to the phase of each origin.

The training segment is folded at the (possibly non-integer) period P into ``round(P)`` phase bins to give a
mean cycle. At each origin the phase is re-estimated: the cycle offset that best fits the last
``fit_cycles`` periods of observations in least squares (with a free mean) is taken, and the forecast is the
mean cycle continued from there. A near-periodic series whose phase drifts is thus followed; the amplitude and
shape are those of the average training cycle.

functions.name: dominant_period
functions.sig: (y, min_period: float = 2.0, max_frac: float = 0.25) -> float
functions.doc:
Period (in samples) of the highest periodogram peak of ``y`` after removing the mean and a linear trend,
searched between ``min_period`` samples and ``max_frac`` of the series length.

children.summary: Baselines every other forecaster must beat: persistence, climatology, AR(p), ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and for (near-)periodic series the seasonal-naive forecast and a phase-aligned mean cycle.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.hybrid
children.doc:
Hybrid forecasters: a physical model plus something learned.

* :class:`ResidualCorrectionForecaster` -- physics forecast + statistical error correction: a gradient-boosting
  model (or MLP) learns y_{t+h} - physics_{t+h} from the lagged observations and the physical forecast itself.
* :class:`UDEForecaster` -- universal differential equation (Rackauckas et al. 2020, arXiv:2001.04385):
  dx/dt = f_known(x; theta) + g_NN(x), with theta estimated first by an :class:`ODEForecaster` on the training data
  and the neural closure g trained through the RK4 integrator on short windows of the training trajectory
  (multiple shooting). The SDE counterpart (drift closure) is
  :class:`~pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.physical.SDEDriftForecaster` with ``closure=...``.

classes.name: ResidualCorrectionForecaster
classes.sig: (physical: Forecaster, corrector: str = 'gbm', n_lags: int = 8, lag_step: int = 1, max_iter: int = 200, learning_rate: float = 0.05, max_leaf_nodes: int = 15, min_samples_leaf: int = 20, hidden: int = 64, layers: int = 2, epochs: int = 100, patience: int | None = 10, weight_decay: float = 0.0001, seed: int = 0, name: str | None = None)
classes.doc: physical forecast + corrector(lags, physical forecast). ``corrector`` is ``"gbm"`` or ``"mlp"``.

classes.name: UDEForecaster
classes.sig: (physical: ODEForecaster, hidden: int = 64, layers: int = 2, window: int = 4, epochs: int = 200, patience: int | None = 20, lr: float = 0.001, weight_decay: float = 1e-05, batch_size: int = 128, max_windows: int = 3000, seed: int = 0, divergence_factor: float = 5.0, name: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
dx/dt = f_known(x; theta_hat) + s * g_NN((x - mu) / sd), trained through RK4 over ``window`` samples.

``physical`` is an (unfitted) :class:`ODEForecaster` with the known, possibly incomplete, vector field; its
parameters are estimated first and kept fixed while the closure is trained (early stopping on windows from the
validation block). ``s`` is the per-variable standard deviation of the known model's one-step derivative
residual, so the closure starts at the scale of what is missing.

children.summary: Hybrid forecasters: a physical model plus something learned.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.learned
children.doc:
Data-driven direct forecasters on lagged windows: gradient boosting and neural networks (MLP, LSTM, TCN,
transformer), with optional physics-derived input features and, for the MLP, a physics residual penalty.

All of them predict the change of the target from the origin, y_{t+h} - y_t, standardised per horizon, from a
window of the last ``n_lags`` observations (every ``lag_step`` samples) of the observed columns. Predicting the
change keeps persistence as the zero output, so an untrained or over-regularised model falls back to the random-
walk forecast instead of to a constant.

Neural networks are trained with :class:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer` (Adam, weight decay), early stopping on
the validation block with the best weights restored, and an optional ensemble of ``n_members`` seeds whose mean
is the forecast.

classes.name: LagFeatures
classes.sig: (n_lags: int = 8, lag_step: int = 1, cols: list[int] | None = None, extra: Callable | None = None)
classes.doc:
Lagged windows of the observed columns, plus optional extra features ``extra(data, origins) -> (n, k)``.

An ``extra`` object with a ``fit(data, train_origins, horizons)`` method is fitted on the training origins
first (physics features whose parameters are estimated from the training data only).

classes.name: GBMForecaster
classes.sig: (n_lags: int = 8, lag_step: int = 1, max_iter: int = 200, learning_rate: float = 0.05, max_leaf_nodes: int = 15, min_samples_leaf: int = 20, l2: float = 0.0, features: Callable | None = None, cols = None, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None, seed: int = 0)
classes.doc:
Histogram gradient boosting (scikit-learn), one regressor per horizon, on lag features.

scikit-learn's own early stopping holds out a *random* fraction of the training rows, which leaks across time
on serial data, so it is switched off; the number of boosting rounds is a hyperparameter for the purged
walk-forward search instead.

classes.name: NeuralForecaster
classes.sig: (arch: str = 'mlp', n_lags: int = 16, lag_step: int = 1, hidden: int = 64, layers: int = 2, dropout: float = 0.0, weight_decay: float = 0.0, lr: float = 0.001, epochs: int = 100, patience: int | None = 10, batch_size: int = 128, n_members: int = 1, seed: int = 0, features: Callable | None = None, cols = None, max_train: int | None = None, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
Direct multi-horizon neural forecaster: ``arch`` in {"mlp", "lstm", "tcn", "transformer"}.

The MLP sees the flattened standardised window (plus any extra features); the sequence models see the window
as a sequence (L, d). ``n_members`` > 1 trains an ensemble from different seeds and averages it.

classes.name: PhysicsLossMLP
classes.sig: (physical, lam: float = 0.1, **kw)
classes.doc:
MLP that predicts the whole observed state at every step 1..max(h) and is penalised for violating a known
vector field: loss = MSE + ``lam`` * mean |(X_{k+1} - X_k) / dt - f((X_{k+1} + X_k) / 2)|^2 / scale^2 along the
predicted path (implicit-midpoint residual, second order in dt; X_0 is the observed state at the origin).

``physical`` is an :class:`~pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.physical.ODEForecaster` (not yet
fitted): its parameters are estimated on the same training origins and its vector field (torch) is the
constraint. Requires every state variable to be observed. ``lam = 0`` is the same network without the penalty.

functions.name: train_torch_regressor
functions.sig: (build: Callable[[], Any], X_tr, Y_tr, X_va = None, Y_va = None, *, epochs: int = 100, lr: float = 0.001, weight_decay: float = 0.0, batch_size: int = 128, patience: int | None = 10, seed: int = 0, loss_fn: Callable | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Train ``build()`` on (X, Y) with :class:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer`.

With ``patience`` (and a validation set) training stops when the validation loss has not improved for that
many epochs and the best weights are restored; ``patience=None`` trains the full ``epochs`` and keeps the last
weights. Returns the model and the history (train / validation loss per epoch).

children.summary: Data-driven direct forecasters on lagged windows: gradient boosting and neural networks (MLP, LSTM, TCN, transformer), with optional physics-derived input features and, for the MLP, a physics ...

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.physical
children.doc:
Physical forecasters: the governing equations with parameters estimated from the training data only.

* :class:`ODEForecaster` -- an ODE whose state is fully observed; parameters by least squares on short
  (multiple-shooting) predictions from the observed training states; forecasts integrate from the observed state
  at the origin. Pass a wrong vector field to measure a misspecified model.
* :class:`DelayODEForecaster` -- a delay differential equation dx/dt = f(x, x(t - tau)) of a scalar series
  (Mackey-Glass), integrated by the method of steps from the interpolated observed history.
* :class:`LinearSSMForecaster` -- linear stochastic models sampled exactly: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and the
  noise-driven damped oscillator, with observation noise. Parameters by maximum likelihood through the Kalman
  filter; forecasts are the exact Gaussian predictive distribution from the filtered state at the origin (data
  assimilation of a linear model).
* :class:`SDEDriftForecaster` -- dx = f(x) dt + sigma dW with f in a polynomial basis, estimated by regressing the
  increments on the basis (first Kramers-Moyal coefficient; Friedrich et al. 2011, Phys. Rep. 506:87);
  Euler-Maruyama ensemble forecasts. An optional neural closure of the drift makes it a hybrid.
* :class:`EnKFForecaster` -- ensemble Kalman filter (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman.
  EnsembleKalmanFilter`) with a fitted :class:`ODEForecaster` as the model; forecast ensembles start from the
  analysis ensemble at each origin.
* :class:`SINDyForecaster` -- equations discovered by sparse regression (:class:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.
  rom.sindy.SINDy`) on the training trajectory.

Forecasts that leave the range of the training data by more than ``divergence_factor`` training standard
deviations (or are not finite) are counted in ``info["diverged_fraction"]`` and replaced by the training mean; the
fraction is reported with the scores, so a model that blows up is visible rather than silently clipped.

classes.name: ODEForecaster
classes.sig: (rhs: Callable, params: dict[str, float], fit_params: Sequence[str] | None = None, sub: int = 5, fit_steps: int = 2, max_fit_origins: int = 1500, divergence_factor: float = 5.0, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
dx/dt = rhs(x, **params) with every state variable observed (the columns of ``data.obs``).

``params`` are the initial guesses; the names in ``fit_params`` are estimated (the rest stay fixed) by
minimising the standardised error of RK4 predictions ``fit_steps`` samples ahead from the observed states at
up to ``max_fit_origins`` training origins.

methods.name: integrate
methods.sig: (x0: np.ndarray, n_samples: int, dt: float, params = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: States after 1..n_samples sampling intervals from x0 (B, d): returns (B, n_samples, d).

methods.name: physics_features
methods.doc: The fitted vector field at the observed state at the origin, times dt.

classes.name: DelayODEForecaster
classes.sig: (rhs: Callable, params: dict[str, float], tau: float, fit_params: Sequence[str] | None = None, dt_int: float = 0.1, fit_steps: int = 2, max_fit_origins: int = 1500, divergence_factor: float = 5.0, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
dx/dt = rhs(x, x(t - tau), **params) for a scalar series sampled every dt; integrated with RK4 at
``dt_int`` (dt and tau must be multiples of it), the history taken from the observations by linear
interpolation.

classes.name: LinearSSMForecaster
classes.sig: (kind: str = 'ou', max_fit_length: int = 4000, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
Linear Gaussian state-space model of a scalar observation y = mu + x_0 + noise.

``kind="ou"``: dx = -theta x dt + sigma dW. ``kind="oscillator"``: x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x =
sigma xi(t) with the velocity hidden. Exact discretisation at the sampling step, maximum likelihood through the
Kalman filter on the training segment (Nelder-Mead on log-parameters), Gaussian forecasts from the filtered
state.

methods.name: physics_features
methods.doc: Filtered state at the origin (position and, for the oscillator, velocity) and the oscillator energy.

classes.name: SDEDriftForecaster
classes.sig: (degree: int = 3, n_samples: int = 200, sub: int = 10, closure: dict | None = None, seed: int = 0, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
dx = f(x) dt + sigma dW for a scalar series, f(x) = sum_k c_k x^k (k <= ``degree``) fitted to the increments,
optionally plus a neural closure g(x) fitted to what the polynomial leaves (``closure=dict(hidden=..,
epochs=..)``). Forecast: ``n_samples`` Euler-Maruyama paths with ``sub`` substeps per sample.

Observation noise on y inflates the estimated diffusion and biases the drift towards zero; that is part of
what the comparison measures (the stated assumption is that the observation noise is small).

classes.name: EnKFForecaster
classes.sig: (physical: ODEForecaster, n_ens: int = 50, inflation: float = 1.02, q_frac: float = 0.1, spinup: int = 200, seed: int = 0, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
Stochastic EnKF over the observations with a fitted :class:`ODEForecaster` as the model.

The observation-noise variance is estimated as half the mean square one-sample prediction error of the fitted
model (an assumption: model error over one sample is negligible next to the observation noise); the process
noise is ``q_frac`` times that. Filtering starts ``spinup`` samples before the first origin, so a forecast
uses only observations up to its origin.

classes.name: SINDyForecaster
classes.sig: (threshold: float = 0.05, l2: float = 0.0001, library: str = 'poly', sub: int = 5, divergence_factor: float = 5.0, name: str | None = None, family: str | None = None)
classes.doc:
Equations discovered by SINDy (STLSQ, polynomial library of degree 2) on the training trajectory of a fully
observed state; forecasts integrate them (RK4, ``sub`` substeps per sample) from the observed state.

classes.name: PhysicsFeatures
classes.sig: (physical: Forecaster)
classes.doc:
Input features for a data-driven model computed by a physical forecaster (fitted on the training origins
when the data model is fitted): its ``physics_features(data, origins)`` -- the fitted vector field or drift at
the origin state, or the filtered state and energy of a linear model.

children.summary: Physical forecasters: the governing equations with parameters estimated from the training data only.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.pipeline
children.doc:
One call per study case, and the tables of the guide, built from the stored results.

* :func:`run_case` -- predictability before modelling, the whole zoo under the protocol, the surrogate-trained
  twins, fan-chart data; returns a JSON-able dict.
* :func:`run_overfitting` -- the anti-overfitting study of a case.
* :func:`markdown_tables` -- the result tables (Markdown) from a list of case results and overfitting studies, so
  every number in the guide is read from the committed JSON.

functions.name: fan_panels
functions.sig: (zoo: dict, data, title: str, n_origins: int = 2, families = ('physical', 'hybrid', 'data')) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Fan-chart data for the representatives of ``families`` at ``n_origins`` test origins (spread over the
test period).

functions.name: surprise_record
functions.sig: (zoo: dict, data, horizon_index: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any] | None
functions.doc:
Per test origin: the absolute error at one horizon of the best non-baseline model (by validation score) and
of the best baseline at that horizon (by validation RMSE), with the target dates when ``data.meta["dates"]``
exists. Feeds :func:`~.plots.plot_surprise_calendar`.

functions.name: run_case
functions.sig: (name: str, *, n: int = 6000, budget: int = BUDGET, seed: int = 0, cache_dir: str | None = None, n_surrogates: int = 99, log: Callable[[str], None] = print) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: run_overfitting
functions.sig: (name: str, *, n: int = 6000, seed: int = 0, cache_dir: str | None = None, schemes = ('shuffled_kfold', 'walk_forward_no_purge', 'purged_walk_forward', 'purged_kfold'), log: Callable[[str], None] = print) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: lyapunov_study
functions.sig: (dt_ints = (0.1, 0.05), total_times = (10000.0, 50000.0, 200000.0), seeds = (0, 1, 2), log: Callable[[str], None] = print) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Convergence of the Benettin estimate of the Mackey-Glass (tau = 17) largest Lyapunov exponent with the
integration step, the length of the run and the seed (initial history and perturbation direction).

functions.name: memorise_vs_learn
functions.sig: (name: str, variants = ('overfit: MLP 512x3, 32 lags, no early stop', 'MLP 64x2 + early stopping'), *, horizon_index: int = 0, window: int = 200, n: int = 6000, seed: int = 0, cache_dir: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Refit two training variants of :func:`~.presets.overfitting_variants` on the final split of case ``name``
and return, for one horizon, the truth and both forecasts over the last ``window`` training origins and the
first ``window`` test origins, with each variant's RMSE on the whole training and test sets.

functions.name: markdown_tables
functions.sig: (results: Sequence[dict], overfit: Sequence[dict] = ()) -> dict[str, str]
functions.doc:
Markdown tables: predictability, skill horizon per family, scores of the representatives, the zoo (wall
time, parameters), surrogate-trained twins, and the overfitting study.

children.summary: One call per study case, and the tables of the guide, built from the stored results.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.plots
children.doc:
Figures of a forecasting study (matplotlib, static PNG).

Families keep one colour everywhere (fixed order, never re-assigned when a family is missing from a panel); the
baseline is drawn as a neutral grey reference line at skill 0.

functions.name: plot_skill_vs_horizon
functions.sig: (results: Sequence[dict], path: str, *, lyapunov: dict[str, float] | None = None, ncols: int = 4, floor: float = -0.5, titles: dict[str, str] | None = None, reference: str = 'best_baseline') -> str
functions.doc:
One panel per series: RMSE skill of each family's representative (chosen on the validation block) against

wrong structure), initial guesses that are off by 20-30 % for the parameters that are estimated, and which
parameters are taken as known (the Mackey-Glass delay and exponent, the Lorenz-96 dimension).

3-D renders of a forecasting study (Blender Cycles through :mod:`pinneapple_blender.cycles`).

Each render has a data function (pure NumPy, tested without Blender, returns the numbers that are drawn) and a
scene function that draws them:

* :func:`landscape_tiles` / :func:`render_landscape` -- skill against the best baseline as a surface over horizon
  (Lyapunov times for chaotic series) x model family, one tile per series, with a translucent sea at skill 0.
* :func:`dense_forecast` / :func:`render_cones` -- a direct forecaster refitted at every horizon 1..H, so the
  predictive fan exists at every step; the observed series as a glowing line and the forecast as translucent
  50 % and 90 % bands; optional clip that reveals the fan step by step.
* :func:`embedding_views` / :func:`render_attractors` -- the delay-embedded series next to its IAAFT and shuffled
  surrogates (tube, tube, point cloud).
* :func:`ensemble_fibres` / :func:`render_ensembles` -- members started from one perturbed initial state, drawn as
  fibres over time, with a marker at one Lyapunov time.

Lyapunov times when the series is chaotic, else log10 of samples) and the skill against the best baseline of
each family's representative at every horizon, clipped below at ``floor``.

studio floor, each with a translucent sea at skill 0 bounded by a glowing waterline. The families share
one labelled axis per row (a tile with a single family is a narrow strip on that family's row); each title
stands in front of its tile.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.study
children.doc:
The evaluation protocol: fix the test period first, tune on purged walk-forward folds of the rest, fit once,
score once on the untouched test period, and test the differences.

* :class:`Protocol` -- the split: the last ``test_frac`` of the series is the test period, chosen before any
  tuning; the development part ends with a validation block (early stopping, spread calibration, choosing a
  family's representative). Training labels never reach into the validation block (purge = largest horizon by
  construction), validation labels never reach into the test period.
* :func:`tune` -- the same configuration budget for every model, scored by purged walk-forward cross-validation
  on the development part (each fold with its own purged inner early-stopping block).
* :func:`evaluate` -- MAE, RMSE, CRPS, central-interval coverage and PIT per horizon.
* :func:`run_zoo` -- all of it for a list of :class:`ModelSpec`, plus skill against persistence and climatology,
  Diebold-Mariano tests against persistence and against the best baseline on the validation block, Holm (per
  horizon, across the zoo) and Benjamini-Hochberg (all model x horizon tests) adjustments, and for each family the
  last horizon with significant skill.
* :func:`overfitting_study` -- train / cross-validation / test errors of training variants under several
  cross-validation schemes (shuffled k-fold, walk-forward without purge, purged walk-forward, purged k-fold with
  embargo), so the train-test gap and each scheme's optimism are measured.
* :func:`surrogate_trained` -- the same model trained on an IAAFT (or shuffled) surrogate of the development data
  and scored on the real test period: a model that does not beat its surrogate-trained twin has learned nothing
  beyond the linear correlations (or nothing at all).

classes.name: Protocol
classes.doc:
Split of a series of length ``n`` into development (train + validation) and an untouched test period.

``min_history`` is the first usable origin for every model (the longest input window in the zoo), so all
models train and are scored on the same origins. ``n_folds`` purged walk-forward folds of ``fold_frac`` of the
development origins each are used for tuning. ``test_stride`` thins the test origins (consecutive h-step
errors are correlated anyway; the DM test accounts for the overlap).

methods.name: inner
methods.doc: Split training origins into inner-train / inner-validation (early stopping) with a purge of H.

classes.name: ModelSpec
classes.doc:
A forecaster in the zoo: ``factory(**config)`` builds an unfitted model; ``grid`` lists the configurations
to try (one entry means no tuning).

functions.name: tune
functions.sig: (spec: ModelSpec, data: SeriesData, protocol: Protocol, *, budget: int | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Score every configuration (or ``budget`` of them, drawn at random) by purged walk-forward CV.

functions.name: evaluate
functions.sig: (model: Forecaster, data: SeriesData, origins, *, levels = LEVELS, keep: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Point and probabilistic scores per horizon on ``origins``.

functions.name: skill_horizon
functions.sig: (horizons, skill, p_values = None, alpha: float = 0.05) -> int | None
functions.doc:
Largest horizon h such that the skill is positive (and, with ``p_values``, significant) at every horizon
up to h; None when there is no skill at the first horizon.

functions.name: run_zoo
functions.sig: (data: SeriesData, specs: Sequence[ModelSpec], protocol: Protocol, *, budget: int | None = None, keep_forecasts: Sequence[str] = (), keep_models: bool = False, log: Callable[[str], None] = print, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Tune, fit and score every model of the zoo on one series. Returns a JSON-able dict (``_forecasts`` holds
the test forecasts of ``keep_forecasts`` for figures, ``_models`` the fitted models when ``keep_models``; both
are dropped by ``to_jsonable(drop_private=True)``). Zoos run in parts (e.g. one process per model) are
combined by :func:`merge_zoo`.

functions.name: merge_zoo
functions.sig: (parts: Sequence[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Combine :func:`run_zoo` results of the same series and protocol run in parts (each with its models' test
forecasts kept): the models and forecasts are pooled and the comparisons (skill, DM tests against persistence
and the best baseline, Holm and BH adjustments, family representatives) are recomputed over the whole zoo.

functions.name: overfitting_study
functions.sig: (data: SeriesData, protocol: Protocol, variants: dict[str, Callable[[], Forecaster]], *, schemes: Sequence[str] = ('purged_walk_forward',), schemes_for: Sequence[str] | None = None, log: Callable[[str], None] = print) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
For each training variant: its error on its training origins, on the validation block and on the untouched
test period, the gap test - train, and the cross-validation estimate under each scheme with its optimism
(test - CV). The error is the mean over horizons of RMSE / RMSE of persistence *on the same origins* (1 = no
better than persistence), so periods of different volatility compare; ``rmse_over_std`` also gives the mean
RMSE divided by the standard deviation of the whole series.

Schemes: ``"purged_walk_forward"`` (the protocol's folds), ``"walk_forward_no_purge"``, ``"purged_kfold"``
(contiguous folds, purge H before and embargo H after each validation fold), ``"shuffled_kfold"``. They are run
for the variants in ``schemes_for`` (all when None).

functions.name: surrogate_trained
functions.sig: (make: Callable[[], Forecaster], data: SeriesData, protocol: Protocol, *, kind: str = 'iaaft', seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Skill (vs persistence, mean over horizons and per horizon) on the real test period of a univariate model
trained on the real development data and of the same model trained on a surrogate of it.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.foundation_models
children.doc:
Pretrained time-series *foundation model* forecasters.

Everywhere else in this repo, forecasters are architectures you train
yourself: ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.transformers`` has
Informer/Autoformer/FEDformer/TFT/TimesNet trained from scratch on your
data, ``pinneapple_systems.time_series.classical_ts`` has ARIMA/Kalman/VAR/
TCN fit on your series, and ``pinneapple_systems.time_series.baselines``
has the simple ``NaiveForecaster`` family. This module is different: it
wraps REAL, openly published, **pre-trained** checkpoints that a research
lab trained on large heterogeneous time-series corpora and released on the
HuggingFace Hub, so a forecast can be produced zero-shot -- with little or
no fitting on the series at hand.

Wrapped models
---------------
* :class:`ChronosForecaster` -- Amazon's Chronos, a T5-based pretrained
  probabilistic time-series forecaster:

      Ansari, A. F. et al. "Chronos: Learning the Language of Time
      Series." arXiv:2403.07815 (2024).

  Backed by the real ``chronos-forecasting`` PyPI package
  (``pip install chronos-forecasting``) and real checkpoints published at
  https://huggingface.co/amazon (e.g. ``amazon/chronos-t5-tiny``, ~8M
  params -- the smallest real variant, used here for testability).

* :class:`TimesFMForecaster` -- Google's TimesFM, a decoder-only pretrained
  foundation model for time-series forecasting:

      Das, A. et al. "A decoder-only foundation model for time-series
      forecasting." arXiv:2310.10688 (2024).

  Backed by the real ``timesfm`` PyPI package (``pip install timesfm``)
  and a real checkpoint published at
  https://huggingface.co/google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch (the current
  actively maintained TimesFM release for the installed ``timesfm``
  package; ~200M params -- the smallest currently-published TimesFM
  weights).

Interface convention
---------------------
Both classes follow this package's ``NaiveForecaster``-style convention
(see ``pinneapple_systems.time_series.baselines.naive``): ``fit(y) -> self``
and ``predict(horizon) -> np.ndarray``. Since both underlying models are
zero-shot pretrained forecasters, ``fit()`` does **not** train any weights
-- it stores the context series and eagerly loads/downloads the real
pretrained checkpoint, so a broken install/network surfaces at ``fit()``
time rather than silently at ``predict()`` time. That is documented
explicitly on each class rather than pretended away. Because both Chronos
and TimesFM are genuinely *probabilistic* forecasters (unlike the point-
estimate-only naive baselines), this module also exposes the real
quantile/sample forecasts the upstream packages compute, via
``predict_quantiles()`` / ``predict_samples()`` / ``predict_with_uncertainty()``.

classes.name: ChronosForecaster
classes.sig: (model_id: str = 'amazon/chronos-t5-tiny', device_map: str = 'cpu', dtype: Optional['torch.dtype'] = None, **pipeline_kwargs)
classes.doc:
Wraps Amazon's real, pretrained Chronos forecasting pipeline.

Chronos (Ansari et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.07815) tokenizes a scaled time
series into a fixed vocabulary and forecasts autoregressively with a
T5-style encoder-decoder trained on a large corpus of public and
synthetic time series. It is genuinely probabilistic: sampling the
decoder autoregressively multiple times yields a distribution over
future paths, from which point forecasts and quantiles are derived.

``fit()`` is honestly a **no-op with respect to model weights** -- this
is a zero-shot pretrained forecaster, not something trained here. It
stores the context series `y` that `predict()` conditions on, and
eagerly loads (downloading on first use) the real pretrained checkpoint
from the HuggingFace Hub, so a missing dependency or unreachable network
fails loudly at `fit()` rather than silently at `predict()`.

No fine-tuning hook is implemented: the upstream project documents a
separate fine-tuning script (see the Chronos repo's
``scripts/training``), and wiring that up was out of scope for this
zero-shot integration -- claiming a "light fine-tune" path here without
actually exercising it would be dishonest.

classes.doc:
Wraps Google's real, pretrained TimesFM forecasting model.

TimesFM (Das et al., 2024, arXiv:2310.10688) is a decoder-only
transformer pretrained on a large corpus of real and synthetic time
series for zero-shot forecasting. The default checkpoint here,
``google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch`` (~200M params), is the smallest
currently-published TimesFM release for the installed ``timesfm``
PyPI package (the paper's original 1.0-200m checkpoint predates the
package's current API; this wrapper targets the real, currently
loadable checkpoint rather than an unloadable legacy id).

Like :class:`ChronosForecaster`, this is zero-shot: ``fit()`` does not
train any weights, it stores the context series and eagerly loads
(downloading + compiling on first use) the real pretrained checkpoint.

Mean Absolute Percentage Error (%).

The denominator uses a small epsilon (1e-8) for numerical stability, so
a zero (or near-zero) target does not raise or produce NaN -- instead
it contributes a very large but finite term that can dominate the mean.
Avoid this metric when the target series contains zeros or values near
zero; prefer sMAPE in that case.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.metrics_ext.comparison
children.doc:
Comparing forecasts: skill scores, the Diebold-Mariano test and multiple-comparison control.

* :func:`skill_score` -- 1 - score / score_reference (positive: better than the reference).
* :func:`diebold_mariano` -- equal predictive accuracy of two forecasts of the same targets (Diebold & Mariano
  1995, J. Bus. Econ. Stat. 13:253) with the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold (1997, Int. J.
  Forecast. 13:281). An h-step forecast error is serially correlated up to lag h - 1, so the variance of the mean
  loss difference uses the autocovariances up to that lag.
* :func:`holm` (Holm 1979, Scand. J. Stat. 6:65, family-wise error) and :func:`benjamini_hochberg` (Benjamini &
  Hochberg 1995, JRSS B 57:289, false discovery rate) adjust a family of p-values.

functions.name: skill_score
functions.sig: (score, reference) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: 1 - score / reference, elementwise (for errors and other negatively oriented scores).

functions.name: diebold_mariano
functions.sig: (e1, e2, *, h: int = 1, loss: str = 'se', max_lag: int | None = None, hln: bool = True) -> DMResult
functions.doc:
Test E[L(e1)] = E[L(e2)] for two error series on the same targets (in time order).

``loss`` is ``"se"`` (squared error), ``"ae"`` (absolute error) or ``"raw"`` (``e1``, ``e2`` are already losses,
e.g. CRPS). ``max_lag`` defaults to h - 1. When the truncated (rectangular) long-run variance is not positive the
Bartlett (Newey-West) weights are used instead. With ``hln`` the statistic is scaled by the Harvey-Leybourne-
Newbold factor and referred to Student's t with n - 1 degrees of freedom; otherwise to the normal.

functions.name: holm
functions.sig: (p_values: dict[str, float] | Sequence[float])
functions.doc: Holm step-down adjusted p-values (same keys / order as given); NaNs are left out of the family.

functions.name: benjamini_hochberg
functions.sig: (p_values: dict[str, float] | Sequence[float])
functions.doc: Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values (q-values); NaNs are left out of the family.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictability
children.doc:
Is there anything to predict? Measures of predictability to compute before fitting any forecaster.

* :func:`fit_ar` -- least-squares AR(p) with the order chosen by AIC or BIC, and its one-step R^2.
* :func:`permutation_entropy` -- Bandt & Pompe (2002), Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:174102; 1 for an i.i.d. series.
* :func:`sample_entropy` -- Richman & Moorman (2000), Am. J. Physiol. 278:H2039.
* :func:`rosenstein_lyapunov` -- largest Lyapunov exponent from a scalar series (Rosenstein, Collins & De Luca
  1993, Physica D 65:117). It returns a positive slope for noise too; read it only next to the surrogate test.
* :func:`iaaft_surrogate`, :func:`phase_randomized_surrogate`, :func:`shuffle_surrogate` -- surrogate data
  (Theiler et al. 1992, Physica D 58:77; Schreiber & Schmitz 1996, Phys. Rev. Lett. 77:635).
* :func:`nonlinear_prediction_error`, :func:`time_reversal_asymmetry` -- discriminating statistics.
* :func:`surrogate_test` -- rank test of a statistic against surrogates: does the series have more structure than
  an i.i.d. process (shuffle) or a linear Gaussian process seen through a static monotone transform (IAAFT)?
* :func:`predictability_report` -- all of the above for one series, with the persistence and climatology errors.

functions.name: fit_ar
functions.sig: (x, max_order: int = 20, criterion: str = 'aic') -> ARFit
functions.doc:
Least-squares AR(p), p = 0..max_order, all fitted on the same sample (the first ``max_order`` values are
dropped for every p) so the information criteria are comparable.

functions.name: permutation_entropy
functions.sig: (x, order: int = 5, delay: int = 1, normalize: bool = True) -> float
functions.doc: Shannon entropy of the ordinal patterns of length ``order`` (ties broken by position).

functions.name: sample_entropy
functions.sig: (x, m: int = 2, r: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
-log(A / B): B = template pairs of length m within tolerance r (Chebyshev), A = the same for m + 1; self
matches excluded and the same N - m templates used for both lengths. ``r`` defaults to 0.2 std(x).

functions.name: delay_embedding
functions.sig: (x, dim: int, delay: int) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: first_acf_zero
functions.sig: (x, max_lag: int | None = None) -> int
functions.doc: First lag at which the autocorrelation drops below 1/e (a common embedding-delay rule).

functions.name: rosenstein_lyapunov
functions.sig: (x, *, dim: int = 5, delay: int | None = None, dt: float = 1.0, min_tsep: int | None = None, n_steps: int = 40, fit: tuple = (5, 30), max_points: int = 3000) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Largest Lyapunov exponent per unit time from a scalar series.

Each embedded point is paired with its nearest neighbour at least ``min_tsep`` samples away (default: the
mean period from the power spectrum); the mean log separation over the next ``n_steps`` samples is fitted by
a straight line on ``fit`` = (first, last) step. Returns the exponent, the divergence curve and the choices.

functions.name: shuffle_surrogate
functions.sig: (x, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Random permutation: keeps the amplitude distribution, destroys all temporal structure.

functions.name: phase_randomized_surrogate
functions.sig: (x, rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Fourier-transform surrogate: same power spectrum, random phases (a linear Gaussian process).

functions.name: iaaft_surrogate
functions.sig: (x, rng: np.random.Generator, n_iter: int = 200, tol: float = 1e-08) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Iterative amplitude-adjusted Fourier transform surrogate (Schreiber & Schmitz 1996): the same amplitude
distribution as ``x`` exactly and nearly the same power spectrum.

functions.name: nonlinear_prediction_error
functions.sig: (x, *, dim: int = 4, delay: int = 1, horizon: int = 1, k: int = 10, train_frac: float = 0.5) -> float
functions.doc:
Out-of-sample error of a local-constant (nearest-neighbour) predictor, divided by std(x).

The library is the first ``train_frac`` of the delay vectors, the predictions are made for the rest: each test
vector is predicted as the mean future of its ``k`` nearest library vectors (Sugihara & May 1990, Nature
344:734; Theiler et al. 1992). ~1 when nothing is predictable, < 1 when it is.

functions.name: time_reversal_asymmetry
functions.sig: (x, lag: int = 1) -> float
functions.doc:
Normalised third moment of the lag-``lag`` increments; 0 in expectation for any time-reversible process
(every linear Gaussian process is).

functions.name: surrogate_test
functions.sig: (x, statistic: Callable[[np.ndarray], float], *, kind: str = 'iaaft', n_surrogates: int = 99, alternative: str = 'less', seed: int = 0, name: str | None = None) -> SurrogateTest
functions.doc:
Rank test of ``statistic(x)`` against ``n_surrogates`` surrogates of the given ``kind``.

``alternative="less"``: the original is more predictable (smaller statistic) than the surrogates, p = (1 +
#{s_i <= s_0}) / (n + 1). ``"two-sided"`` compares |s - median(s_i)|. With 99 surrogates the smallest
attainable p is 0.01.

functions.name: baseline_errors
functions.sig: (x, horizons, train_frac: float = 0.8) -> dict[str, dict[int, float]]
functions.doc:
RMSE of persistence (x_{t+h} = x_t) and climatology (x_{t+h} = mean of the first ``train_frac``) on the last
1 - ``train_frac`` of the series, per horizon, both divided by std(x).

functions.name: predictability_report
functions.sig: (x, *, horizons = (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), dt: float = 1.0, max_ar_order: int = 20, pe_order: int = 5, embed_dim: int = 4, n_surrogates: int = 99, seed: int = 0, lyapunov: bool = True, lyapunov_kwargs: dict | None = None, difference_if_unit_root: bool = True) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Predictability of a scalar series before any modelling.

The surrogate tests use the nonlinear prediction error at horizon 1 (one-sided: is the series more predictable
by nearest neighbours than its surrogates?) and the time-reversal asymmetry (two-sided). When the AR(1)
coefficient exceeds 0.99 and ``difference_if_unit_root`` is set, the tests and entropies run on the first
differences, because Fourier surrogates of a non-stationary series are not a valid null (Schreiber & Schmitz
2000, Physica D 142:346); ``tested_on`` says which.

children.summary: Is there anything to predict? Measures of predictability to compute before fitting any forecaster.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.preparation.outliers
children.doc: Outlier detection and treatment for time series.

classes.name: OutlierDetector
classes.sig: (method: DetectionMethod = 'rolling_iqr', window: int = 20, iqr_factor: float = 1.5, z_threshold: float = 3.0, treatment: TreatmentMethod = 'interpolate', winsorize_pct: float = 0.05)
classes.doc:
Outlier detection (Rolling IQR / Z-Score) with 6 treatment options.

All rolling windows are trailing/causal (they only look at the current
point and points before it), and `interpolate` only fills using past
values (`limit_direction="forward"`). This matters because this
detector is commonly fit on a full series before it is split into
train/val/test for a forecasting pipeline: a centered window or a
both-directions fill would let a flagged point in the training portion
be "cleaned" using values from the validation/test period, leaking
information that would not be available at real deployment time.
Note that linear interpolation of a single isolated flagged point still
uses the next valid observation as one of its two anchors (that is
inherent to linear interpolation, not to the rolling windows here);
when strict causality for every flagged point matters, prefer
treatment="mean_replace" or a forward-fill instead.

Detection methods:
  rolling_iqr    — IQR computed in a rolling window; flags points outside
                   [Q1 - iqr_factor*IQR, Q3 + iqr_factor*IQR]
  zscore         — flags |z| > threshold using rolling mean/std
  modified_zscore — MAD-based robust Z-score (Iglewicz-Hoaglin)
  both           — union of rolling_iqr and zscore flags

Treatment options:
  clip         — clamp to [lower_fence, upper_fence]
  remove       — replace with NaN (use imputer afterward)
  interpolate  — linear interpolation over flagged points
  winsorize    — same as clip but uses percentile-based bounds
  flag         — no change, just return mask (call treat() explicitly)
  mean_replace — replace with rolling window mean

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.solar_cycle
children.doc:
Solar-cycle envelope from the daily sunspot number: (E)EMD, the IMF nearest 11 years, its Hilbert amplitude, and
a fit of that amplitude by an extreme learning machine (ELM) with the end-point equality f(0) = f(1) built into the
basis (a constrained expression of the Theory of Functional Connections), then extended past the data.

Data. :func:`fetch_silso_daily` downloads SILSO's daily total sunspot number V2.0 (``SN_d_tot_V2.0.csv``,
Royal Observatory of Belgium, Brussels; licence CC BY-NC 4.0: cite "SILSO data/image, Royal Observatory of
Belgium, Brussels" and do not use it commercially). Nothing from SILSO is shipped here; :func:`synthetic_daily`
makes a series of the same shape for tests and offline demos.

Method.
1. Min-max scale to [0, 1] on a normalised time axis t in [0, 1].
2. Decompose with EMD or EEMD (``PyEMD`` from the ``EMD-signal`` package, Apache-2.0, when installed; otherwise
   :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.eemd`, whose IMFs plus the returned residue also sum to the
   signal). IMFs run from high to low frequency, and which index lands near 11 years depends on the series length
   and ``max_imf``: on a 2005-2025 SILSO slice the source app measured IMF 0 at ~3.6 days and the ~10-year
   component last. :func:`closest_to_schwabe_cycle` therefore picks the IMF whose measured period (median Hilbert
   instantaneous frequency) is nearest 11 years and warns when even that one is more than 40 % off.
3. Hilbert amplitude of that IMF (``scipy.signal.hilbert``).
4. :func:`periodic_elm_fit`: with g(x) = H(x) xi (H: random tanh features), f(x) = g(x) + x (g(0) - g(1))
   satisfies f(0) = f(1) for every xi (Mortari, "The Theory of Connections", 2017), so the fit is ordinary least
   squares on Hc(x) = H(x) + x (H(0) - H(1)). Only the two end values are tied (no derivative continuity);
   ``backend="tfc"`` uses the ``tfc`` package's ``ELMTanh`` basis instead of the NumPy one.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``solar_cycle_forecasting`` product (HelioTFC), which reconstructed this from
an older script whose ``tfc.decorators.constrained_expression`` / ``tfc.utils.elm_fit`` calls do not exist in
``tfc`` 1.4.0.

children.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.synthetic
children.doc:
Synthetic time series with known ground truth, for forecasting studies.

Every generator returns a :class:`SyntheticSeries`: the clean state, the noisy observation that a forecaster sees,
the true parameters, and (for the chaotic systems) the largest Lyapunov exponent computed from the equations with
:func:`largest_lyapunov_benettin`, so a forecast horizon can be stated in Lyapunov times.

Systems
-------
* Lorenz-63 (Lorenz 1963, J. Atmos. Sci. 20:130), sigma=10, rho=28, beta=8/3.
* Lorenz-96 (Lorenz 1996, ECMWF Seminar on Predictability), cyclic, forcing F.
* Mackey-Glass delay equation (Mackey & Glass 1977, Science 197:287), dx/dt = beta x_tau / (1 + x_tau^n) - gamma x.
* Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process dx = -theta x dt + sigma dW, sampled exactly (an AR(1)).
* Stochastically forced damped oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = sigma xi(t), sampled exactly
  (matrix exponential and Van Loan's integral for the process-noise covariance).
* Double-well Langevin equation dx = (x - x^3) dt + sigma dW: noise-driven switching between two regimes.
* White noise and a Gaussian random walk (controls where nothing can beat the baseline).

The vector fields (:func:`lorenz63_rhs`, :func:`lorenz96_rhs`, :func:`mackey_glass_rhs`, :func:`double_well_drift`)
accept NumPy arrays or torch tensors of shape (..., d), so the same definition drives data generation, the fitted
physical models, and the known part of a universal differential equation.

functions.name: mackey_glass_step
functions.sig: (hist: np.ndarray, dt: float, beta: float = 0.2, gamma: float = 0.1, n: float = 10.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Advance Mackey-Glass histories by one RK4 step of size ``dt`` (method of steps).

``hist`` has shape (B, m + 1): the last m + 1 values on a grid of spacing dt, with tau = m dt; the newest value
is ``hist[:, -1]``. The delayed value at the half step is the mean of its two grid neighbours. Returns the
shifted history (B, m + 1).

functions.name: largest_lyapunov_benettin
functions.sig: (step: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], x0: np.ndarray, *, step_time: float, n_steps: int = 20000, transient: int = 2000, d0: float = 1e-08, seed: int = 0) -> float
functions.doc:
Largest Lyapunov exponent (per unit time) of a deterministic map ``x -> step(x)`` by two-trajectory
renormalisation (Benettin, Galgani, Giorgilli & Strelcyn 1980, Meccanica 15:9).

``step`` acts on a batch (B, d); ``step_time`` is the time one call advances. The separation is renormalised to
``d0`` after every step and the exponent is the mean log growth rate.

functions.name: mackey_glass_lyapunov
functions.sig: (*, dt_int: float = 0.1, total_time: float = 50000.0, transient_time: float = 2000.0, tau: float = 17.0, beta: float = 0.2, gamma: float = 0.1, n: float = 10.0, seed: int = 0) -> float
functions.doc:
Largest Lyapunov exponent (per unit time, natural log) of the Mackey-Glass delay equation.

The state of a delay equation is its history on [t - tau, t]; here the tau / dt_int + 1 grid values. A random
perturbation of the whole history is followed with :func:`largest_lyapunov_benettin` (renormalised every
step, Euclidean norm over the grid) after a spin-up of 500 time units and a further ``transient_time``.

classes.name: PurgedWalkForwardSplitter
classes.doc:
Walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation over forecast origins with purge and embargo.

``times`` passed to :meth:`split` are the sorted origin times of the samples. The last ``n_folds`` blocks of
``val_size`` samples are the validation blocks (oldest first). Training uses only samples whose origin is more
than ``purge`` time steps before the block (set ``purge`` to the largest horizon so no training label falls in
the block). ``window`` limits training to the most recent samples (a rolling instead of an expanding window).

doc:
pinneapple_systems — Multi-component physical systems (time series, co-simulation, digital twins).

Sub-modules
-----------
time_series    (was pinneapple_timeseries)
    Time-series forecasting for physical signals: LSTM, GRU, NBeats, TCN,
    TFT, XGBoost, classical decomposition (FFT, HHT), data preparation,
    EDA, backtesting, and visualization.

cosimulation   (was pinneapple_cosim)
    Graph-based differentiable co-simulation engine: compose nodes
    (AnalyticalNode, PINNNode, SymbolicPDENode, TimeSeriesCoSimNode) into
    a CoSimGraph, run with CoSimEngine, train with CoSimTrainer.

digital_twin   (pinneapple_digital_twin — same name, clearer context)
    Digital twin framework: wrap a surrogate model as a live twin, ingest
    real-time sensor streams (MQTT, Kafka, HTTP, file), fuse observations
    with Kalman filters (EKF, EnKF), and detect anomalies.

component_modeling
    Control, optimization, and uncertainty-quantification tooling that
    works on any differentiable component model: PID control, gradient-based
    MPC, SWAG/ensemble/MC-Dropout uncertainty, generic PDE residuals, and
    ONNX edge-deployment packaging.

process_components
    Physical unit-operation models for process/plant digital twins: real-gas
    thermodynamic properties (GERG-2008 via CoolProp), turbomachinery
    (real-gas polytropic compression/expansion + nondimensional similarity
    maps), control valves (IEC 60534-2-1), heat exchangers
    (effectiveness-NTU), and 1D pipe networks (quasi-steady momentum +
    transient continuity).

Integration helpers
-------------------
``forecast(data, horizon, ...)``
    Fit the best auto-selected time-series model and return a forecast.
``cosim_from_models(models_dict, connections)``
    Quick factory that builds a CoSimGraph from a dict of named models.
``build_digital_twin(model, ...)``
    Shortcut for digital_twin.build_digital_twin.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_systems import build_digital_twin, cosim_from_models, forecast
>>> twin = build_digital_twin(surrogate, field_names=["u", "v", "p"])
>>> graph = cosim_from_models({"fluid": pinn, "thermal": lstm}, [("fluid.T", "thermal.T_in")])
>>> pred = forecast(signal_df, horizon=24, model="lstm")
